category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: In the etiological classification of Diabetes Mellitus, the form characterized by an absolute deficiency of insulin due to autoimmune destruction of beta cells is [___].
back:
• Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus (T1DM)
• Mediated by T-cell attack on beta-cell autoantigens
• Strongly associated with HLA-DR3 or DR4 haplotypes

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: A 22-year-old non-obese male presents with mild hyperglycemia. Genetic testing identifies a mutation in the glucokinase (GCK) gene. The most likely etiological category is [___].
back:
• Maturity-Onset Diabetes of the Young (MODY)
• A monogenic form of diabetes
• Primary genetic defect in pancreatic beta-cell function

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: Explain the biological function of 'Insulin Resistance' as an etiological step in the development of Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus.
back:
• Failure of target tissues (liver, muscle, fat) to respond to insulin
• Leads to decreased glucose uptake and uninhibited gluconeogenesis
• Compensatory hyperinsulinemia occurs before eventual beta-cell failure

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: Contrast the primary immune mechanisms involved in Type 1A versus Type 1B (Idiopathic) Diabetes Mellitus.
back:
• Type 1A: T-cell mediated autoimmune destruction; circulating islet autoantibodies (anti-GAD, anti-ICA512) present
• Type 1B: No evidence of autoimmunity or autoantibodies; cause is unknown/idiopathic

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: Identify three specific endocrinopathies that can etiologically cause secondary Diabetes Mellitus by antagonizing insulin action.
back:
• Cushing Syndrome (Excess Cortisol)
• Acromegaly (Excess Growth Hormone)
• Pheochromocytoma (Excess Catecholamines)
• Hyperthyroidism

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: Secondary diabetes resulting from iron deposition in the islets in a patient with hereditary hemochromatosis is etiologically classified as [___].
back:
• 'Bronze' Diabetes
• Classified under Exocrine Pancreatic Defects
• Involves physical destruction of islet architecture

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: A pregnant woman with no history of hyperglycemia presents with glucose intolerance in her third trimester. This specific etiological category is [___].
back:
• Gestational Diabetes Mellitus (GDM)
• Results from metabolic stress of pregnancy and placental hormones
• Most cases resolve postpartum, though risk for T2DM increases later

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: How do genetic defects in the KCNJ11 and ABCC8 genes contribute to the etiology of Neonatal Diabetes?
back:
• Mutations involve the K+ ATP channel proteins (Kir6.2 and SUR1)
• Prevents channel closure in response to ATP
• Blocks membrane depolarization and inhibits insulin release from beta cells

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: Contrast the etiological role of obesity in Type 1 versus Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus.
back:
• Type 2: Obesity is the primary driver through adipokines and free fatty acids inducing insulin resistance
• Type 1: Obesity is not a primary etiological factor; patients are typically normal weight

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: List two drug classes that frequently cause secondary Diabetes Mellitus by impairing insulin sensitivity or secretion.
back:
• Glucocorticoids (Increase gluconeogenesis)
• Protease Inhibitors (used in HIV treatment)
• Thiazide diuretics
• Atypical antipsychotics

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: The primary underlying mechanism in Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus involves [___] destruction of pancreatic ̢-cells, typically resulting in absolute insulin deficiency.
back:
• Autoimmune-mediated destruction
 • Loss of self-tolerance to islet antigens
 • T-cell mediated injury (CD4+ and CD8+ cells)

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: A 45-year-old male with a history of alcohol-induced chronic pancreatitis presents with polyuria and a fasting blood glucose of 145 mg/dL. This specific etiological classification of diabetes is [___].
back:
• Pancreatogenic Diabetes (Type 3C)
 • Caused by exocrine pancreatic defects
 • Results in secondary islet cell destruction

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: Explain the role of the pancreatic ̢-cell during the early versus late stages of Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus development.
back:
• Early: ̢-cell compensation via hyperinsulinemia to overcome peripheral resistance
 • Late: ̢-cell failure/exhaustion leading to relative insulin deficiency

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: Contrast the islet histopathology of long-standing Type 1 Diabetes with Type 2 Diabetes.
back:
• Type 1: ̢-cell depletion, islet atrophy, and early insulitis (lymphocytic infiltrate)
 • Type 2: Amyloid deposition (amylin) within islets and mild ̢-cell depletion

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: List three distinct classes of pharmacological agents known to induce secondary Diabetes Mellitus.
back:
• Glucocorticoids
 • Thiazide diuretics
 • Protease inhibitors (HIV therapy)
 • Thyroid hormones

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: Diabetes Mellitus occurring in a previously euglycemic woman that is first recognized during the second or third trimester of pregnancy is classified as [___].
back:
• Gestational Diabetes Mellitus (GDM)
 • Driven by pregnancy-induced insulin resistance
 • Increases risk for future Type 2 DM in the mother

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: A 15-year-old female presents with severe insulin resistance and dark, velvety skin patches on her neck (acanthosis nigricans). Genetic analysis would most likely reveal a mutation in the [___].
back:
• Insulin Receptor (Type A Insulin Resistance)
 • Impairs tissue response to insulin
 • Often associated with hyperandrogenism and polycystic ovaries

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: Explain the biological mechanism by which Glucokinase (GCK) mutations cause Maturity-Onset Diabetes of the Young (MODY 2).
back:
• GCK acts as the primary 'glucose sensor'
 • Mutations raise the threshold for glucose-stimulated insulin release
 • Results in stable, mild fasting hyperglycemia

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: Contrast Stage 1 and Stage 2 in the natural history of Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus progression.
back:
• Stage 1: Multiple autoantibodies present; normal blood glucose; asymptomatic
 • Stage 2: Multiple autoantibodies present; dysglycemia (impaired tolerance); asymptomatic

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: Identify three classic endocrinopathies that are classified as causes of secondary Diabetes Mellitus.
back:
• Acromegaly (Excess Growth Hormone)
 • Cushing Syndrome (Excess Cortisol)
 • Pheochromocytoma (Excess Catecholamines)
 • Hyperthyroidism

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus is primarily characterized by an absolute deficiency of insulin caused by autoimmune destruction of pancreatic [___].
back:
• ̢ cells (Islets of Langerhans)
• Results from a failure of self-tolerance in T cells
• Leads to total loss of insulin production

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: A 15-year-old non-obese patient presents with mild hyperglycemia and an autosomal dominant family history of diabetes. Name the likely classification of this condition.
back:
• Maturity-Onset Diabetes of the Young (MODY)
• Caused by primary genetic defects in ̢-cell function
• Most common mutations involve Glucokinase (GCK) or HNF genes

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: Explain the dual metabolic defects required to produce the clinical phenotype of Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus.
back:
• Insulin Resistance: Failure of target tissues (liver, muscle, fat) to respond to insulin
• ̢-cell Dysfunction: Inadequate insulin secretion to compensate for the resistance

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: Contrast the microscopic islet pathology of Type 1 vs Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus.
back:
• Type 1: Insulitis (lymphocytic infiltrate) and ̢-cell depletion
• Type 2: Amyloid deposition (amylin) and mild ̢-cell reduction
• Type 2 lacks the autoimmune inflammatory component

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: Identify three specific endocrinopathies that cause secondary diabetes by increasing counter-regulatory hormones.
back:
• Acromegaly (Excess Growth Hormone)
• Cushing Syndrome (Excess Cortisol)
• Pheochromocytoma (Excess Catecholamines)
• Hyperthyroidism (Excess Thyroid Hormone)

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: Secondary diabetes resulting from extensive damage to the exocrine pancreas (e.g., chronic pancreatitis or cystic fibrosis) is etiologically classified as [___].
back:
• Type 3c Diabetes (Pancreatogenic Diabetes)
• Caused by loss of islet mass secondary to exocrine destruction
• Common in chronic alcoholics or patients with pancreatic cancer

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: A 30-year-old female at 26 weeks gestation shows impaired glucose tolerance that was not present before pregnancy. State the classification and long-term risk.
back:
• Gestational Diabetes Mellitus (GDM)
• Caused by pregnancy-induced insulin resistance
• Increased risk (50%+) of developing overt Type 2 DM within 10-20 years

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: How do glucocorticoid medications etiologically contribute to the development of 'Drug-Induced' Diabetes?
back:
• Increase hepatic gluconeogenesis
• Antagonize peripheral insulin action
• Commonly seen in patients on long-term steroid therapy for chronic inflammation

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: Contrast the HLA associations of Type 1 DM with the genetic patterns of Type 2 DM.
back:
• Type 1: Strong linkage to HLA-DR3 and HLA-DR4 haplotypes
• Type 2: No HLA linkage; polygenic inheritance related to TCF7L2, PPARG, and obesity genes

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: Name the surrogate peptide marker released in equimolar amounts with insulin that distinguishes endogenous from exogenous insulin levels.
back:
• C-peptide
• Decreased in Type 1 DM (absolute deficiency)
• Increased early in Type 2 DM (insulin resistance/hyperinsulinemia)

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus is etiologically characterized by the [___] destruction of pancreatic beta-cells, leading to an absolute deficiency of insulin.
back:
• Autoimmune (Type 1A)
• Mediated by T-cell attack
• Results in total loss of insulin production.

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: A non-obese 18-year-old male presents with mild fasting hyperglycemia and a strong family history of early-onset diabetes. Genetic testing shows a mutation in Hepatocyte Nuclear Factor 1-alpha. Identify the etiological category.
back:
• Maturity-Onset Diabetes of the Young (MODY)
• Subtype: MODY3
• Classification: Genetic defect of beta-cell function.

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: Explain the biological mechanism by which patients with Cushing Syndrome or Acromegaly develop secondary Diabetes Mellitus.
back:
• Cortisol and GH are insulin-antagonistic
• Stimulate hepatic gluconeogenesis
• Inhibit peripheral glucose uptake, causing insulin resistance.

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
coreConcept: Genetic and Environmental DM Risk Factors
front: Contrast the etiological roles of HLA association and obesity in Type 1 versus Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus.
back:
• Type 1: Strong HLA-DR3/DR4 linkage; no obesity link
• Type 2: No HLA linkage; strongly linked to visceral obesity.

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: List three specific conditions classified under "Exocrine Pancreas Defects" (Type 3C Diabetes) in the etiological classification.
back:
• Chronic pancreatitis
• Cystic fibrosis
• Hemochromatosis (iron overload).

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: Hyperglycemia that is first recognized during the second or third trimester of pregnancy is etiologically classified as [___].
back:
• Gestational Diabetes Mellitus (GDM)
• Induced by pregnancy-related insulin resistance
• Increases long-term maternal risk for Type 2 DM.

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: A patient with systemic lupus erythematosus treated with chronic high-dose Prednisolone presents with new-onset polyuria and elevated blood sugar. This etiological subtype is known as [___].
back:
• Drug-induced Diabetes Mellitus
• Glucocorticoid-induced hyperglycemia
• Results from increased insulin resistance and gluconeogenesis.

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: Describe the specific mechanism leading to the etiological subtype MODY2 (Glucokinase mutations).
back:
• Glucokinase acts as a beta-cell glucose sensor
• Mutation raises the threshold for insulin release
• Causes stable, mild fasting hyperglycemia.

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: Contrast the primary metabolic defect in "Genetic defects of beta-cell function" with "Genetic defects in insulin action."
back:
• Beta-cell defects: Impaired insulin secretion (e.g., MODY)
• Insulin action defects: Target tissue resistance (e.g., Type A resistance).

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: Identify two viral infections etiologically associated with the development of secondary Diabetes Mellitus.
back:
• Congenital Rubella
• Cytomegalovirus (CMV)
• Coxsackie B virus.

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: The most common form of monogenic diabetes resulting from a defect in the rate-limiting step of oxidative glucose metabolism is [___].
back:
• MODY2 (Maturity-Onset Diabetes of the Young).
• Caused by mutations in the Glucokinase (GCK) gene.
• Impairs the glucose-sensing mechanism of pancreatic beta-cells.

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: A 12-year-old male presents with rapid weight loss, intense thirst, and frequent urination. Laboratory tests reveal positive glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD) autoantibodies. Identify the etiology.
back:
• Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus (Immune-mediated).
• Characterized by autoimmune destruction of pancreatic beta-cells.
• Leads to an absolute deficiency of insulin.

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: Explain the role of the 'incretin effect' in insulin regulation and its status in Type 2 Diabetes.
back:
• Oral glucose triggers intestinal GIP and GLP-1 release.
• These hormones stimulate insulin secretion from beta-cells.
• In T2DM, this effect is significantly blunted, contributing to hyperglycemia.

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: A 19-year-old non-obese female presents with mild hyperglycemia and a strong family history of early-onset DM. Contrast her likely condition with Type A Insulin Resistance.
back:
• This patient likely has MODY (genetic beta-cell dysfunction).
• Type A Insulin Resistance involves insulin receptor mutations and presents with acanthosis nigricans.
• MODY primarily affects insulin secretion, not receptor signaling.

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: List three exocrine pancreatic disorders that can cause secondary 'Pancreatogenic' (Type 3c) Diabetes.
back:
• Chronic pancreatitis.
• Cystic Fibrosis.
• Hemochromatosis (Bronze Diabetes).
• Result from physical destruction of the pancreatic parenchyma and islets.

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: Diabetes caused by a combination of peripheral tissue resistance to insulin and an inadequate secretory response is classified as [___].
back:
• Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus.
• Associated with relative (not absolute) insulin deficiency.
• Strongly linked to obesity and metabolic syndrome.

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: A 50-year-old obese patient has fasting glucose of 115 mg/dL. Identify the clinical classification and the 5-year risk significance.
back:
• Prediabetes (Impaired Fasting Glucose).
• Fasting glucose ranges from 100 to 125 mg/dL.
• Carries a 25% risk of progressing to frank T2DM within 5 years.

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: Explain how chronic hyperglycemia and free fatty acids (FFAs) lead to beta-cell failure in Type 2 Diabetes.
back:
• Glucotoxicity: Chronic high glucose exhausts secretory capacity.
• Lipotoxicity: FFAs compromise cell function and induce inflammation.
• Amyloid deposition: Islet amyloid polypeptide (amylin) accumulates, causing beta-cell apoptosis.

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: Contrast the underlying mechanisms of secondary diabetes seen in Cushing Syndrome versus Acromegaly.
back:
• Cushing Syndrome: Excess cortisol stimulates gluconeogenesis and antagonizes insulin action.
• Acromegaly: Excess Growth Hormone (GH) increases hepatic glucose output and induces peripheral insulin resistance.

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: Name the specific glucose transporter responsible for glucose uptake into pancreatic beta-cells to initiate insulin release.
back:
• GLUT-2.
• It is an insulin-independent transporter.
• Facilitates glucose entry that generates ATP, closing K+ channels and opening Ca2+ channels.

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: The etiological category of diabetes resulting from primary destruction of the exocrine pancreas is specifically termed [___] diabetes.
back: • Type 3c (Pancreatogenic) diabetes. • Caused by chronic pancreatitis, trauma, cystic fibrosis, or hemochromatosis. • Results from collateral islet damage during exocrine tissue destruction.

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: A 10-year-old child presents with sudden polyuria, thirst, and weight loss. Serum labs show anti-GAD antibodies and ketonemia. Identify the etiological classification.
back: • Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus (T1D). • Characterized by autoimmune-mediated pancreatic beta-cell destruction. • Leads to absolute insulin deficiency and high ketoacidosis risk.

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: Explain the two fundamental metabolic defects that characterize the etiology of Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus.
back: • Insulin resistance: Peripheral tissues (muscle, fat, liver) fail to respond to insulin. • Beta-cell dysfunction: Secretory response is inadequate to overcome resistance. • Results in relative insulin deficiency.

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: Contrast Maturity-Onset Diabetes of the Young (MODY) with Type 2 Diabetes regarding their underlying genetic etiology.
back: • MODY: Monogenic (single-gene) inheritance affecting beta-cell function (e.g., GCK mutation). • T2D: Polygenic and multifactorial inheritance. • MODY typically lacks the obesity-linked resistance seen in T2D.

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: List three non-pancreatic endocrinopathies that can etiologically cause secondary diabetes.
back: • Cushing syndrome (excess cortisol). • Acromegaly (excess growth hormone). • Pheochromocytoma (excess catecholamines). • These conditions promote hyperglycemia by directly opposing insulin action.

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: Genetic syndromes associated with an increased risk of diabetes due to chromosomal or developmental abnormalities include Down syndrome, Turner syndrome, and [___].
back: • Klinefelter syndrome. • Also includes Prader-Willi syndrome. • These syndromes are associated with impaired glucose tolerance and metabolic syndrome.

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: A patient with systemic lupus erythematosus on long-term high-dose prednisone develops new-onset hyperglycemia. What is the etiological classification of this condition?
back: • Drug-induced diabetes. • Classified under "Other Specific Types." • Glucocorticoids increase hepatic gluconeogenesis and induce significant peripheral insulin resistance.

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: Describe the physiological mechanism by which pregnancy acts as an etiological trigger for Gestational Diabetes Mellitus.
back: • Pregnancy is a naturally "diabetogenic" state. • Hormonal changes increase systemic insulin resistance. • DM occurs when beta-cell compensation fails to meet increased metabolic demands.

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: Distinguish the genetic susceptibility loci of Type 1 Diabetes from that of Type 2 Diabetes.
back: • T1D: Strongly linked to MHC Class II genes (HLA-DR3 and HLA-DR4). • T2D: No HLA linkage; associated with obesity-related genes (e.g., TCF7L2, FTO).

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: Identify the primary genetic defect and associated clinical sign in "Type A Insulin Resistance."
back: • Defect: Mutation in the insulin receptor gene. • Mechanism: Impaired receptor synthesis or tyrosine kinase activity. • Clinical sign: Acanthosis nigricans (velvety skin hyperpigmentation).

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus is primarily an autoimmune disease characterized by the immune-mediated destruction of pancreatic [___].
back:
• β-cells (within the islets of Langerhans)
• Leads to an absolute insulin deficiency
• Often associated with HLA-DR3 or DR4 haplotypes

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: A 15-year-old non-obese male presents with mild hyperglycemia. He has a strong family history of early-onset diabetes in his father and grandfather. Genetic testing reveals a mutation in the Glucokinase (GCK) gene. Diagnosis?
back:
• Maturity-Onset Diabetes of the Young (MODY), specifically MODY2
• Represents a primary genetic defect in β-cell function
• Autosomal dominant inheritance pattern

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: Explain the dual metabolic defects that characterize the development of Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus.
back:
• Insulin resistance: Target tissues (liver, muscle, fat) fail to respond normally to insulin
• β-cell dysfunction: Secretory response is inadequate to overcome resistance (relative insulin deficiency)

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: Contrast the genetic association patterns of Type 1 and Type 2 Diabetes regarding linkage to the Major Histocompatibility Complex (MHC).
back:
• Type 1 DM: Strong linkage to MHC Class II genes (HLA-DR and DQ)
• Type 2 DM: No HLA linkage; associated with polygenic risk alleles like TCF7L2 and FTO

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: List three specific endocrinopathies, excluding primary pancreatic disorders, that can lead to the development of secondary Diabetes Mellitus.
back:
• Cushing Syndrome (excess cortisol)
• Acromegaly (excess growth hormone)
• Pheochromocytoma (excess catecholamines)
• Hyperthyroidism (excess thyroid hormone)

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: Hyperglycemia first recognized during pregnancy that usually resolves following parturition is classified as [___].
back:
• Gestational Diabetes Mellitus (GDM)
• Caused by pregnancy-induced insulin resistance
• Increases long-term risk of overt Type 2 DM in the mother

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: A 45-year-old chronic alcoholic presents with steatorrhea and hyperglycemia. Imaging shows extensive calcification of the pancreas. Identify the etiological category of his diabetes.
back:
• Exocrine pancreatic defect (Type 3C Diabetes)
• Results from chronic pancreatitis causing structural destruction of islets
• Part of the 'other specific types' of DM

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: Explain how chronic administration of high-dose glucocorticoids results in the induction of secondary Diabetes Mellitus.
back:
• Increases hepatic gluconeogenesis
• Inhibits peripheral glucose uptake in muscle and fat
• Promotes a state of systemic insulin resistance

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: Distinguish between the primary defects in 'Genetic defects of β-cell function' versus 'Genetic defects in insulin action'.
back:
• Defects of β-cell function: Impaired insulin secretion/synthesis (e.g., MODY, Neonatal DM)
• Defects in insulin action: End-organ resistance due to receptor/signaling mutations (e.g., Type A Insulin Resistance)

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: Identify two viral infections that are etiologically linked to the triggering of β-cell destruction in Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus.
back:
• Coxsackie B virus
• Congenital Rubella
• Mumps or Cytomegalovirus (CMV)

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: Diabetes mellitus characterized by absolute insulin deficiency resulting from autoimmune destruction of pancreatic ̢-cells is etiologically classified as [___].
back:
• Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus (T1DM)
 • Often associated with islet autoantibodies (anti-GAD, anti-insulin)
 • Strong linkage to HLA-DR3 and HLA-DR4 haplotypes

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: A 16-year-old non-obese male presents with mild hyperglycemia. His medical history reveals three generations of early-onset diabetes in his family. No islet autoantibodies are present. This clinical picture suggests [___].
back:
• Maturity-Onset Diabetes of the Young (MODY)
 • Caused by primary genetic defects in ̢-cell function
 • Most common form is MODY3 (HNF1A mutation) or MODY2 (Glucokinase)

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: Explain the two fundamental metabolic defects that define the etiology of Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus.
back:
• Peripheral insulin resistance: Decreased tissue response to insulin (muscle, liver, fat)
 • Relative insulin deficiency: ̢-cell failure to compensate for increased insulin demand

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: Contrast the diagnostic markers and genetic patterns of Type 1 DM with Type 2 DM.
back:
• T1DM: HLA-linked (MHC II); presence of autoantibodies; absolute insulin loss
 • T2DM: No HLA linkage; no autoantibodies; linked to obesity and metabolic syndrome genes

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: List four specific endocrinopathies that can lead to the secondary development of diabetes mellitus.
back:
• Cushing syndrome (excess cortisol)
 • Acromegaly (excess growth hormone)
 • Pheochromocytoma (excess catecholamines)
 • Glucagonoma (excess glucagon)

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: Diabetes resulting from exocrine pancreatic injury such as chronic pancreatitis, cystic fibrosis, or hemochromatosis is etiologically categorized as [___].
back:
• Exocrine pancreatic defects (Pancreatogenic or Type 3c DM)
 • Occurs due to direct destruction of islet cells by exocrine pathology

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: A 30-year-old female presents with elevated blood glucose for the first time during her 24th week of pregnancy. This condition is etiologically classified as [___].
back:
• Gestational Diabetes Mellitus (GDM)
 • Induced by the metabolic stress of pregnancy and hormonal insulin antagonism
 • Associated with high risk of developing T2DM later in life

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: Describe the mechanism by which glucocorticoids and thiazide diuretics etiologically induce secondary diabetes.
back:
• Glucocorticoids: Increase gluconeogenesis and antagonize insulin action (insulin resistance)
 • Thiazides: Impair insulin secretion and decrease peripheral sensitivity

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: Contrast neonatal diabetes with MODY regarding the age of clinical onset.
back:
• Neonatal Diabetes: Presents within the first 6 months of life
 • MODY: Typically presents in young adults or adolescents, usually before age 25

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: Name the specific viral infections associated with the etiological destruction of ̢-cells.
back:
• Coxsackie B virus
 • Cytomegalovirus (CMV)
 • Congenital rubella
 • Mumps

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: Diabetes resulting from an absolute deficiency of insulin primarily caused by autoimmune destruction of pancreatic beta-cells is classified as [___].
back:
• Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus (T1D).
• Includes Immune-mediated and Idiopathic subtypes.
• Fundamental lesion is the progressive destruction of islet beta-cells.

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: A 16-year-old non-obese male presents with mild hyperglycemia discovered during a physical. His father and grandmother were both diagnosed with diabetes in their late teens. The most likely etiologic category is [___].
back:
• Maturity-Onset Diabetes of the Young (MODY).
• Classified as a genetic defect of beta-cell function.
• Usually follows an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern.

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: Explain the role of 'Beta-cell failure' in the pathogenesis of Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus.
back:
• Compensation: Early beta-cell hyperfunction occurs to counter insulin resistance.
• Exhaustion: Secretory capacity eventually fails to meet increasing demands.
• Relative deficiency: Insulin levels become inadequate for the degree of hyperglycemia.

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: Contrast Type 1 and Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus regarding their association with HLA genes and islet histopathology.
back:
• Genetics: T1D is strongly linked to HLA-DR3/DR4; T2D has no HLA linkage.
• Pathology: T1D shows lymphocytic insulitis; T2D shows islet amyloid deposition.
• Beta-cells: T1D involves severe depletion; T2D shows mild depletion.

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: List four endocrinopathies that can result in secondary diabetes mellitus by producing hormones that oppose insulin action.
back:
• Acromegaly (Growth Hormone excess).
• Cushing Syndrome (Cortisol excess).
• Pheochromocytoma (Catecholamine excess).
• Hyperthyroidism (Thyroid hormone excess).

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: The form of secondary diabetes caused by structural damage to the endocrine pancreas in conditions like Chronic Pancreatitis or Cystic Fibrosis is categorized as [___].
back:
• Exocrine Pancreatic Defects.
• Often referred to as Type 3C Diabetes.
• Results from diffuse destruction of pancreatic parenchyma.

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: A 30-year-old woman at 26 weeks gestation undergoes a glucose tolerance test with a result of 215 mg/dL at 2 hours. Identify her etiologic classification and the primary underlying mechanism.
back:
• Gestational Diabetes Mellitus (GDM).
• Mechanism: Pregnancy-induced insulin resistance exceeds beta-cell compensatory capacity.
• Risks: Increased likelihood of fetal macrosomia and future maternal Type 2 DM.

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: Outline how glucocorticoid therapy carries out its biological function in inducing a 'drug-induced' diabetic state.
back:
• Increases Gluconeogenesis: Stimulates hepatic glucose output.
• Induces Resistance: Antagonizes the actions of insulin in peripheral tissues.
• Promotes Hyperglycemia: Often necessitates increased insulin dosing in known diabetics.

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: Contrast 'Genetic Defects of Beta-Cell Function' with 'Genetic Defects in Insulin Action' in the classification of diabetes.
back:
• Beta-cell function: Mutations (e.g., MODY, GCK) impair insulin production/secretion.
• Insulin action: Mutations (e.g., Insulin receptor) impair receptor signaling/responsiveness.
• Presentation: Receptor defects often present with Acanthosis Nigricans.

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: Identify the specific etiologic sub-category for diabetes mellitus triggered by Cytomegalovirus or Congenital Rubella.
back:
• Infections.
• Classified under 'Other Specific Types' of diabetes.
• Believed to involve direct viral-mediated injury to pancreatic islets.

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: In the etiological classification of DM, genetic defects in beta-cell function that lead to Maturity-Onset Diabetes of the Young (MODY) type 3 involve mutations in the [___] gene.
back:
* HNF1A (Hepatocyte nuclear factor 1 alpha)
* Most common form of MODY
* Results in progressive beta-cell dysfunction and impaired glucose-induced insulin secretion

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: A 10-year-old child presents with rapid weight loss, polyuria, and polydipsia. Laboratory tests confirm hyperglycemia and the presence of glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD) autoantibodies. Identify the specific etiologic category.
back:
* Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus (Immune-mediated)
* Caused by T-cell mediated autoimmune destruction of pancreatic beta cells
* Leads to absolute insulin deficiency and susceptibility to ketoacidosis

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: Explain how the mechanism of insulin deficiency differs etiologically between Type 1 and Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus.
back:
* Type 1: Absolute insulin deficiency due to autoimmune-driven beta-cell destruction.
* Type 2: Relative insulin deficiency caused by peripheral insulin resistance combined with inadequate beta-cell compensatory secretion.

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: A 45-year-old chronic alcoholic with recurrent epigastric pain presents with hyperglycemia. Contrast the underlying etiology of his diabetes with that of a patient with Cushing syndrome.
back:
* Chronic Alcoholic: Type 3C (Pancreatogenic) DM due to direct exocrine tissue destruction.
* Cushing Syndrome: Endocrinopathy-associated DM where excess cortisol induces peripheral insulin resistance and gluconeogenesis.

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: Summarize the role of Dipeptidyl Peptidase-4 (DPP-4) inhibitors in the treatment of Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus.
back:
* Inhibits degradation of endogenous incretins (GLP-1 and GIP).
* Extends the half-life of hormones that stimulate glucose-dependent insulin secretion.
* Helps suppress inappropriate postprandial glucagon release.

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: Current WHO/ADA criteria for the diagnosis of Diabetes Mellitus include a fasting plasma glucose level ≥ [___] mg/dL or a 2-hour plasma glucose ≥ [___] mg/dL during an OGTT.
back:
* Fasting: 126 mg/dL
* 2-hour (OGTT): 200 mg/dL
* Diagnosis requires repeat confirmation or a concurrent HbA1c ≥ 6.5%

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: A 50-year-old male with skin hyperpigmentation, cirrhosis, and hyperglycemia is suspected of having 'Bronze Diabetes.' This condition is classified etiologically under [___].
back:
* Exocrine Pancreatic Defects (Secondary DM)
* Specifically: Hereditary Hemochromatosis
* Iron deposition causes direct toxic damage to both exocrine parenchyma and endocrine islets.

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: Analyze how activating mutations in the KCNJ11 and ABCC8 genes result in neonatal diabetes and why this differs from Type 1 DM.
back:
* Mechanism: Mutations keep ATP-sensitive K+ channels permanently open, preventing cell depolarization and insulin release.
* Contrast: This is a monogenic functional defect rather than autoimmune beta-cell destruction.

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: Contrast the acute metabolic complications typically seen in Type 1 versus Type 2 Diabetes regarding the 'Hyperosmolar' and 'Ketotic' states.
back:
* Type 1: Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA); absolute insulin lack drives ketogenesis.
* Type 2: Hyperosmolar Hyperglycemic State (HHS); residual insulin prevents ketosis but allows extreme hyperglycemia and dehydration.

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: Identify the equimolar byproduct of proinsulin cleavage that serves as a useful clinical biomarker for endogenous insulin production.
back:
* C-peptide
* Formed during proteolytic cleavage in the Golgi complex/secretory granules
* Useful for distinguishing T1D (low C-peptide) from T2D (normal/high C-peptide).

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: In Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus, the genetic susceptibility is most strongly linked to the [___] gene cluster.
back:
• MHC Class II
• Specifically HLA-DR3 and HLA-DR4 haplotypes
• Contributes nearly 50% of the heritable risk.

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: A 12-year-old child presents with weight loss despite increased appetite, frequent urination, and a fruity odor on the breath. Identify the most likely underlying pathophysiology.
back:
• Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus
• T-cell mediated autoimmune destruction of pancreatic β-cells
• Resulting in absolute insulin deficiency.

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: Explain the role of free fatty acids (FFAs) in the development of insulin resistance in Type 2 Diabetes.
back:
• Excess FFAs overwhelm intracellular oxidation pathways
• Accumulation of DAG and ceramides attenuates insulin signaling
• Compete with glucose as oxidation substrates.

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: Contrast the acute metabolic emergencies typically seen in poorly controlled Type 1 versus Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus.
back:
• DM-I: Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA); characterized by ketonemia and metabolic acidosis.
• DM-II: Hyperosmolar Hyperglycemic State (HHS); marked by extreme hyperglycemia (>600 mg/dL) and severe dehydration.

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: Describe how GLP-1 receptor agonists utilize the "incretin effect" to manage Type 2 Diabetes.
back:
• Stimulate insulin secretion from β-cells post-feeding
• Suppress inappropriate glucagon release from α-cells
• Delay gastric emptying to promote satiety.

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: According to current diagnostic criteria, a patient is diagnosed with Diabetes Mellitus if their Glycated Hemoglobin (HbA1c) level is ≥ [___].
back:
• 6.5%
• Reflects average glycemic control over the past 120 days
• Repeat testing required for confirmation.

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: A 55-year-old obese male with long-standing Type 2 Diabetes presents with decreased vision. Fundoscopy reveals neovascularization. Identify the growth factor responsible for this complication.
back:
• Vascular Endothelial Growth Factor (VEGF)
• Hypoxia-induced expression leads to proliferative retinopathy
• Key target for antiangiogenic therapies.

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: Detail the distinctive histological changes found in the Islets of Langerhans when comparing Type 1 and Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus.
back:
• DM-I: Insulitis (lymphocytic infiltrates); progressive β-cell depletion.
• DM-II: Amyloid (amylin) deposition within islets; mild β-cell loss late in disease.

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: Contrast the metabolic effects of insulin in the liver versus skeletal muscle.
back:
• Liver: Inhibits gluconeogenesis/glycogenolysis; promotes glycogen synthesis.
• Muscle: Increases glucose uptake (GLUT-4 translocation) and protein synthesis.

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: Identify the pathognomonic glomerular lesion of diabetic nephropathy characterized by ovoid PAS-positive mesangial nodules.
back:
• Kimmelstiel-Wilson lesions
• Also known as Nodular Glomerulosclerosis
• Results from chronic microangiopathy.

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus is strongly linked to the [___] locus on chromosome 6, specifically involving the DR3 and DR4 haplotypes.
back:
• MHC Class II (HLA)
• Contributes nearly 50% of genetic susceptibility
• Involves failure of self-tolerance in islet-specific T-cells

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
coreConcept: Clinical Presentation and Histology of T1DM
front: A 12-year-old child presents with sudden weight loss, polyuria, and a fruity breath odor. Lab tests show blood glucose of 400 mg/dL and ketonuria. Identify the diagnosis and the expected islet histology.
back:
• Diagnosis: Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus (DKA)
• Histology: Insulitis
• Characterized by lymphocytic infiltration (T-cells) and β-cell depletion

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: Explain the role of free fatty acids (FFAs) in the pathogenesis of peripheral insulin resistance in Type 2 Diabetes.
back:
• Excess FFAs overwhelm fatty acid oxidation pathways
• Accumulation of DAG and ceramide intermediates
• These metabolites attenuate signaling through the insulin receptor (IRS proteins)

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: A patient with Type 2 Diabetes presents with a glucose of 900 mg/dL, severe dehydration, and altered mental status but no ketosis. Contrast this complication with its Type 1 counterpart.
back:
• Type 2: Hyperosmolar Hyperglycemic State (HHS)
• Type 1: Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA)
• HHS has higher glucose and minimal ketones due to residual insulin

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: Identify the two fundamental metabolic defects that must coexist to result in the development of overt Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus.
back:
• Insulin Resistance: Decreased response of peripheral tissues
• β-cell Dysfunction: Secretory failure relative to insulin demand

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: According to standard criteria, a diagnosis of Diabetes Mellitus requires a fasting plasma glucose level equal to or greater than [___] mg/dL.
back:
• 126 mg/dL
• Must be confirmed on a separate day
• Alternative: HbA1c ≥ 6.5% or random glucose ≥ 200 mg/dL

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: A 55-year-old diabetic patient presents with microalbuminuria and blurred vision. The thickening of capillary basement membranes in these organs is primarily driven by the interaction of [___] with their specific receptor (RAGE).
back:
• Advanced Glycation End products (AGEs)
• Stimulates TGF-β and VEGF production
• Leads to excessive basement membrane matrix deposition

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: How does the polyol pathway lead to oxidative stress in tissues like the lens and nerves during chronic hyperglycemia?
back:
• Aldose reductase converts glucose to sorbitol
• Reaction consumes NADPH
• Depleted NADPH prevents regeneration of reduced glutathione (GSH)
• Resulting oxidative stress causes cellular damage

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: Contrast the microscopic islet findings between long-standing Type 1 and long-standing Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus.
back:
• Type 1: β-cell depletion, islet atrophy, and fibrosis
• Type 2: Amyloid deposition (amylin)
• Amyloid starts in capillaries and eventually obliterates islets

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: Name the pathognomonic glomerular lesion of diabetic nephropathy characterized by ovoid, PAS-positive mesangial matrix deposits.
back:
• Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules
• Also called Nodular Glomerulosclerosis
• Found in 15-30% of long-term diabetics

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: In Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus, the fundamental immune abnormality is a failure of self-tolerance in T cells specific for islet antigens, which often correlates with the presence of [___] and [___] HLA haplotypes.
back:
• HLA-DR3
• HLA-DR4
• These major histocompatibility complex (MHC) class II alleles contribute to nearly 50% of the genetic susceptibility for Type 1 disease.

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: A 14-year-old child presents with a three-week history of polyuria, polydipsia, and significant weight loss despite increased appetite. What is the most likely microscopic finding in this patient's pancreatic islets?
back:
• Insulitis
• Characterized by lymphocytic inflammatory infiltrates (T cells and macrophages)
• Results in progressive autoimmune destruction of the insulin-secreting beta cell population.

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: Explain how C-peptide levels are utilized to distinguish between Type 1 and Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus during diagnostic workup.
back:
• C-peptide is co-secreted with insulin in equimolar amounts
• Low/absent in DM-I due to absolute insulin deficiency
• Normal or high in early DM-II reflecting insulin resistance and hyperinsulinemia.

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: Contrast the acute metabolic emergencies typically seen in a non-compliant 20-year-old DM-I patient versus an elderly, dehydrated 70-year-old DM-II patient.
back:
• DM-I: Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA) with severe ketonemia and Kussmaul breathing
• DM-II: Hyperosmolar Hyperglycemic State (HHS) with extreme dehydration and absence of significant ketoacidosis.

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: Describe the blunting of the 'incretin effect' and its contribution to the metabolic failure in Type 2 Diabetes.
back:
• Reduced secretion/action of GIP and GLP-1 after food intake
• Leads to inadequate postprandial insulin release
• Results in impaired suppression of glucagon and loss of satiety signals.

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: According to the standard diagnostic criteria for Diabetes Mellitus, a patient is diagnosed if their glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) level is greater than or equal to [___]%.
back:
• 6.5%
• This value reflects the average glycemic control over the 120-day lifespan of a red blood cell via nonenzymatic glycation.

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: An obese 50-year-old male with persistent hyperglycemia shows velvety, hyperpigmented plaques on his neck and axillae. Identify the skin condition and its underlying association.
back:
• Acanthosis nigricans
• It is a clinical marker of severe peripheral insulin resistance
• Frequently associated with Type 2 Diabetes and metabolic syndrome.

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: Contrast the characteristic islet morphology of long-standing Type 2 Diabetes with that of Type 1 Diabetes.
back:
• DM-II: Amyloid deposition (amylin) often obliterating the islets
• DM-I: Islet atrophy and marked reduction in the total number and size of islets.

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: Contrast the impact of hyperglycemia on the polyol pathway in tissues that do not require insulin for glucose transport.
back:
• Excess glucose is converted to sorbitol via aldose reductase
• This process depletes NADPH, increasing susceptibility to oxidative stress
• Results in cataracts and contributes to diabetic neuropathy/nephropathy.

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: Identify the most common cause of death in patients with long-standing Diabetes Mellitus across both types.
back:
• Myocardial Infarction
• Driven by accelerated atherosclerosis (macrovascular disease)
• Risk is significantly exacerbated by hyperglycemia-induced endothelial dysfunction, hypertension, and dyslipidemia.

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: The most significant genetic susceptibility for Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus involves the [___] gene cluster, specifically the DR3 and DR4 haplotypes.
back:
* HLA (Human Leukocyte Antigen) class II.
* High association with DR3/DR4 compound heterozygosity.
* Contributes nearly 50% of the total genetic risk.

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: A 14-year-old child presents with sudden-onset weight loss, abdominal pain, and Kussmaul breathing. Laboratory results reveal severe metabolic acidosis and ketonuria. Identify the likely condition and its primary pathophysiology.
back:
* Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus (Diabetic Ketoacidosis).
* Absolute insulin deficiency.
* Leads to unchecked lipolysis and hepatic oxidation of free fatty acids into ketone bodies.

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: Explain the role of the 'incretin effect' in glucose homeostasis and its status in Type 2 Diabetes.
back:
* GIP and GLP-1 are secreted by intestines to stimulate post-meal insulin release.
* Blunted incretin response in T2D contributes to relative insulin deficiency.
* DPP-4 inhibitors work by preserving these endogenous hormones.

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: Contrast the classic histopathological findings in the pancreatic islets of long-standing Type 1 vs. Type 2 Diabetes.
back:
* DM-I: Insulitis (T-lymphocytic infiltration), progressive beta-cell depletion, and islet atrophy.
* DM-II: Amyloid deposition (amylin) within islets and mild to moderate reduction in beta-cell mass.

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: List the three cardinal metabolic abnormalities identified in 'Metabolic Syndrome' that increase risk for Type 2 Diabetes.
back:
* Visceral (central) obesity.
* Insulin resistance (hyperglycemia).
* Dyslipidemia (increased triglycerides, low HDL) and hypertension.

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: According to current diagnostic criteria, a glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) level of [___]% or higher is diagnostic for Diabetes Mellitus.
back:
* 6.5%.
* Reflects average blood glucose over the preceding 120 days (lifespan of a red blood cell).

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: An elderly, obese male presents with severe dehydration and a blood glucose of 850 mg/dL, but no detectable ketones. Identify the likely complication and why ketosis is absent.
back:
* Hyperosmolar Hyperglycemic State (HHS).
* Occurs in Type 2 Diabetes.
* Residual insulin levels are sufficient to inhibit hepatic fatty acid oxidation and ketogenesis.

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: Explain how Advanced Glycation End-products (AGEs) contribute to diabetic macrovascular injury.
back:
* AGEs bind RAGE on endothelium, inducing ROS and pro-inflammatory cytokines.
* Cross-linking of Type I collagen reduces vessel elasticity.
* Trapping of LDL in the basement membrane accelerates atherosclerosis.

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: Distinguish between Diffuse Mesangial Sclerosis and Nodular Glomerulosclerosis in diabetic nephropathy.
back:
* Diffuse: Symmetric increase in mesangial matrix with GBM thickening.
* Nodular (Kimmelstiel-Wilson): Pathognomonic ovoid, PAS-positive laminated matrix deposits at the glomerular periphery.

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: Identify the primary mechanism behind polydipsia in uncontrolled diabetic patients.
back:
* Hyperglycemia causes osmotic diuresis (glycosuria).
* Profound renal water loss causes intracellular dehydration.
* Dehydration stimulates hypothalamic thirst centers.

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: The primary genetic susceptibility locus for Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus, which involves alleles like DR3 and DR4, is the [___] gene cluster.
back:
• HLA (Human Leukocyte Antigen)
• Specifically MHC Class II (HLA-DR and HLA-DQ)

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: A 12-year-old child presents with sudden weight loss, polydipsia, and fruity-smelling breath. Name the acute metabolic complication and its primary cause.
back:
• Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA)
• Absolute insulin deficiency leading to increased free fatty acids and ketone body production

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: Explain the cellular event triggered by an increased intracellular ATP/ADP ratio that lead to insulin release from pancreatic β-cells.
back:
• Closure of ATP-sensitive K+ channels
• Depolarization of the cell membrane
• Influx of Ca2+ through voltage-gated channels triggering exocytosis

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: Contrast the characteristic microscopic findings in the pancreatic islets of a patient with long-standing Type 1 vs. Type 2 Diabetes.
back:
• Type 1: Insulitis (T-cell lymphocytic infiltrate) and β-cell depletion
• Type 2: Islet amyloid (amylin) deposition and mild β-cell loss

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: Identify the acute metabolic complication in elderly Type 2 Diabetics characterized by severe dehydration and glucose levels >600 mg/dL without significant ketosis.
back:
• Hyperosmolar Hyperglycemic State (HHS)
• Residual insulin prevents lipolysis and ketogenesis but fails to control hyperglycemia

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: According to the WHO and ADA diagnostic criteria, a patient is classified as having Diabetes Mellitus if their Glycated Hemoglobin (HbA1c) is [___] or higher.
back:
• 6.5%
• Reflects average glycemic control over the preceding 120 days

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: A 45-year-old obese female presents with acanthosis nigricans and a fasting glucose of 140 mg/dL. State the primary mechanism of her hyperglycemia.
back:
• Insulin resistance in peripheral tissues (skeletal muscle/adipocytes)
• Inadequate compensatory β-cell insulin secretion

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: Explain how elevated circulating free fatty acids (FFAs) in obesity cause peripheral insulin resistance in skeletal muscle.
back:
• Excess FFAs generate toxic intermediates (DAG/ceramides)
• These activate kinases that inhibit insulin receptor substrate (IRS) signaling
• Results in blunted GLUT-4 translocation to the membrane

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: Distinguish between Type 1 and Type 2 Diabetes using circulating C-peptide levels.
back:
• Type 1: Low to absent (indicates absolute insulin deficiency)
• Type 2: Normal to high initially (reflects hyperinsulinemia to counter resistance)

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: Name the pathognomonic glomerular lesion in diabetic nephropathy characterized by ovoid, PAS-positive nodules in the mesangium.
back:
• Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules
• Also called nodular glomerulosclerosis

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: The primary genetic susceptibility for Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus is linked to the [___] gene cluster, specifically the DR3 and DR4 haplotypes.
back:
• HLA (Human Leukocyte Antigen) class II
• Specifically haplotypes DR3-DQ2 and DR4-DQ8
• Contributes up to 50% of the genetic risk for T1D

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: A 14-year-old presents with sudden polyuria, weight loss, and fruity breath. Labs show autoantibodies against glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD). Identify the underlying pathophysiology.
back:
• Autoimmune-mediated T-cell destruction of pancreatic β-cells
• Results in an absolute insulin deficiency
• Progresses to Stage 3 symptomatic Type 1 Diabetes

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: Explain the role of Free Fatty Acids (FFAs) in the induction of insulin resistance in Type 2 Diabetes.
back:
• Intracellular lipid intermediates (DAG, ceramides) accumulate
• These attenuate insulin receptor signaling pathways (IRS/PI3K)
• FFAs also compete with glucose for oxidation (Randle cycle)

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: Contrast the acute metabolic complications typically seen in Type 1 versus Type 2 Diabetes regarding clinical presentation and labs.
back:
• Type 1: Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA); presents with Kussmaul breathing, ketonemia, and metabolic acidosis
• Type 2: Hyperosmolar Hyperglycemic State (HHS); presents with extreme hyperglycemia (>600 mg/dL) and profound dehydration without ketosis

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: Name the specific islet of Langerhans lesion characteristic of long-standing Type 2 Diabetes that is absent in Type 1.
back:
• Amyloid deposition
• Derived from islet amyloid polypeptide (IAPP or Amylin)
• Results in progressive replacement and obliteration of islets

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: To satisfy the WHO/ADA diagnostic criteria for Diabetes Mellitus, the glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) level must be greater than or equal to [___]%.
back:
• 6.5%
• Reflects glycemic control over the preceding 120 days
• Does not require fasting state for measurement

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: A 55-year-old diabetic presents with microalbuminuria. Renal biopsy reveals ovoid, PAS-positive hyaline nodules in the glomerular periphery. Identify this finding.
back:
• Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules
• Pathognomonic for Nodular Glomerulosclerosis
• Part of diabetic microangiopathy affecting the mesangium

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: Describe the mechanism by which persistent intracellular hyperglycemia leads to oxidative stress via the Polyol Pathway.
back:
• Glucose is converted to sorbitol by Aldose Reductase
• This reaction consumes NADPH
• Depleted NADPH prevents regeneration of Reduced Glutathione (GSH), increasing ROS susceptibility

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: Distinguish between the histological findings in the pancreatic islets of a patient with Type 1 vs. Type 2 Diabetes.
back:
• Type 1: Insulitis (lymphocytic T-cell infiltration) and β-cell depletion
• Type 2: Amyloid (amylin) deposition and mild β-cell mass reduction; no inflammatory infiltrate

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: Identify the three clinical manifestations comprising the 'Classic Triad' of symptomatic Diabetes.
back:
• Polyuria (excessive urination due to osmotic diuresis)
• Polydipsia (excessive thirst due to volume depletion)
• Polyphagia (excessive hunger due to catabolic state)

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: Genetic susceptibility to Type 1 Diabetes (DM-I) is most strongly linked to the [___] gene cluster, particularly the DR3 and DR4 haplotypes.
back:
• HLA (Human Leukocyte Antigen) class II
• Specifically HLA-DR and HLA-DQ loci
• Contributes approximately 50% of genetic susceptibility.

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: A 12-year-old child presents with rapid weight loss, polyuria, and fruity breath odor. The primary underlying pathophysiology involves [___].
back:
• Autoimmune destruction of pancreatic β-cells
• Absolute insulin deficiency
• T-cell mediated (Type IV) hypersensitivity response to islet antigens.

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: Explain the characteristic microscopic differences in the pancreatic islets between long-standing Type 1 and Type 2 Diabetes.
back:
• DM-I: Insulitis (lymphocytic T-cell infiltrate) followed by β-cell depletion and atrophy.
• DM-II: Amyloid (amylin) deposition within islets and mild/variable β-cell reduction.

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: Contrast the acute metabolic crisis of a 15-year-old DM-I patient with that of a 70-year-old obese DM-II patient with restricted water intake.
back:
• 15yo (DKA): Ketosis, metabolic acidosis, Kussmaul breathing, glucose <600 mg/dL.
• 70yo (HHS): Severe dehydration, no ketosis, glucose >600 mg/dL, high serum osmolarity.

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: State the pharmacological relevance of the "incretin effect" in managing Type 2 Diabetes.
back:
• GIP and GLP-1 promote postprandial insulin secretion.
• This effect is blunted in DM-II.
• Targeted by GLP-1 receptor agonists and DPP-4 inhibitors.

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: According to current diagnostic criteria, Diabetes Mellitus is confirmed if the Glycated Hemoglobin (HbA1c) level is ≥ [___] %.
back:
• 6.5%
• Reflects glycemic control over the previous 120 days (lifespan of RBCs).

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: An obese 45-year-old female presents with velvety, hyperpigmented patches in her axilla. This clinical finding is a marker for [___].
back:
• Acanthosis nigricans
• Severe insulin resistance
• Compensatory hyperinsulinemia in Type 2 Diabetes.

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: How does persistent hyperglycemia lead to osmotic damage and cataract formation in non-insulin-dependent tissues like the lens?
back:
• Polyol Pathway: Glucose is converted to sorbitol via aldose reductase.
• Sorbitol accumulation causes osmotic swelling.
• NADPH depletion leads to oxidative stress.

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: Contrast the role of Free Fatty Acids (FFAs) in the metabolic loop of insulin resistance in DM-II.
back:
• Excess FFAs overwhelmed fatty acid oxidation.
• Toxic intermediates (DAG, ceramides) accumulate.
• These attenuate insulin receptor signaling by phosphorylating IRS proteins.

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: Identify the most common cause of death in patients with long-standing Diabetes Mellitus of either type.
back:
• Myocardial Infarction
• Due to accelerated macrovascular atherosclerosis.

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus is strongly linked to the [___] and [___] haplotypes of the Major Histocompatibility Complex (MHC).
back:
• HLA-DR3
• HLA-DR4
• Linked to 50% of genetic susceptibility in Caucasians

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: A 14-year-old child presents with extreme thirst, frequent urination, and weight loss despite increased appetite. Lab tests show autoantibodies against Glutamic Acid Decarboxylase (GAD). Identify the most likely underlying pathogenesis.
back:
• Autoimmune T-cell mediated destruction of pancreatic beta-cells
• Th1 and CD8+ cytotoxic T-cell injury
• Results in absolute insulin deficiency

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: Explain the role of Free Fatty Acids (FFAs) in the induction of peripheral insulin resistance in Type 2 Diabetes.
back:
• Excess FFAs generate toxic lipid intermediates (diacylglycerol)
• Attenuates insulin receptor substrate (IRS) signaling
• Competes with glucose as an oxidation substrate

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: Contrast the acute metabolic crises of Type 1 and Type 2 Diabetes regarding their primary hormonal state and typical plasma glucose range.
back:
• Type 1: Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA); absolute insulin deficiency; glucose 250–600 mg/dL
• Type 2: Hyperosmolar Hyperglycemic State (HHS); relative insulin deficiency + severe dehydration; glucose 600–1200 mg/dL

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: List three metabolic effects of insulin on adipose tissue that are typically impaired in the insulin-resistant state of Type 2 Diabetes.
back:
• Inhibition of hormone-sensitive lipase (increased lipolysis)
• Glucose uptake via GLUT-4 translocation
• Lipogenesis (triglyceride synthesis)

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: The diagnostic threshold for Diabetes Mellitus using Glycated Hemoglobin (HbA1c) is a level greater than or equal to [___].
back:
• 6.5%
• Reflects glycemic control over 120 days
• Not affected by day-to-day glucose variation

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: An obese 50-year-old patient with chronic hyperglycemia presents with proteinuria. Renal biopsy reveals laminated, PAS-positive ovoid nodules in the glomerular periphery. Identify the lesion.
back:
• Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules
• Feature of Nodular Glomerulosclerosis
• Pathognomonic for diabetic nephropathy

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: Explain how the Polyol pathway leads to cataract formation and oxidative stress in tissues like the lens and nerves during chronic hyperglycemia.
back:
• Aldose reductase converts excess glucose to sorbitol (osmotic swelling)
• NADPH depletion during the reaction prevents glutathione regeneration
• Increases susceptibility to reactive oxygen species (ROS)

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: Contrast the histopathological findings of pancreatic islets in long-standing Type 1 versus Type 2 Diabetes.
back:
• Type 1: Insulitis (T-lymphocytic infiltration) and marked beta-cell depletion
• Type 2: Amyloid (amylin) deposition and mild/moderate beta-cell reduction

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: Name the insulin-independent glucose transporter responsible for 'glucose sensing' within pancreatic beta-cells.
back:
• GLUT-2
• Facilitates glucose entry to trigger insulin release
• Operates via ATP generation and calcium channel activation

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: The primary genetic susceptibility locus for Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus, contributing nearly 50% of the inherited risk, is the [___] gene cluster.
back:
• HLA (Human Leukocyte Antigen) class II
• Specifically associated with HLA-DR3 and HLA-DR4 haplotypes
• Affects peptide binding and T-cell selection/tolerance

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: A 10-year-old child presents with rapid weight loss, polyuria, and polydipsia. Lab tests show low C-peptide levels. Identify the underlying pathophysiology.
back:
• T-cell mediated autoimmune destruction of pancreatic β-cells
• Th1 and CD8+ cytotoxic T-lymphocyte attack
• Resulting in an absolute insulin deficiency

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: Explain the role of free fatty acids (FFAs) in the pathogenesis of insulin resistance in Type 2 Diabetes.
back:
• Excess FFAs overwhelm fatty acid oxidation pathways
• Accumulation of cytoplasmic intermediates (DAG, ceramides)
• These toxic metabolites attenuate insulin receptor signaling cascades

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: Contrast the islet-specific microscopic findings in long-standing Type 1 versus Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus.
back:
• DM-I: Insulitis (lymphocytic infiltrate) followed by marked β-cell depletion/atrophy
• DM-II: Amyloid deposition (amylin) within islets and mild β-cell reduction

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: Enumerate the three cardinal metabolic defects that define the pathophysiology of Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus.
back:
• Peripheral insulin resistance (muscle/fat)
• Inadequate insulin secretion by β-cells (relative deficiency)
• Increased endogenous glucose production in the liver

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: To diagnose Diabetes Mellitus, the Fasting Plasma Glucose must be [___] mg/dL or higher, or the HbA1c must be at least [___]%.
back:
• Fasting Plasma Glucose: 126 mg/dL
• HbA1c: 6.5%
• Requires confirmation by repeat testing on a separate day

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: A 60-year-old obese female with a history of recurrent skin infections presents with a blood glucose of 850 mg/dL and severe dehydration, but no ketones. Identify the specific acute complication.
back:
• Hyperosmolar Hyperglycemic State (HHS)
• Typical of DM-II where residual insulin prevents lipolysis/ketogenesis
• Severe osmotic diuresis leading to profound dehydration

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: Explain how hyperglycemia leads to microvascular basement membrane thickening via the Advanced Glycation End-products (AGEs) pathway.
back:
• Glucose metabolites bind amino groups on proteins
• AGEs bind RAGE receptors on endothelium
• Triggers pro-inflammatory cytokines, ROS, and excess matrix synthesis (TGF-β)

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: Distinguish between the characteristic metabolic drivers of Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA) versus normal postprandial states.
back:
• DKA: Severe insulin deficiency + glucagon excess
• Stimulates hormone-sensitive lipase in fat
• FFAs reach liver and undergo oxidation to ketone bodies

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: Identify the pathognomonic glomerular lesion seen in diabetic nephropathy upon microscopic examination.
back:
• Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules
• Nodular glomerulosclerosis (ovoid, PAS-positive matrix deposits)
• Accompanied by diffuse mesangial sclerosis and capillary membrane thickening

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: In Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus, the strongest genetic association is with the [___] gene cluster, specifically the DR3 and DR4 haplotypes.
back:
• HLA (Human Leukocyte Antigen) class II
• Contributes ~50% of genetic susceptibility
• Linked to failure of T-cell self-tolerance

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
coreConcept: C-peptide as a Marker of β-cell Function
front: A 12-year-old boy presents with sudden weight loss, polyuria, and fruity breath. Lab tests show extremely low C-peptide levels. Identify the likely diagnosis and explain the lab finding.
back:
• Diagnosis: Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus
• Low C-peptide: Indicates absolute insulin deficiency
• Reflects autoimmune destruction of >90% of pancreatic β-cells

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: Explain the role of amylin/amyloid deposition in the pathogenesis of Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus.
back:
• Found in >90% of T2DM islets
• Represents β-cell 'burnout' or failure
• Contributes to progressive loss of functional β-cell mass

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: Contrast the typical acute metabolic crises associated with Type 1 versus Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus.
back:
• Type 1: Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA); characterized by ketonemia and Kussmaul breathing
• Type 2: Hyperosmolar Hyperglycemic State (HHS); characterized by severe dehydration without significant ketosis

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: Identify the three primary tissues where insulin resistance manifests to cause hyperglycemia in Type 2 Diabetes.
back:
• Skeletal muscle (failure of glucose uptake)
• Liver (failure to inhibit gluconeogenesis)
