• Adipose tissue (failure to inhibit lipolysis, increasing FFAs)

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: The pathognomonic glomerular lesion characterized by ovoid, PAS-positive hyaline masses in diabetic nephropathy is [___].
back:
• Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules
• Also known as Nodular Glomerulosclerosis
• Results from increased mesangial matrix deposition

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: An obese 45-year-old female with acanthosis nigricans presents with a fasting glucose of 145 mg/dL. Explain how obesity contributes to her insulin resistance.
back:
• Excess FFAs: Intracellular lipid metabolites interfere with insulin signaling
• Adipokines: Decreased adiponectin and increased pro-inflammatory cytokines
• Chronic inflammation: Macrophage activation via the inflammasome

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: Describe the mechanism by which Advanced Glycation End-products (AGEs) cause diabetic microangiopathy.
back:
• Binding RAGE: Stimulates VEGF (causing retinopathy) and TGF-β (basement membrane thickening)
• Cross-linking: Trap LDL in vessel walls and resist proteolytic digestion
• Result: Pro-coagulant activity and ROS generation

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: Contrast the islet histology between Type 1 and Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus.
back:
• Type 1: Insulitis (T-cell lymphocytic infiltrate) with β-cell depletion
• Type 2: Amyloid deposition within islets and mild β-cell loss

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: List the four official WHO/ADA diagnostic criteria thresholds for Diabetes Mellitus.
back:
• HbA1c ≥6.5%
• Fasting Plasma Glucose ≥126 mg/dL
• 2-hour OGTT ≥200 mg/dL
• Random Glucose ≥200 mg/dL with symptoms

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: The fundamental immune abnormality in Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus involves a failure of self-tolerance in T-cells specifically targeting [___] antigens.
back:
• Islet autoantigens (e.g., Insulin, GAD).
• Leads to progressive autoimmune destruction of pancreatic β-cells.
• Characterized by absolute insulin deficiency.

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: A 14-year-old female presents with polyuria, weight loss, and deep, labored breathing. Lab results reveal severe metabolic acidosis and hyperglycemia. Identify the immediate metabolic complication.
back:
• Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA).
• Caused by absolute insulin deficiency and glucagon excess.
• Leads to increased free fatty acid oxidation and ketone body formation.

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: Explain how intracellular hyperglycemia leads to diabetic microangiopathy through the Protein Kinase C (PKC) pathway.
back:
• Stimulates de novo synthesis of Diacylglycerol (DAG).
• Activates PKC, increasing VEGF and TGF-β production.
• Results in basement membrane thickening and procoagulant activity.

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: Contrast the microscopic islet morphology typically seen in long-standing Type 1 vs. Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus.
back:
• DM-I: Insulitis (T-cell lymphocytic infiltrates) and β-cell depletion.
• DM-II: Amyloid deposition (amylin) and mild β-cell mass reduction.
• Amylin is co-secreted with insulin in resistant states.

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: Identify the primary clinical utility of measuring Glycated Hemoglobin (HbA1c) compared to a random blood glucose test.
back:
• Measures glycemic control over the lifespan of red cells (120 days).
• Not affected by day-to-day glucose fluctuations.
• Diagnostic threshold for Diabetes is ≥ 6.5%.

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: To confirm a diagnosis of Diabetes Mellitus, a patient's fasting plasma glucose must be equal to or greater than [___] mg/dL on at least two separate occasions.
back:
• 126 mg/dL.
• Fasting is defined as no caloric intake for at least 8 hours.
• Alternative: Random glucose ≥ 200 mg/dL with classic symptoms.

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: An obese 60-year-old male presents with severe dehydration and a plasma glucose of 900 mg/dL, but lacks Kussmaul breathing or a fruity breath odor. What is the most likely diagnosis?
back:
• Hyperosmolar Hyperglycemic State (HHS).
• Characteristic of Type 2 Diabetes due to relative insulin deficiency.
• Absence of ketoacidosis due to residual portal insulin inhibiting lipolysis.

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: Describe the mechanism by which the 'Polyol Pathway' contributes to the development of diabetic cataracts.
back:
• Aldose reductase converts glucose to sorbitol.
• Reaction consumes NADPH, depleting reduced glutathione (GSH).
• Increases oxidative stress and osmotic pressure within the lens.

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: Contrast the genetic predispositions of DM-I and DM-II regarding HLA linkage and concordance in identical twins.
back:
• DM-I: Strong HLA-DR3/DR4 linkage; ~50% twin concordance.
• DM-II: No HLA linkage; >90% twin concordance (higher genetic component).
• DM-II is primarily related to polymorphisms in metabolic/obesity genes.

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: What is the hallmark glomerular lesion seen in diabetic nodular glomerulosclerosis?
back:
• Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules.
• Ovoid, PAS-positive laminated matrix deposits in the glomerular periphery.
• Result of chronic microangiopathy and mesangial matrix expansion.

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: In Type 1 Diabetes, the fundamental immune abnormality is a failure of self-tolerance in [___] specific for islet antigens.
back:
• T cells (specifically CD4+ Th1 and CD8+ CTLs)
• These cells react against endogenous beta-cell antigens (e.g., insulin, GAD)
• Leads to progressive autoimmune destruction of islets.

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: A 12-year-old child presents with abdominal pain, Kussmaul breathing, and a fruity breath odor. Lab shows blood glucose 450 mg/dL. Identify the acute complication and its primary driver.
back:
• Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA)
• Primary driver: Absolute insulin deficiency
• Pathophysiology: Unchecked lipolysis leads to excess acetyl-CoA and ketone body formation.

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: Explain the role of Glycated Hemoglobin (HbA1c) in the long-term diagnosis and monitoring of Diabetes Mellitus.
back:
• Measures nonenzymatic covalent addition of glucose to hemoglobin
• Reflects average glycemic control over the RBC lifespan (~120 days)
• Diagnostic threshold: ≥ 6.5%.

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: Contrast the histological appearance of pancreatic islets in long-standing Type 1 vs. Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus.
back:
• Type 1: Insulitis (lymphocytic infiltrate) early, followed by atrophy and near-total loss of beta cells
• Type 2: Amyloid deposition (amylin) within islets; mild to moderate reduction in beta-cell mass.

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: Identify the two primary metabolic defects that must coexist to transition from prediabetes to overt Type 2 Diabetes.
back:
• Insulin resistance: Decreased peripheral tissue response (muscle, liver, fat)
• Beta-cell dysfunction: Inadequate insulin secretion to compensate for resistance.

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: According to standard diagnostic criteria, a fasting plasma glucose level of [___] mg/dL or higher, confirmed on repeat testing, is diagnostic for Diabetes Mellitus.
back:
• 126 mg/dL
• Prediabetes range: 100–125 mg/dL
• Fasting is defined as no caloric intake for at least 8 hours.

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: A diabetic patient's renal biopsy reveals ovoid, PAS-positive hyaline nodules in the glomerular periphery. What is the specific name of this lesion?
back:
• Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules
• Also called nodular glomerulosclerosis
• Pathognomonic for diabetic nephropathy.

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: Describe theRandle cycle (competition mechanism) by which elevated Free Fatty Acids (FFAs) contribute to insulin resistance in Type 2 Diabetes.
back:
• Excess FFAs are oxidized in muscle, competing with glucose for substrate oxidation
• Intracellular lipid metabolites (DAG, ceramides) inhibit insulin receptor signaling pathways (IRS-1).

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: Contrast the genetic associations of Type 1 vs. Type 2 Diabetes regarding HLA linkage and twin concordance.
back:
• Type 1: Strong linkage to HLA-DR3/DR4; 50% monozygotic twin concordance
• Type 2: No HLA linkage; >90% monozygotic twin concordance (stronger genetic component).

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: Identify the most common cause of death in patients with long-standing Diabetes Mellitus.
back:
• Myocardial Infarction
• Caused by accelerated atherosclerosis (macrovascular disease)
• Risk is significantly increased by concurrent hypertension and dyslipidemia.

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: The primary genetic susceptibility for Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus is linked to the [___] gene cluster, which accounts for nearly 50% of the inherited risk.
back:
* HLA (Human Leukocyte Antigen) class II
* Specifically HLA-DR3 and HLA-DR4 haplotypes
* Polymorphisms affect peptide-binding pockets and T-cell selection

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: A 12-year-old child presents with sudden weight loss, polyuria, and fatigue. Lab tests reveal circulating antibodies against glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD). Identify the underlying pathophysiology.
back:
* Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus
* Autoimmune destruction of pancreatic ̢-cells
* Mediated by CD8+ cytotoxic T-cells and Th1 cytokines
* Results in absolute insulin deficiency

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
coreConcept: C-peptide as a measure of endogenous insulin
front: Describe the diagnostic utility of serum C-peptide levels in distinguishing between Type 1 and Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus.
back:
* C-peptide is produced in equimolar amounts with insulin
* Type 1: Low or absent levels (indicates ̢-cell loss)
* Type 2: High or normal levels early in disease (indicates insulin resistance)

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: A 70-year-old obese patient with Type 2 Diabetes presents with a glucose of 1000 mg/dL and severe dehydration but no ketones. Contrast this with the typical metabolic emergency of Type 1 Diabetes.
back:
* Type 2: Hyperosmolar Hyperglycemic State (HHS); no ketosis because residual insulin inhibits lipolysis
* Type 1: Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA); absolute insulin deficiency causes unrestricted ketogenesis and metabolic acidosis

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: Explain the role of GLP-1 receptor agonists in addressing the blunted 'incretin effect' seen in Type 2 Diabetes management.
back:
* Mimic gut-derived GLP-1 to amplify glucose-dependent insulin secretion
* Suppress postprandial glucagon release
* Delay gastric emptying and promote satiety, aiding weight loss

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: According to the American Diabetes Association (ADA), a confirmed diagnosis of Diabetes Mellitus requires a fasting plasma glucose level greater than or equal to [___] mg/dL.
back:
* 126 mg/dL
* Requires confirmation on a separate day
* Alternative: HbA1c ̢ 6.5% or random glucose ̢ 200 mg/dL with symptoms

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: A biopsy of the pancreatic islets from a 60-year-old male with a long history of poorly controlled blood sugar shows deposition of pink, acellular material. Name the lesion and the associated diabetes type.
back:
* Islet Amyloid (Amylin deposition)
* Characteristic of Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus
* Reflects ̢-cell exhaustion and chronic secretory stress

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: Detail the mechanism by which the Polyol Pathway contributes to diabetic complications like cataracts and neuropathy in the setting of chronic hyperglycemia.
back:
* Aldose reductase converts glucose to sorbitol, consuming NADPH
* Depletes NADPH needed to regenerate reduced glutathione (GSH)
* Reduced GSH increases oxidative stress and cellular susceptibility to ROS

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: Contrast the islet-specific inflammatory and structural changes seen in the early stages of Type 1 vs. Type 2 Diabetes.
back:
* Type 1: Insulitis (T-lymphocyte infiltration) and rapid reduction in number/size of islets
* Type 2: No insulitis; characterized by amyloid deposition and subtle reduction in ̢-cell mass

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: Name the three components of the 'classic triad' of symptoms appearing at the clinical onset of insulin-deficient diabetes.
back:
* Polyuria (osmotic diuresis due to glycosuria)
* Polydipsia (intracellular dehydration triggering thirst centers)
* Polyphagia (catabolic state with negative energy balance)

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus shows a strong genetic association with the [___] gene cluster, specifically the DR3 and DR4 haplotypes.
back:
* HLA (Major Histocompatibility Complex)
* Linked to approximately 50% of genetic susceptibility
* Involves MHC Class II alleles

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: A 12-year-old child presents with sudden weight loss, polyuria, and fruity breath. The most likely underlying pathophysiology is [___].
back:
* Autoimmune destruction of pancreatic ̢̢β-cells
* T-cell mediated (Th1 and CD8+ CTLs)
* Leads to absolute insulin deficiency

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: Explain the role of central obesity in the induction of insulin resistance in Type 2 Diabetes.
back:
* Excess free fatty acids (FFAs) impair insulin signaling pathways
* Reduced adiponectin levels (insulin-sensitizing hormone)
* Chronic inflammation via IL-1β secretion from inflammasomes

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: Contrast the acute metabolic crises typically seen in uncontrolled Type 1 versus Type 2 Diabetes.
back:
* Type 1: Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA); severe ketosis, Kussmaul breathing
* Type 2: Hyperosmolar Hyperglycemic State (HHS); profound dehydration, minimal ketosis, extreme hyperglycemia (>600 mg/dL)

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: Identify the characteristic histologic finding in the pancreatic islets of long-standing Type 2 Diabetes.
back:
* Amyloid deposition
* Derived from Islet Amyloid Polypeptide (Amylin)
* Results in progressive loss of β-cell mass

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: According to standard diagnostic criteria, a patient is diagnosed with Diabetes Mellitus if their glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) level is [___] or higher.
back:
* 6.5%
* Confirmed on a separate day
* Reflects glycemic control over roughly 120 days

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: A long-term diabetic patient presents with claudication and a non-healing foot ulcer. This presentation is primarily a consequence of [___].
back:
* Diabetic Macrovascular Disease
* Accelerated atherosclerosis of large/medium arteries
* Results in limb ischemia and gangrene risk

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: How does persistent hyperglycemia lead to basement membrane thickening in diabetic microangiopathy?
back:
* Formation of Advanced Glycation End-products (AGEs)
* Non-enzymatic glycation of proteins
* Increased cross-linking of Type IV collagen and trapping of plasma proteins (LDL, albumin)

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: Distinguish the characteristic islet inflammatory pathology of early Type 1 Diabetes from Type 2 Diabetes.
back:
* Type 1: Insulitis (lymphocytic T-cell infiltrate)
* Type 2: Absence of insulitis; characterized by amyloid or β-cell burnout

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: Explain the utility of measuring C-peptide levels in a diabetic patient.
back:
* Surrogate marker for endogenous insulin secretion
* Low/absent in Type 1 (absolute deficiency)
* High early in Type 2 (compensatory hyperinsulinemia)

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: The primary immune mediators responsible for the progressive destruction of pancreatic ̢β-cells in Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus are [___].
back:
* T-lymphocytes (specifically CD8+ Cytotoxic T-cells)
* Th1 cells secreting inflammatory cytokines (IFN-γ, TNF)
* Localized inflammatory infiltrate termed "Insulitis"

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: A 12-year-old child presents with a 2-week history of polyuria, weight loss, and severe dehydration. Laboratory findings show a serum glucose of 350 mg/dL and ketonuria. Identify the underlying genetic susceptibility alleles most likely present.
back:
* HLA-DR3
* HLA-DR4
* Strongest risk associated with DR3/DR4 compound heterozygosity

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: How does the role of islet amyloid polypeptide (amylin) deposition differ in the diagnostic pathology of Type 2 DM compared to Type 1 DM?
back:
* Type 2 DM: Characteristic amyloid deposition within islets in >90% of long-standing cases
* Type 1 DM: Amyloid is absent; pathology is defined by lymphocytic insulitis and β-cell loss

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: A 45-year-old patient with long-standing hyperglycemia is undergoing evaluation. Contrast the likely islet morphology if her condition were Type 1 (autoimmune) versus Type 2 (metabolic) on microscopic examination.
back:
* Type 1: Insulitis (lymphocytic infiltrate) and profound β-cell depletion
* Type 2: Amyloid deposition (fibrosis in late stages) and focal/mild β-cell reduction

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: Explain the therapeutic rationale for using GLP-1 receptor agonists (Incretin mimetics) specifically in the management of Type 2 Diabetes.
back:
* Enhances glucose-dependent insulin secretion
* Suppresses inappropriately elevated post-prandial glucagon
* Delays gastric emptying and increases satiety (promoting weight loss)

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: According to current WHO diagnostic criteria, a confirmed diagnosis of Diabetes Mellitus requires a Glycated Hemoglobin (HbA1c) level of [___]% or higher.
back:
* 6.5%
* Must be confirmed with a second test unless symptomatic
* Reflects average glycemia over the previous 120 days

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: An older diabetic patient presents with nephrotic-range proteinuria. Biopsy reveals ovoid, PAS-positive, laminated mesangial nodules in the glomerular periphery. Applying these findings, determine the pathognomonic complication.
back:
* Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules
* Feature of Nodular Glomerulosclerosis
* Indicates advanced Diabetic Nephropathy

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: Explain why absolute insulin deficiency in Type 1 DM leads to Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA), whereas residual insulin in Type 2 DM typically results in Hyperosmolar Hyperglycemic State (HHS).
back:
* Type 1: Zero insulin allows unrestricted hepatic fatty acid oxidation to ketones
* Type 2: Residual portal insulin inhibits ketogenesis but permits severe hyperglycemia and osmotic dehydration

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: Contrast the insulin-glucose physiological loops during the "fasting state" between healthy individuals and those with long-standing Type 2 Diabetes.
back:
* Healthy: Low insulin allows basal gluconeogenesis to maintain euglycemia
* Type 2: Insulin resistance prevents inhibition of gluconeogenesis/glycogenolysis, resulting in fasting hyperglycemia

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: Identify the primary biochemical mediator responsible for neovascularization in proliferative diabetic retinopathy.
back:
* Vascular Endothelial Growth Factor (VEGF)
* Induced by retinal ischemia/hypoxia
* Leads to fragile new vessel formation and potential hemorrhage

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: The strongest genetic linkage for susceptibility to Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus (DM-I) is located within the [___] locus on chromosome 6.
back:
• HLA Class II genes
• Specifically HLA-DR3 and HLA-DR4 haplotypes
• Contributes up to 50% of the genetic susceptibility for DM-I development.

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: A 10-year-old child presents with a 2-week history of polyuria, weight loss, and fatigue. If a pancreatic biopsy were performed, identify the hallmark histopathological feature likely present in the islets.
back:
• Insulitis
• Characterized by a lymphocytic inflammatory infiltrate (primarily T-cells)
• Results in progressive autoimmune destruction of beta-cells.

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: Explain the role of insulin resistance in the liver during the pathogenesis of Type 2 Diabetes.
back:
• Failure to inhibit gluconeogenesis
• Unchecked hepatic glucose production occurs despite hyperglycemia
• Major contributor to elevated fasting blood glucose levels.

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: A 14-year-old lean male and a 55-year-old obese female both present with polyuria. Contrast the expected histological findings of their pancreatic islets if both are confirmed diabetics.
back:
• 14-year-old (DM-I): Islet atrophy, beta-cell depletion, and insulitis
• 55-year-old (DM-II): Amyloid deposition (amylin) within islets and mild beta-cell reduction.

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: Name the two specific adipokines that are typically reduced in obesity, thereby contributing to insulin resistance in Type 2 Diabetes.
back:
• Adiponectin (primary insulin sensitizer)
• Leptin (regulates energy balance)
• Low levels fail to suppress glucose production and enhance insulin sensitivity.

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: According to standard diagnostic criteria, a random plasma glucose concentration of [___] mg/dL or higher in a symptomatic patient is sufficient for a diagnosis of Diabetes Mellitus.
back:
• 200 mg/dL
• Must be accompanied by classic symptoms (polyuria, polydipsia, unexplained weight loss).

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: A long-term diabetic patient presents with decreased visual acuity and funduscopic evidence of neovascularization. Identify the molecular driver of this specific microvascular complication.
back:
• VEGF (Vascular Endothelial Growth Factor)
• Stimulated by retinal ischemia/hypoxia
• Leads to Proliferative Diabetic Retinopathy.

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: Describe the metabolic sequence in the liver that converts absolute insulin deficiency into systemic metabolic ketoacidosis.
back:
• 1. Absolute insulin lack activates hormone-sensitive lipase
• 2. Massive release of Free Fatty Acids (FFAs) to the liver
• 3. Hepatic oxidation of FFAs produces acetoacetic and beta-hydroxybutyric acids.

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: Contrast the diagnostic threshold of HbA1c for 'Prediabetes' versus 'Frank Diabetes Mellitus'.
back:
• Prediabetes: 5.7% to 6.4%
• Frank Diabetes: 6.5% or higher
• Reflects average glycemic control over the preceding 120 days.

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: Identify the pathognomonic renal lesion characterized by ovoid, PAS-positive glomerular hyaline masses in diabetic nephropathy.
back:
• Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules
• Also known as Nodular Glomerulosclerosis
• Results from chronic mesangial matrix expansion and microangiopathy.

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus is strongly linked to the [___] locus on chromosome 6, specifically alleles DR3 and DR4.
back:
• HLA (Human Leukocyte Antigen)
• Specifically MHC Class II molecules
• Key genetic differentiator from Type 2 Diabetes

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: A 12-year-old child presents with sudden weight loss, polyuria, and ketoacidosis. The primary pathophysiological mechanism involves [___].
back:
• Autoimmune destruction of pancreatic beta cells
• T-cell mediated (Type IV hypersensitivity)
• Results in an absolute insulin deficiency

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: Explain the diagnostic utility of C-peptide levels in distinguishing between Type 1 and Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus.
back:
• C-peptide is co-secreted with endogenous insulin
• Low/absent levels indicate Type 1 (beta-cell loss)
• High/normal levels suggest Type 2 (insulin resistance)

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: Contrast the genetic risk factors for Type 1 versus Type 2 Diabetes based on twin concordance and familial patterns.
back:
• Type 1: Moderate twin concordance; requires environmental trigger
• Type 2: Very high twin concordance (>90%)
• Type 2 has a much stronger genetic/familial basis

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: Identify the intestinal hormones responsible for the 'incretin effect' and their status in Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus.
back:
• GIP and GLP-1 hormones
• They stimulate insulin secretion post-feeding
• This effect is significantly blunted in T2D

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: The diagnostic threshold for fasting plasma glucose (FPG) to confirm Diabetes Mellitus is at or above [___] mg/dL.
back:
• 126 mg/dL
• Must be confirmed on two separate occasions
• Values 100–125 mg/dL indicate prediabetes

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: An obese 45-year-old female presents with velvety hyperpigmented patches on her neck (acanthosis nigricans). This finding is most commonly associated with [___].
back:
• Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus
• Severe insulin resistance
• Compensatory hyperinsulinemia

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: Explain the role of Advanced Glycation End Products (AGEs) in the development of diabetic microvascular complications.
back:
• AGEs bind RAGE on endothelium
• Induces ROS and TGF-beta (basement membrane thickening)
• AGEs cross-link Type IV collagen, trapping plasma proteins

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: Contrast the typical islet morphology seen in Type 1 vs Type 2 Diabetes after long-standing disease.
back:
• Type 1: Insulitis (lymphocytic infiltrate) and beta-cell depletion
• Type 2: Amyloid (amylin) deposition within islets
• Type 2: Fibrosis in late stages

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: Identify the primary insulin-independent glucose transporter used by pancreatic β-cells to monitor blood glucose levels.
back:
• GLUT-2 transporter
• Facilitates glucose entry into beta cells
• Triggers insulin synthesis and Ca-dependent release

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: The primary genetic susceptibility locus for Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus involves the [___] gene cluster on chromosome 6p21, specifically the DR3 and DR4 haplotypes.
back:
• HLA (Human Leukocyte Antigen) class II
• Accounts for 50% of genetic susceptibility
• Linked to failure of T-cell self-tolerance

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: A 12-year-old child presents with sudden weight loss, polyuria, and a fruity odor on his breath. Identify the likely diagnosis and the fundamental immune abnormality.
back:
• Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus (Stage 3)
• Failure of self-tolerance in T-cells
• Absolute insulin deficiency from beta-cell destruction

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: Explain the role of Free Fatty Acids (FFAs) in the induction of insulin resistance in Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus.
back:
• Overwhelm intracellular oxidation pathways
• Generate toxic intermediates (diacylglycerol)
• Attenuate insulin receptor substrate (IRS) signaling

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: A pancreatic biopsy shows 'insulitis' in Slide A and 'islet amyloid deposition' in Slide B. Contrast these findings by associating them with the correct DM type.
back:
• Slide A (Insulitis): Type 1 DM (T-cell infiltrates)
• Slide B (Amyloid): Type 2 DM
• Amyloid is composed of amylin (IAPP)

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: Name the intestinally-derived hormones responsible for the 'Incretin Effect' and their clinical relevance in DM-II therapy.
back:
• GIP and GLP-1 (Incretins)
• Promote insulin secretion following oral intake
• Targeted by DPP-4 inhibitors and GLP-1 agonists

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: According to standard criteria, a diagnosis of Diabetes Mellitus is confirmed if the Glycated Hemoglobin (HbA1c) level is equal to or greater than [___] percent.
back:
• 6.5%
• Reflects glycemic control over 120 days
• Not affected by daily glucose fluctuations

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: A 50-year-old obese patient with Type 2 DM presents with severe dehydration and a blood glucose of 800 mg/dL, but no ketones in the urine. Identify the acute complication.
back:
• Hyperosmolar Hyperglycemic State (HHS)
• Sustained osmotic diuresis leads to profound dehydration
• Relative insulin prevents ketogenesis

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: How does the 'Polyol Pathway' lead to diabetic cataracts in insulin-independent tissues like the lens?
back:
• Aldose reductase converts glucose to sorbitol
• Depletes NADPH and reduced glutathione (GSH)
• Sorbitol causes osmotic swelling and oxidative stress

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: Contrast the vascular distribution and primary outcomes of 'Macrovascular' versus 'Microvascular' complications in Diabetes.
back:
• Macrovascular: Large arteries; leads to MI and stroke
• Microvascular: Capillary basement membranes; leads to Retinopathy and Nephropathy
• Driven by Advanced Glycation End-products (AGEs)

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: List the three hallmark glomerular lesions found in Diabetic Nephropathy.
back:
• Capillary basement membrane (GBM) thickening
• Diffuse mesangial sclerosis
• Nodular glomerulosclerosis (Kimmelstiel-Wilson lesions)

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: The most common overall cause of Cushing syndrome is [___] administration of glucocorticoids.
back:
• Exogenous (iatrogenic)
• Results in bilateral adrenocortical atrophy
• Suppresses the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: A 35-year-old female presents with truncal obesity and purple striae. Labs reveal elevated 24-hour urinary free cortisol and a suppressed serum ACTH. Identify the likely anatomical source of the excess cortisol.
back:
• Adrenal cortex
• Diagnosis: ACTH-independent Cushing syndrome
• Causes: Adrenal adenoma or carcinoma

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: Explain the role of the High-Dose Dexamethasone Suppression Test (HDDST) in distinguishing endogenous causes of hypercortisolism.
back:
• Cushing Disease (Pituitary): Shows >50% cortisol suppression because the adenoma retains some feedback sensitivity.
• Ectopic ACTH: No suppression because the tumor (e.g., small cell lung cancer) is completely autonomous.

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: Contrast the serum ACTH levels and skin pigmentation findings in Cushing Disease versus primary adrenal Cushing syndrome.
back:
• Cushing Disease: High/Normal ACTH; hyperpigmentation present (due to MSH/POMC).
• Adrenal Cushing: Suppressed ACTH; no hyperpigmentation (atrophic pituitary).

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: Enumerate the three most common first-line screening tests used to confirm a diagnosis of hypercortisolism.
back:
• 24-hour urinary free cortisol
• Late-night salivary cortisol
• Overnight low-dose (1mg) dexamethasone suppression test

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: In the pituitary gland of patients with chronic hypercortisolism, normal granular basophilic cytoplasm is replaced by homogeneous keratin filaments, a feature known as [___] hyaline change.
back:
• Crooke hyaline change
• Occurs in ACTH-producing cells
• Result of high circulating glucocorticoid levels

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: A patient with small-cell lung carcinoma presents with hypokalemia, hypertension, and weight gain. Labs show extremely high ACTH and cortisol levels that fail to suppress with high-dose dexamethasone. What is the diagnosis?
back:
• Ectopic ACTH Syndrome
• Paraneoplastic manifestation
• Characterized by rapid clinical onset and severe hypercortisolism

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: Describe the mechanism by which the Low-Dose Dexamethasone Suppression Test (LDDST) screen produces a 'normal' result.
back:
• 1mg dexamethasone provides negative feedback to the pituitary.
• Suppresses pituitary ACTH release in healthy individuals.
• Leads to a drop in endogenous cortisol (<1.8 µg/dL).

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: Contrast the adrenal morphology found in Cushing Disease versus an adrenal cortical adenoma.
back:
• Cushing Disease: Bilateral diffuse or nodular cortical hyperplasia.
• Adrenal Adenoma: Solitary circumscribed yellow nodule with contralateral adrenal cortical atrophy.

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: Identify the rare clinical condition where hypercortisolism is absent but a pituitary mass grows rapidly after bilateral adrenalectomy.
back:
• Nelson Syndrome
• Loss of adrenal feedback on pre-existing corticotroph microadenoma
• Presents with mass effects and severe hyperpigmentation

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: The most common cause of endogenous Cushing syndrome, responsible for 60% to 70% of cases, is an ACTH-secreting [___].
back:
• Pituitary microadenoma
  • Known specifically as Cushing disease
  • More common in women and young adults

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: A 40-year-old female presents with moon facies, truncal obesity, and hypertension. Labs show elevated cortisol that suppresses with high-dose dexamethasone but not low-dose. Identify the underlying lesion.
back:
• ACTH-secreting pituitary adenoma (Cushing disease)
  • Pituitary tumors retain partial sensitivity to glucocorticoid feedback, unlike ectopic or adrenal sources.

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: Explain the role of the high-dose dexamethasone suppression test in the differential diagnosis of ACTH-dependent Cushing syndrome.
back:
• Distinguishes Pituitary source from Ectopic source.
  • Pituitary: Cortisol suppresses by >50%.
  • Ectopic: No suppression (autonomous secretion).

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: Contrast the adrenal gland morphology and plasma ACTH levels in Iatrogenic Cushing syndrome versus Cushing Disease.
back:
• Iatrogenic: Bilateral cortical atrophy; Low/suppressed ACTH.
  • Cushing Disease: Bilateral diffuse/nodular hyperplasia; Elevated ACTH.

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: Enumerate the two most common non-pituitary malignancies responsible for ectopic ACTH-dependent Cushing syndrome.
back:
• Small-cell carcinoma of the lung (most common)
  • Carcinoid tumors (lung, thymus, or pancreas)
  • Medullary thyroid carcinoma

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: In the initial screening for Cushing syndrome, the biochemical 'sine qua non' for an ACTH-independent cause is high serum cortisol and [___] serum ACTH.
back:
• Low or undetectable serum ACTH
  • Indicates primary adrenal pathology (adenoma or carcinoma) or exogenous steroid use.

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: A patient with suspected hypercortisolism exhibits high ACTH levels and failure to suppress cortisol on both low-dose and high-dose dexamethasone. What is the most likely diagnosis?
back:
• Ectopic ACTH secretion
  • Commonly associated with small-cell lung cancer.
  • Lacks feedback inhibition seen in pituitary adenomas.

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: How does an adrenal adenoma lead to hypercortisolism and what is the effect on the contralateral adrenal gland?
back:
• Adenoma secretes cortisol autonomously.
  • High cortisol suppresses pituitary ACTH via negative feedback.
  • Low ACTH causes atrophy of the contralateral gland.

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: Distinguish between the 24-hour urine free cortisol test and the late-night salivary cortisol test in screening for Cushing syndrome.
back:
• 24-hr Urine: Measures cumulative free cortisol excretion (increased).
  • Salivary: Detects loss of the normal diurnal rhythm (cortisol should be lowest at night).

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
coreConcept: Most Common Cause of Cushing Syndrome
front: Enumerate the most common cause of Cushing syndrome overall in clinical practice.
back:
• Exogenous (Iatrogenic) administration of glucocorticoids
  • Used for inflammatory or autoimmune disorders (e.g., RA, Asthma).

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: The most frequent overall cause of Cushing syndrome in clinical practice is the [___] administration of glucocorticoids.
back:
• Exogenous (Iatrogenic)
• Results in bilateral adrenocortical atrophy due to suppressed ACTH levels.

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: A 35-year-old female presents with buffalo hump, abdominal striae, and amenorrhea. Labs show elevated plasma ACTH which suppresses following high-dose dexamethasone. The most likely diagnosis is [___].
back:
• Cushing Disease
• Specifically refers to an ACTH-secreting pituitary microadenoma.

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: Explain the biological basis for the response to the High-Dose Dexamethasone Suppression Test (HDDST) in pituitary versus ectopic ACTH production.
back:
• Pituitary adenomas (Cushing Disease) retain partial sensitivity to negative feedback at high doses.
• Ectopic tumors (e.g., Small Cell Lung CA) are completely autonomous and fail to suppress.

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: Contrast the biochemical findings of primary adrenal Cushing syndrome (e.g., adenoma) with pituitary-derived Cushing disease regarding ACTH levels.
back:
• Adrenal Adenoma: Low ACTH (due to negative feedback from autonomous cortisol).
• Pituitary Adenoma: Elevated or inappropriately normal ACTH.

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: List the three standard initial screening investigations used to confirm a state of hypercortisolism.
back:
• 24-hour urinary free cortisol (increased).
• Late-night salivary cortisol (loss of diurnal rhythm).
• Low-dose dexamethasone suppression test (failure to suppress below 1.8 mcg/dL).

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: The most common non-pituitary malignant neoplasm responsible for the secretion of ectopic ACTH is [___].
back:
• Small-cell carcinoma of the lung
• Other sources include bronchial carcinoids and medullary thyroid carcinoma.

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: A patient with clinical Cushing syndrome presents with very high cortisol, virilization, and a large, necrotic adrenal mass (250g) on CT. This scenario is most characteristic of [___].
back:
• Adrenocortical carcinoma
• Distinguished from adenomas by larger size, necrosis, and tendency to secrete multiple steroid types (e.g., androgens).

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: Describe the mechanism of Nelson Syndrome in patients previously treated for Cushing disease.
back:
• Occurs after bilateral adrenalectomy.
• Loss of cortisol-mediated negative feedback causes rapid enlargement of a pre-existing pituitary microadenoma.
• Presents with mass effects and severe hyperpigmentation.

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: Distinguish the adrenal morphology found in Cushing Disease from that found in exogenous steroid use.
back:
• Cushing Disease: Bilateral diffuse or nodular cortical hyperplasia.
• Exogenous Use: Bilateral cortical atrophy (specifically zona fasciculata and reticularis).

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: Identify the common hormone precursor responsible for skin hyperpigmentation in ACTH-dependent Cushing syndrome.
back:
• Pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC)
• Cleavage of POMC produces both ACTH and Melanocyte-Stimulating Hormone (MSH).

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: The most common cause of Cushing syndrome overall is the administration of [___].
back:
• Exogenous glucocorticoids (Iatrogenic).
• Leads to bilateral adrenocortical atrophy due to suppression of endogenous ACTH.
• The zona glomerulosa is typically spared.

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: A 40-year-old female presents with moon facies, truncal obesity, and proximal muscle weakness. Laboratory testing reveals elevated urinary free cortisol and low serum ACTH. Identify the likely endogenous cause.
back:
• Primary adrenocortical neoplasm (Adenoma or Carcinoma).
• Classified as ACTH-independent Cushing syndrome.
• The contralateral adrenal gland will show atrophy.

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: Explain the role of the Low-dose Dexamethasone Suppression Test (LDDST) in the evaluation of suspected Cushing syndrome.
back:
• Used as an initial screening test to confirm hypercortisolism.
• Normal response: Suppression of cortisol to <1.8 μg/dL.
• Cushing syndrome: Failure to suppress cortisol regardless of the etiology.

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: Contrast the results of a High-Dose Dexamethasone Suppression Test (HDDST) in Cushing Disease versus Ectopic ACTH Syndrome.
back:
• Cushing Disease (Pituitary): Cortisol suppresses (usually >50% reduction).
• Ectopic ACTH (e.g., Small cell lung cancer): Cortisol fails to suppress.
• Pituitary adenomas retain some sensitivity to feedback, whereas ectopic tumors do not.

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: Enumerate the three first-line laboratory screening tests for diagnosing Cushing syndrome.
back:
• 24-hour urinary free cortisol (UFC).
• Late-night salivary cortisol level.
• Overnight low-dose dexamethasone suppression test (LDDST).

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: The characteristic accumulation of keratin intermediate filaments in the pituitary corticotrophs of patients with hypercortisolism is known as [___].
back:
• Crooke hyaline change.
• Represents a cellular reaction to high circulating glucocorticoid levels.
• Basophilic granules are replaced by homogeneous, pale material.

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: A patient with a lung mass presents with skin hyperpigmentation and severe hypokalemia. Lab shows very high ACTH levels and high cortisol that is not suppressed by high-dose dexamethasone. What is the diagnosis?
back:
• Ectopic ACTH Syndrome.
• Commonly caused by Small Cell Carcinoma of the lung.
• Hyperpigmentation is due to MSH-like activity in the ACTH precursor (POMC).

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: How do serum ACTH levels differentiate the primary types of endogenous Cushing syndrome?
back:
• Low ACTH: Indicates ACTH-independent causes (Adrenal adenoma/carcinoma).
• High ACTH: Indicates ACTH-dependent causes (Pituitary adenoma or Ectopic ACTH).

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: Distinguish the adrenal gland morphology between Cushing Disease and Ectopic ACTH Syndrome.
back:
• Cushing Disease: Bilateral diffuse cortical hyperplasia (glands up to 30g).
• Ectopic ACTH: Rapid progression often results in less prominent hyperplasia or weight gain, but glands are still bilaterally enlarged.

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: Name the specific genetic mutation most commonly associated with Primary Pigmented Nodular Adrenocortical Disease (PPNAD) and Carney Complex.
back:
• PRKAR1A mutation.
• Encodes the regulatory subunit of protein kinase A.
• Results in increased cAMP signaling and autonomous cortisol secretion.

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: The most common cause of Cushing syndrome overall is [___].
back:
• Exogenous glucocorticoid administration (Iatrogenic).
• Results in suppressed ACTH and bilateral adrenal atrophy.

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: A 35-year-old female presents with moon facies, truncal obesity, and abdominal striae. Lab results show undetectable serum ACTH and elevated 24-hour urinary free cortisol. Identify the likely source of hypercortisolism.
back:
• ACTH-independent Cushing syndrome.
• Likely a Primary Adrenal Neoplasm (Adenoma or Carcinoma).

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: Explain the mechanism of the high-dose dexamethasone suppression test (HDDST) in differentiating pituitary vs. ectopic ACTH sources.
back:
• Pituitary adenomas (Cushing Disease) retain partial sensitivity to feedback, suppressing cortisol levels by >50%.
• Ectopic tumors (e.g., Small Cell Lung Cancer) are fully autonomous and show no suppression.

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: Contrast the expected biochemical findings in Cushing Disease vs. Ectopic ACTH syndrome regarding CRH stimulation.
back:
• Cushing Disease: Responds to exogenous CRH with increased ACTH and cortisol.
• Ectopic ACTH: No response to CRH stimulation (autonomous secretion).

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: List the three first-line screening tests used to confirm hypercortisolism.
back:
• 24-hour urinary free cortisol.
• Late-night salivary cortisol.
• Low-dose dexamethasone suppression test (LDDST).

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: In the laboratory diagnosis of hypercortisolism, the diagnostic cut-off for a positive 1mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test is a cortisol level > [___] µg/dL.
back:
• 1.8 µg/dL (50 nmol/L).
• Failure to suppress indicates autonomous cortisol production.

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: A heavy smoker presents with rapid-onset hypercortisolism, severe hypokalemia, and hyperpigmentation. Identify the most probable underlying cause.
back:
• Ectopic ACTH secretion.
• Usually secondary to Small Cell Lung Carcinoma.

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: Explain why serum ACTH measurement is the essential second step after confirming hypercortisolism.
back:
• Distinguishes ACTH-dependent causes (Pituitary/Ectopic) from ACTH-independent causes (Adrenal tumor/Exogenous steroids).
• High ACTH (>20 pg/mL) indicates dependent; Low ACTH (<5 pg/mL) indicates independent.

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: Contrast the gross adrenal morphology found in Cushing Disease versus iatrogenic Cushing syndrome.
back:
• Cushing Disease: Bilateral diffuse or nodular hyperplasia.
• Iatrogenic: Bilateral adrenocortical atrophy.

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: Identify the rare cause of Cushing syndrome associated with germline mutations in PRKAR1A and pigmented adrenal nodules.
back:
• Primary Pigmented Nodular Adrenocortical Disease (PPNAD).
• Often a component of Carney Complex.

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: The most common cause of Cushing syndrome overall is [___] administration of glucocorticoids.
back:
• Exogenous (iatrogenic) glucocorticoids
• Results in bilateral adrenocortical atrophy
• Feedback inhibition of the pituitary-adrenal axis

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: A 35-year-old female presents with moon facies, truncal obesity, and purple striae. Labs show elevated serum ACTH and suppression of cortisol with high-dose dexamethasone. What is the most likely diagnosis?
back:
• Cushing Disease
• Caused by an ACTH-secreting pituitary microadenoma
• Leads to bilateral diffuse or nodular adrenal hyperplasia

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: Explain the role of Pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC) in the hyperpigmentation seen in ACTH-dependent Cushing syndrome.
back:
• POMC is the precursor for both ACTH and Melanocyte-Stimulating Hormone (MSH)
• Pituitary hypersecretion leads to excess MSH derivatives
• These stimulate melanocytes, causing skin darkening

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: Contrast the biochemical response to high-dose dexamethasone in a patient with a pituitary adenoma versus one with ectopic ACTH-secreting small cell lung carcinoma.
back:
• Pituitary Adenoma: Cortisol levels suppress as tumor cells retain some feedback sensitivity
• Ectopic ACTH: Cortisol levels remain elevated as non-pituitary tumors are completely resistant to feedback

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: Identify the primary screening tests used to confirm a diagnosis of hypercortisolism.
back:
• 24-hour urinary free-cortisol (increased)
• Late-night salivary cortisol (loss of diurnal rhythm)
• Low-dose dexamethasone suppression test

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: In Cushing syndrome caused by primary adrenal neoplasms, serum ACTH levels are [___].
back:
• Low or undetectable
• Due to strong feedback inhibition of the pituitary by autonomous cortisol production

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: A patient with persistent hypertension and weight gain has elevated urinary cortisol, low serum ACTH, and no suppression on high-dose dexamethasone. What is the underlying cause?
back:
• Primary Adrenal Neoplasm
• Adrenocortical adenoma or carcinoma
• Characterized by autonomous cortisol production

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: Describe the cellular mechanism behind 'Crooke hyaline change' observed in the anterior pituitary.
back:
• Result of chronic high glucocorticoid levels
• Accumulation of intermediate keratin filaments in the cytoplasm
• Normal granular basophilic cytoplasm becomes homogeneous and pale

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: Contrast the macroscopic adrenal findings in Cushing disease versus iatrogenic Cushing syndrome.
back:
• Cushing Disease: Bilateral diffuse or nodular cortical hyperplasia
• Iatrogenic: Bilateral cortical atrophy (zona fasciculata and reticularis)

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: Which gene mutation is most frequently associated with ACTH-independent bilateral macronodular adrenal hyperplasia (BMAH)?
back:
• ARMC5 mutation
• Encodes a tumor suppressor protein
• Involved in 50% of sporadic BMAH cases

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: The most common overall cause of Cushing syndrome in modern medical practice is the [___] administration of glucocorticoids.
back:
• Exogenous (Iatrogenic)
• Results in suppressed ACTH levels
• Causes bilateral adrenocortical atrophy

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: A 35-year-old female with moon facies and striae has elevated ACTH levels. Her urinary cortisol suppresses by 65% following high-dose dexamethasone. The most likely diagnosis is [___].
back:
• Cushing Disease
• Specifically caused by an ACTH-secreting pituitary microadenoma
• Adrenals show bilateral diffuse hyperplasia

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: Explain why the high-dose dexamethasone suppression test is used to differentiate pituitary adenomas from ectopic ACTH-secreting tumors.
back:
• Pituitary adenomas retain partial sensitivity to negative feedback
• Ectopic tumors (e.g., small cell lung cancer) are fully autonomous
• High doses suppress pituitary ACTH but fail to suppress ectopic ACTH

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: Contrast the biochemical serum ACTH findings in primary adrenal cortical adenoma versus ectopic ACTH syndrome.
back:
• Adrenal Adenoma: ACTH is low/suppressed due to feedback inhibition
• Ectopic ACTH: ACTH is markedly elevated/high
• Both show high serum cortisol

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: Identify the biochemical 'sine qua non' laboratory finding required to diagnose ACTH-independent Cushing syndrome.
back:
• Elevated serum cortisol
• Low/suppressed serum ACTH levels
• Indicates the source is the adrenal gland itself or exogenous

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: The initial screening test used to confirm hypercortisolism, measuring cortisol that is not bound to corticosteroid-binding globulin, is [___].
back:
• 24-hour urine free cortisol
• Measures bioactive cortisol levels
• Loss of normal diurnal rhythm is also characteristic

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: A 60-year-old male smoker presents with rapid-onset hypercortisolism and hyperpigmentation. ACTH levels are 400 pg/mL (Normal < 60) and do not suppress with high-dose dexamethasone. This suggests [___].
back:
• Ectopic ACTH secretion
• Most commonly Small Cell Carcinoma of the Lung
• Hyperpigmentation is due to pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC) elevation

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: Explain the role of Pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC) in the development of hyperpigmentation in primary Addison disease and ACTH-dependent Cushing.
back:
• POMC is a common precursor for ACTH and MSH
• High ACTH production involves increased POMC
• MSH activity stimulates melanocytes causing skin darkening

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: Contrast the adrenal morphology seen in Cushing disease with that of iatrogenic (steroid-induced) Cushing syndrome.
back:
• Cushing Disease: Bilateral diffuse or nodular cortical hyperplasia
• Iatrogenic: Bilateral cortical atrophy (excluding zona glomerulosa)
• Both exhibit high circulating glucocorticoid effects

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: Identify the characteristic histologic pituitary change involving keratin filament accumulation in basophils in response to high cortisol levels.
back:
• Crooke hyaline change
• Normal granular basophilic cytoplasm becomes homogeneous/pale
• Occurs in both endogenous and exogenous hypercortisolism

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
coreConcept: ACTH suppression in primary adrenal disease
front: The biochemical sine qua non of ACTH-independent Cushing syndrome is elevated serum cortisol accompanied by [___] levels of ACTH.
back:
• Suppressed or undetectable plasma ACTH levels.
• Results from negative feedback inhibition of the anterior pituitary by excess cortisol.

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: A 45-year-old female presents with central obesity, moon facies, and abdominal striae. Lab findings show elevated cortisol that suppresses after high-dose dexamethasone. The underlying diagnosis is [___].
back:
• Cushing disease.
• Specifically caused by an ACTH-secreting pituitary microadenoma.
• Leads to bilateral diffuse adrenal cortical hyperplasia.

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: Explain the role of the CRH stimulation test in distinguishing pituitary Cushing disease from ectopic ACTH secretion.
back:
• Pituitary Disease: Shows an exaggerated rise in ACTH and cortisol.
• Ectopic ACTH: Shows no response (ACTH and cortisol remain unchanged) as the tumor focus is autonomous.

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: Contrast the response to high-dose dexamethasone suppression between a patient with a cortisol-secreting adrenal adenoma and a patient with a pituitary microadenoma.
back:
• Pituitary Microadenoma: Cortisol levels suppress (retains some sensitivity).
• Adrenal Adenoma: Cortisol fails to suppress (secretion is completely autonomous and ACTH is already low).

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: List the three first-line screening tests used to confirm hypercortisolism during the initial workup of Cushing syndrome.
back:
• 24-hour urine free cortisol.
• Late-night salivary cortisol (evaluates loss of diurnal rhythm).
• Low-dose dexamethasone suppression test (LDDST).

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: The characteristic histopathologic change in the pituitary of Cushing syndrome patients, where granular basophilic cytoplasm is replaced by homogeneous keratin filaments, is [___].
back:
• Crooke hyaline change.
• Result of high circulating levels of endogenous or exogenous glucocorticoids acting on ACTH-producing cells.

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: A 55-year-old male smoker presents with rapid-onset hypertension, weight loss, and hyperpigmentation. Labs show very high ACTH that fails to suppress with high-dose dexamethasone. Diagnosis: [___].
back:
• Ectopic ACTH syndrome.
• Most commonly caused by small-cell carcinoma of the lung.
• Hyperpigmentation is due to MSH activity in POMC-derived ACTH precursors.

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: How does exogenous glucocorticoid administration lead to the unique finding of bilateral adrenal cortical atrophy?
back:
• Excess exogenous steroids suppress CRH and ACTH via negative feedback.
• Prolonged lack of ACTH leads to atrophy of the zona fasciculata and zona reticularis.

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: Contrast the adrenal gland morphology in Cushing disease with that found in primary adrenocortical neoplasms.
back:
• Cushing Disease: Bilateral diffuse or nodular hyperplasia due to excess ACTH.
• Adrenocortical Neoplasms: Unilateral tumor (adenoma/carcinoma) with atrophy of the contralateral gland and adjacent cortex.

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: Identify the most common cause of Cushing syndrome overall and its effect on endogenous ACTH levels.
back:
• Iatrogenic (exogenous glucocorticoid administration).
• Causes low (suppressed) endogenous ACTH levels due to pituitary feedback inhibition.

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: The most common cause of endogenous Cushing syndrome is a/an [___] pituitary adenoma, a condition specifically referred to as Cushing disease.
back:
• ACTH-secreting
• Accounts for 60–70% of endogenous cases
• Leads to bilateral adrenal cortical hyperplasia

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: A 45-year-old heavy smoker presents with truncal obesity, hyperpigmentation, and a lung mass. Labs show extremely high ACTH and failure to suppress cortisol with high-dose dexamethasone. Identify the most likely cause.
back:
• Ectopic ACTH Syndrome
• Commonly caused by Small Cell Lung Carcinoma
• ACTH levels are typically higher than in pituitary causes

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: Explain the role of the 24-hour urinary free cortisol test in the initial evaluation of suspected hypercortisolism.
back:
• Measures unbound, metabolically active cortisol
• Acts as a primary screening tool
• High sensitivity for confirming hypercortisolism status

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: Contrast the response of pituitary Cushing Disease versus an Adrenal Adenoma during a High-Dose Dexamethasone Suppression Test (HDDST).
back:
• Cushing Disease: Partial suppression of ACTH/cortisol occurs
• Adrenal Adenoma: No suppression occurs
• Adrenal tumors function autonomously, independent of ACTH feedback

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: Enumerate the ACTH-independent causes of endogenous Cushing syndrome.
back:
• Adrenocortical adenoma
• Adrenocortical carcinoma
• Bilateral macronodular adrenal hyperplasia
• Primary pigmented nodular adrenocortical disease

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: The biochemical hallmark used to differentiate ACTH-dependent from ACTH-independent Cushing syndrome is the measurement of serum [___].
back:
• ACTH (Adrenocorticotropic Hormone)
• High/Normal ACTH: Dependent (Pituitary/Ectopic)
• Low/Suppressed ACTH: Independent (Adrenal source)

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: A patient with long-term steroid use for asthma presents with a 'moon facies' and low serum ACTH. Describe the expected morphologic state of their adrenal glands.
back:
• Bilateral adrenal cortical atrophy
• Caused by chronic suppression of the pituitary-adrenal axis
• Zona glomerulosa is usually spared

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: Explain why hyperpigmentation is a clinical feature of ACTH-dependent Cushing syndrome but not ACTH-independent cases.
back:
• High ACTH (from POMC) has MSH-like activity
• Directly stimulates skin melanocytes
• Adrenal tumors suppress ACTH production via feedback

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: Contrast the diagnostic objectives of the Low-Dose Dexamethasone Suppression Test (LDDST) and the High-Dose Dexamethasone Suppression Test (HDDST).
back:
• LDDST: Screening to confirm hypercortisolism (Cushing Syndrome presence)
• HDDST: Differentiation to identify source (Pituitary vs. Ectopic/Adrenal)

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: List the three first-line screening investigations for a patient suspected of having Cushing syndrome.
back:
• 24-hour urinary free cortisol
• Late-night salivary cortisol
• Low-dose dexamethasone suppression test (LDDST)

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: The most common endogenous cause of Cushing syndrome, accounting for approximately 70% of cases, is an ACTH-secreting [___].
back:
• Pituitary adenoma (specifically called Cushing Disease).
• Most often a microadenoma (<10 mm).
• Leads to bilateral adrenal cortical hyperplasia.

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: A 40-year-old female presents with moon facies, purple striae, and hypertension. Lab tests show elevated cortisol and undetectable serum ACTH. What is the most likely underlying cause?
back:
• ACTH-independent Cushing Syndrome.
• Primary adrenal neoplasm (adenoma or carcinoma).
• Exogenous glucocorticoid intake must also be ruled out.

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: Explain the role of the 1 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test (LDDST) in the initial workup of hypercortisolism.
back:
• Acts as a screening test to confirm Cushing Syndrome.
• Normal response: Suppression of cortisol to <1.8 µg/dL.
• Cushing response: Failure of dexamethasone to suppress cortisol production.

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: Contrast the response of pituitary Cushing disease vs. ectopic ACTH syndrome during a High-Dose Dexamethasone Suppression Test (HDDST).
back:
• Cushing Disease: Cortisol suppresses by >50% (pituitary cells remain somewhat sensitive).
• Ectopic ACTH: No suppression (tumor cells function autonomously).

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: Enumerate the three validated first-line screening tests for Cushing syndrome.
back:
• 24-hour urinary free cortisol (UFC).
• Late-night salivary cortisol.
• Low-dose (1 mg) overnight dexamethasone suppression test (LDDST).

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: In patients with ACTH-dependent Cushing syndrome, a CrH stimulation test that results in a significant rise in ACTH and cortisol indicates [___] as the source.
back:
• Pituitary source (Cushing Disease).
• Ectopic sources (like small cell lung cancer) typically do not respond to CrH stimulation.

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: A patient with a history of bilateral adrenalectomy for Cushing disease presents with sudden visual field defects and intense skin hyperpigmentation. Identify the condition.
back:
• Nelson Syndrome.
• Caused by the loss of inhibitory cortisol feedback, leading to rapid expansion of a pre-existing pituitary microadenoma.

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: How does the morphology of the adrenal glands differ between iatrogenic Cushing syndrome and Cushing disease?
back:
• Iatrogenic: Bilateral cortical atrophy (due to suppression of endogenous ACTH).
• Cushing Disease: Bilateral diffuse or nodular cortical hyperplasia (due to excessive ACTH stimulation).

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: Contrast 'Cushing Syndrome' and 'Cushing Disease' based on their definitions.
back:
• Cushing Syndrome: Any condition causing chronic hypercortisolism.
• Cushing Disease: A specific subtype caused by a pituitary ACTH-secreting adenoma.

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: Name the most common non-endocrine malignancy associated with ectopic ACTH secretion.
back:
• Small cell carcinoma of the lung.
• Others include bronchial carcinoids and medullary thyroid carcinoma.
• Usually associated with rapid onset and cachexia.

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: The most common overall cause of Cushing syndrome is [___].
back:
• Iatrogenic administration of exogenous glucocorticoids.
• Results in bilateral adrenocortical atrophy due to ACTH suppression.
• Zona glomerulosa is typically spared.

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: A 50-year-old male smoker with a lung mass presents with moon facies and hypertension. Laboratory testing reveals very high ACTH levels that are not suppressed by high-dose dexamethasone. Identify the pathophysiology.
back:
• Ectopic ACTH secretion.
• Most commonly caused by Small-Cell Carcinoma of the lung.
• Leads to bilateral adrenocortical diffuse hyperplasia.

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: Explain the role of the 'diurnal rhythm' in the laboratory diagnosis of Cushing syndrome.
back:
• Normal individuals show cortisol peaks in the morning and troughs at night.
• Cushing syndrome is characterized by a loss of this diurnal pattern.
• Elevated late-night salivary or serum cortisol is a primary screening finding.

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: Contrast the serum ACTH levels found in Cushing Disease versus those found in an Adrenocortical Adenoma.
back:
• Cushing Disease (Pituitary): Elevated (ACTH-dependent).
• Adrenocortical Adenoma: Low/Undetectable (ACTH-independent).
• High cortisol in tumors causes feedback inhibition of the pituitary.

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: List the three primary endogenous causes of Cushing syndrome in order of frequency.
back:
• ACTH-secreting pituitary adenoma (Cushing Disease; ~70%).
• Primary adrenal neoplasms (Adenoma or Carcinoma; ~15-20%).
• Ectopic ACTH secretion by non-pituitary tumors (~5-10%).

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: The biochemical 'sine qua non' of ACTH-independent Cushing syndrome is the combination of elevated [___] and low [___].
back:
• Elevated: Serum Cortisol.
• Low: Serum ACTH.
• This pattern indicates a primary adrenal source or exogenous intake.

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: A patient presents with hypercortisolism. Low-dose dexamethasone fails to suppress cortisol, but high-dose dexamethasone results in a 50% reduction of urinary steroids. What is the most likely diagnosis?
back:
• Cushing Disease (ACTH-secreting pituitary adenoma).
• High-dose dexamethasone is sufficient to inhibit ACTH release from pituitary corticotrophs.
• Ectopic ACTH and adrenal tumors do not suppress.

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: How do inactivating mutations in the PRKAR1A gene contribute to the development of Cushing syndrome?
back:
• Causes Carney Complex or Primary Pigmented Nodular Adrenocortical Disease (PPNAD).
• Increases intracellular cAMP signaling.
• Results in ACTH-independent micronodular cortical hyperplasia.

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: Contrast the pituitary morphology in Cushing Disease versus iatrogenic Cushing syndrome.
back:
• Cushing Disease: ACTH-secreting microadenoma (corticotroph cells).
• Iatrogenic/Tumor source: Crooke Hyaline Change (replacement of granular cytoplasm with keratin filaments).
• Crooke change results from high cortisol feedback.

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: Identify the primary screening test used to confirm integrated 24-hour cortisol hyperproduction.
back:
• 24-hour Urinary Free Cortisol (UFC).
• Demonstrates increased total cortisol excretion.
• Must be confirmed with dexamethasone suppression or midnight cortisol testing.

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: The primary enzyme serving as the 'glucose sensor' in pancreatic beta cells, whose mutation results in MODY2, is [___].
back:
• Glucokinase (GCK)
• Catalyzes the rate-limiting step of glucose metabolism
• Mutations raise the threshold for insulin secretion

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: A 10-year-old child presents with polydipsia, polyuria, and sudden weight loss. Lab tests show autoantibodies to glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD). Identify the specific etiological category of this condition.
back:
• Type 1A Diabetes Mellitus
• Characterized by autoimmune destruction of beta cells
• Leads to absolute insulin deficiency

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: Explain the role of free fatty acids (FFAs) in the pathogenesis of insulin resistance in Type 2 Diabetes.
back:
• Excess FFAs overwhelm fatty acid oxidation pathways
• Intracellular metabolites (DAG, ceramides) accumulate
• These toxic lipids inhibit insulin receptor signaling and GLUT-4 translocation

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: Contrast Type 1 and Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus regarding the presence of HLA association and pancreatic islet pathology.
back:
• Type 1: Strong HLA-DR3/DR4 linkage; presents with 'Insulitis' (T-cell infiltrates)
• Type 2: No HLA linkage; presents with Amyloid (Amylin) deposition in islets

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: Name three specific endocrinopathies that cause secondary diabetes by secreting hormones that oppose insulin action.
back:
