• Acromegaly (Growth Hormone)
• Cushing Syndrome (Cortisol)
• Pheochromocytoma (Epinephrine/Catecholamines)
• Hyperthyroidism (Thyroid hormone)

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: According to the American Diabetes Association, the diagnostic threshold for glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) to confirm frank Diabetes Mellitus is [___].
back:
• 6.5% or higher
• Reflects glycemic control over 120 days
• Must be repeated for confirmation if asymptomatic

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: A 30-year-old female develops hyperglycemia for the first time during her second trimester of pregnancy. Identify the classification and the long-term risk for the mother.
back:
• Gestational Diabetes Mellitus (GDM)
• High risk of developing overt Type 2 DM within 10-20 years
• Associated with fetal macrosomia

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: Describe the mechanism of 'Pancreatogenic' (Type 3c) Diabetes in the context of chronic pancreatitis.
back:
• Diffuse destruction of the exocrine pancreas secondary to inflammation
• Secondary loss of both beta cells (insulin) and alpha cells (glucagon)
• High risk of 'brittle' diabetes with frequent hypoglycemia

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: Contrast the metabolic features of Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA) typically seen in Type 1 DM with Hyperosmolar Hyperglycemic State (HHS) in Type 2 DM.
back:
• DKA: Severe ketosis, acidosis, moderate hyperglycemia, Kussmaul breathing
• HHS: Minimal ketosis, severe dehydration, profound hyperglycemia (>600 mg/dL)

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: Define 'Prediabetes' based on fasting plasma glucose levels.
back:
• Fasting glucose between 100 and 125 mg/dL
• Known as 'Impaired Fasting Glucose'
• Significant risk factor for cardiovascular disease and Type 2 DM

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: The most frequent cause of Cushing syndrome in clinical practice overall is the [___] administration of glucocorticoids.
back:
• Exogenous (Iatrogenic)
• Causes bilateral adrenal cortical atrophy
• Suppresses endogenous ACTH production

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: A 45-year-old female presents with truncal obesity and moon facies. Labs reveal elevated serum cortisol and high ACTH. Cortisol levels suppress by 60% following a high-dose dexamethasone test. Identify the most likely diagnosis.
back:
• Cushing disease
• Caused by an ACTH-secreting pituitary microadenoma
• Most common cause of endogenous hypercortisolism

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: Explain the diagnostic significance of measuring serum ACTH levels in a patient with confirmed hypercortisolism.
back:
• Distinguishes ACTH-dependent from independent causes
• Low/Undetectable ACTH: Primary adrenal neoplasm (adenoma/carcinoma)
• High/Normal ACTH: Pituitary adenoma or ectopic source (e.g., lung cancer)

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: A 55-year-old male smoker presents with rapid-onset Cushingoid features, hypokalemia, and hyperpigmentation. Serum ACTH is markedly elevated and fails to suppress with high-dose dexamethasone. What is the likely underlying pathology?
back:
• Ectopic ACTH syndrome
• Most commonly caused by small-cell carcinoma of the lung
• Hyperpigmentation results from elevated POMC/MSH levels

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: Enumerate three first-line screening investigations used to establish a diagnosis of hypercortisolism.
back:
• 24-hour urinary free cortisol concentration
• Late-night salivary cortisol level
• Low-dose dexamethasone suppression test (LDDST)

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: In ACTH-independent Cushing syndrome caused by an adrenal adenoma, the adjacent and contralateral adrenal cortex typically show [___].
back:
• Cortical atrophy
• Caused by feedback inhibition of endogenous ACTH
• Specifically affects zona fasciculata and reticularis

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: A patient presents with hypercortisolism and multiple pigmented skin lesions. Genetic testing identifies a mutation in the PRKAR1A gene. Identify the adrenal cause of the Cushing syndrome.
back:
• Primary pigmented nodular adrenocortical disease (PPNAD)
• Component of the Carney Complex
• Form of ACTH-independent micronodular hyperplasia

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: Explain the biological mechanism by which Bilateral Macronodular Adrenal Hyperplasia (BMAH) causes ACTH-independent Cushing syndrome.
back:
• Ectopic expression of non-ACTH receptors (e.g., GIP, LH, or ADH receptors)
• Cortisol secretion is stimulated by non-pituitary hormones
• Frequently associated with germline ARMC5 mutations

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: Contrast the biochemical utility of the low-dose versus high-dose dexamethasone suppression tests.
back:
• Low-dose: Confirms presence of hypercortisolism (screening)
• High-dose: Differentiates pituitary source (Cushing disease) from ectopic ACTH syndrome
• Cushing disease suppresses with high-dose; Ectopic does not

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: Which characteristic morphologic change is seen in the non-neoplastic pituitary of a patient with chronic Cushing syndrome of any cause?
back:
• Crooke hyaline change
• Accumulation of intermediate keratin filaments in corticotrophs
• Cytoplasm becomes homogeneous and pale

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: Diabetes caused by primary destruction of the exocrine pancreas (e.g., in cystic fibrosis, chronic pancreatitis, or hemochromatosis) is specifically classified as [___] diabetes.
back:
• Type 3c (Pancreatogenic) diabetes.
• Results from loss of islet mass secondary to exocrine tissue damage.

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: A 16-year-old non-obese male presents with mild, asymptomatic hyperglycemia. Genetic testing reveals a mutation in the Glucokinase (GCK) gene. What is the diagnosis?
back:
• MODY 2 (Maturity-Onset Diabetes of the Young, Type 2).
• This is a monogenic form of diabetes affecting beta-cell function without autoimmunity.

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: Explain how the two fundamental metabolic defects in Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus interact to produce clinical disease.
back:
• Insulin resistance: Peripheral tissues (muscle, liver, fat) fail to respond to insulin.
• Beta-cell dysfunction: Compensatory hyperinsulinemia eventually fails, leading to relative insulin deficiency.

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: Contrast Type 1 and Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus regarding the presence of islet autoantibodies and the primary genetic association style.
back:
• Type 1: Positive for autoantibodies (anti-insulin, anti-GAD); linked to HLA-DR3/DR4.
• Type 2: Negative for autoantibodies; linked to multiple polygenic susceptibility loci.

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: Identify three specific endocrinopathies that cause secondary diabetes by secreting hormones that oppose insulin action.
back:
• Acromegaly (Growth Hormone).
• Cushing syndrome (Cortisol).
• Pheochromocytoma (Catecholamines).
• Glucagonoma (Glucagon).

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: Neonatal diabetes, presenting within the first 6 months of life, is frequently caused by activating mutations in the [___] and ABCC8 genes.
back:
• KCNJ11 (encoding the Kir6.2 subunit of the ATP-sensitive K+ channel).
• This represents a monogenic defect in beta-cell function.

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: A previously euglycemic woman at 26 weeks gestation develops impaired glucose tolerance. What is the classification and the long-term risk for the mother?
back:
• Gestational Diabetes Mellitus (GDM).
• Increased risk of developing overt Type 2 DM within 10 to 20 years postpartum.

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: Describe the primary mechanism of beta-cell destruction in Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus.
back:
• T-cell mediated autoimmune attack.
• Involves CD8+ cytotoxic T cells and CD4+ Th1 cells secreting cytokines (IFN-gamma, TNF) that injure islets.

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: Contrast the etiological basis of 'Immune-mediated' versus 'Idiopathic' Type 1 Diabetes.
back:
• Immune-mediated: Evidence of autoimmune markers (majority).
• Idiopathic: Absolute insulin deficiency and permanent ketosis-prone state without detectable autoantibodies (minority).

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: Name a specific class of drugs used in HIV therapy and a class used for inflammation that are high-yield causes of drug-induced diabetes.
back:
• Protease inhibitors (HIV).
• Glucocorticoids (Inflammation/Immunosuppression).
• Both interfere with insulin sensitivity and glucose homeostasis.

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: Diabetes resulting from an absolute deficiency of insulin caused by autoimmune ̠-cell destruction is classified as [___].
back:
* Type 1 Diabetes (T1D)
* Characterized by pancreatic ̠-cell destruction
* Usually results in absolute insulin deficiency and susceptibility to ketoacidosis.

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: A 45-year-old obese male presents with a fasting glucose of 130 mg/dL. This classification of diabetes is caused by [___].
back:
* Type 2 Diabetes (T2D)
* Pathophysiology: Peripheral resistance to insulin action
* Secretory response by ̠-cells is inadequate (relative insulin deficiency).

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: How does exocrine pancreatic disease, such as chronic pancreatitis or cystic fibrosis, lead to the etiological classification of diabetes?
back:
* Classified as "Pancreatogenic" (Type 3C) Diabetes
* Secondary to direct destruction of islet cells by exocrine tissue damage
* Results in acquired insulin deficiency.

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: Contrast the typical age of onset and body habitus between the etiological categories of Type 1 and Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus.
back:
* T1D: Usually childhood/adolescence; normal weight or weight loss preceding diagnosis
* T2D: Usually adult-onset; vast majority (80%) are obese.

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: Identify the etiological category of diabetes characterized by primary genetic defects in ̠-cell function that often mimics Type 2 DM in younger, non-obese patients.
back:
* Maturity-onset diabetes of the young (MODY)
* Caused by germline loss-of-function mutations (e.g., GCK, HNF1A)
* Autosomal dominant inheritance pattern.

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: Glucose intolerance first recognized during pregnancy that typically increases the long-term risk for Type 2 DM is defined as [___].
back:
* Gestational Diabetes Mellitus (GDM)
* Caused by pregnancy-induced insulin resistance exceeding ̠-cell compensation
* Typically resolves following delivery.

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: A patient with Cushing syndrome or Acromegaly develops hyperglycemia. This etiological classification is known as [___].
back:
* Secondary Diabetes (Endocrinopathies)
* Excess hormones (cortisol, growth hormone) oppose insulin action
* Leads to impaired glucose tolerance.

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: Explain the role of the Glucokinase (GCK) gene in the pathogenesis of MODY2.
back:
* GCK serves as the "glucose sensor" in ̠-cells
* Mutations raise the threshold for glucose-stimulated insulin secretion
* Results in stable, mild fasting hyperglycemia.

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: Contrast the role of HLA linkage in the etiological risk for Type 1 versus Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus.
back:
* T1D: Strong linkage to MHC Class II (HLA-DR3/DR4)
* T2D: No HLA linkage; associated with candidate genes like TCF7L2 and obesity-related loci.

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: Name three specific infections recognized by the WHO as rare causes of secondary diabetes mellitus.
back:
* Coxsackie B virus
* Cytomegalovirus (CMV)
* Congenital rubella
* These cause islet cell damage and subsequent hyperglycemia.

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus is primarily classified into immune-mediated and [___] subtypes, both characterized by an absolute deficiency of insulin.
back:
• Idiopathic (Type 1B)
• Involves destruction of pancreatic ̡-cells
• Absence of identifiable autoantibodies
• Strongly associated with Asian and African heritage.

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: A 45-year-old obese male presents with hyperglycemia and hypertension. His C-peptide levels are initially elevated. What is the etiological pathophysiology?
back:
• Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus
• Peripheral insulin resistance in muscle and adipose
• Compensatory ̡-cell hyperinsulinemia (early stage)
• Eventual relative insulin deficiency.

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: Explain the etiological mechanism by which Cushing syndrome or Acromegaly induces secondary Diabetes Mellitus.
back:
• Endocrinopathy-induced DM
• Excess Cortisol/GH promotes gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis
• Hormones act as insulin antagonists
• Increases peripheral insulin resistance.

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: Contrast Maturity-Onset Diabetes of the Young (MODY) with Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus regarding their primary etiological driver.
back:
• MODY: Monogenic defect in ̡-cell function (e.g., HNF-1̱, GCK)
• Type 2 DM: Complex polygenic/environmental interaction
• MODY lacks obesity and insulin resistance.

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: Identify three specific exocrine pancreatic disorders that cause Pancreatogenic (Type 3c) Diabetes Mellitus.
back:
• Chronic pancreatitis
• Cystic fibrosis
• Hemochromatosis ("Bronze Diabetes")
• Pancreatic adenocarcinoma or total pancreatectomy.

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: Diabetes appearing for the first time during pregnancy that typically resolves after parturition is etiologically classified as [___].
back:
• Gestational Diabetes Mellitus (GDM)
• Driven by placental hormones causing insulin resistance
• Increases risk of future overt Type 2 DM
• Requires postpartum follow-up.

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: A patient on long-term high-dose Prednisone for systemic lupus erythematosus develops persistent fasting hyperglycemia. This represents [___].
back:
• Drug-induced Diabetes Mellitus
• Glucocorticoids stimulate hepatic glucose output
• Inhibition of peripheral glucose uptake
• Classified under "Other Specific Types."

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: Describe the etiological mechanism of MODY-2 (Glucokinase mutation) in the regulation of insulin release.
back:
• Glucokinase acts as the ̡-cell "glucose sensor"
• Mutation raises the threshold for insulin secretion
• Causes stable, mild fasting hyperglycemia
• Usually managed without pharmacological intervention.

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: Contrast Type 1A and Type 1B Diabetes Mellitus based on their immunological profile.
back:
• Type 1A: Immune-mediated ̡-cell destruction (positive antibodies like GAD65, ICA)
• Type 1B: Idiopathic destruction; antibody negative; often episodic ketoacidosis.

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: Identify two rare etiological categories of DM involving genetic defects in insulin action rather than ̡-cell failure.
back:
• Type A Insulin Resistance (Insulin receptor mutations)
• Lipoatrophic Diabetes
• Characterized by severe hyperinsulinemia and Acanthosis Nigricans.

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus is etiologically defined as the form of DM characterized by absolute insulin deficiency due to the destruction of [___].
back:
• Pancreatic ̠-cells
• Usually immune-mediated (autoimmune)
• Less commonly idiopathic (no evidence of autoimmunity)

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: A 45-year-old obese male presents with fasting glucose of 135 mg/dL. The etiological classification for this condition involves a combination of peripheral [___] and relative ̠-cell failure.
back:
• Insulin resistance
• Pathophysiology of Type 2 DM
• Overcomes compensatory hyperinsulinemia over time

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: How are Maturity-onset diabetes of the young (MODY) and Neonatal diabetes classified within the etiological framework of DM?
back:
• Genetic defects of ̠-cell function
• Monogenic forms of DM
• Distinct from classic Type 1 or Type 2 DM

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: Contrast the etiological basis of DM in a patient with Acromegaly versus a patient with Chronic Pancreatitis.
back:
• Acromegaly: Secondary to endocrinopathy (GH excess opposes insulin)
• Pancreatitis: Secondary to exocrine pancreatic defects (Type 3c)
• Both are classified as "Other specific types"

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: Identify the class of pharmaceutical agents that frequently causes secondary DM by stimulating hepatic gluconeogenesis and inhibiting peripheral glucose uptake.
back:
• Glucocorticoids (Corticosteroids)
• Other drugs include Thiazides, Protease inhibitors, and Thyroid hormone

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: According to the American Diabetes Association (ADA), the diagnostic threshold for a fasting plasma glucose level indicative of DM is [___] mg/dL or higher.
back:
• 126 mg/dL
• Must be confirmed on a separate day
• Prediabetes range is 100–125 mg/dL

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: A child presenting with congenital rubella develops hyperglycemia. This form of DM is etiologically classified under [___].
back:
• Infections
• Specifically viral induction of ̠-cell damage
• Other examples include Coxsackie B and Cytomegalovirus

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: Explain the role of 'Lipotoxicity' in the development of etiological Type 2 Diabetes.
back:
• Excess Free Fatty Acids (FFAs) overwhelm oxidation pathways
• Intracellular toxic metabolites (DAG/Ceramides) attenuate insulin signaling
• Triggers pro-inflammatory cytokines causing ̠-cell dysfunction

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: Contrast the incretin effect in healthy individuals versus those with Type 2 DM.
back:
• Healthy: GLP-1/GIP amplify insulin release after food intake
• T2DM: Incretin effect is significantly blunted
• Results in reduced insulin secretion postprandially

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: Name the specific genetic locus that contributes as much as 50% of the inherited susceptibility for Type 1 Diabetes.
back:
• HLA gene cluster (MHC Class II)
• Specifically HLA-DR3 and HLA-DR4 haplotypes
• Linked to failure of self-tolerance in T-cells

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: The etiological classification of Diabetes Mellitus identifies [___] as the primary cause of absolute insulin deficiency resulting from autoimmune β-cell destruction.
back:
• Type 1 Diabetes (T1D)
• Characterized by progressive depletion of β-cells
• Usually immune-mediated
• Linked primarily to HLA-DR3 or DR4 haplotypes.

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: A 16-year-old non-obese patient presents with mild hyperglycemia. Genetic testing identifies a germline mutation in the Glucokinase (GCK) gene. This condition is etiologically classified as [___].
back:
• Maturity-Onset Diabetes of the Young (MODY)
• Specifically MODY2
• A genetic defect of β-cell function
• Inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern.

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: Explain the fundamental difference between Type 1 and Type 2 Diabetes regarding the mechanism of insulin deficiency.
back:
• Type 1: Absolute deficiency due to β-cell destruction.
• Type 2: Relative deficiency resulting from peripheral insulin resistance combined with inadequate β-cell compensatory secretion.

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: Contrast the etiological basis of 'Pancreatogenic' (Type 3C) Diabetes with that of Type 1 Diabetes.
back:
• Type 1: Primary autoimmune attack on islets.
• Type 3C: Secondary to exocrine pancreas diseases (e.g., chronic pancreatitis, cystic fibrosis, or hemochromatosis) that destroy islet tissue.

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: Identify three specific endocrinopathies that etiologically cause secondary Diabetes by antagonizing insulin action.
back:
• Acromegaly (Growth Hormone excess)
• Cushing Syndrome (Cortisol excess)
• Pheochromocytoma (Catecholamine excess)
• Hyperthyroidism (Thyroid hormone excess).

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: Glucose intolerance that is first recognized during the state of pregnancy is etiologically classified as [___].
back:
• Gestational Diabetes Mellitus (GDM)
• Results from pregnancy-induced insulin resistance
• Most cases resolve post-delivery
• Increases long-term risk for maternal Type 2 DM.

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: A patient on long-term treatment for HIV presents with new-onset hyperglycemia. Which specific pharmacological class is most likely responsible for this etiological form of DM?
back:
• Protease Inhibitors
• Classified as Drug-induced Diabetes
• Impair glucose metabolism and insulin sensitivity
• Other causes include glucocorticoids and thiazides.

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: Describe the physiological role of the 'Incretin Effect' and how its dysfunction contributes to the etiology of Type 2 DM.
back:
• Incretins (GIP, GLP-1) stimulate insulin release after food intake.
• In T2D, the incretin effect is blunted.
• Results in reduced postprandial insulin secretion and increased glucagon release.

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: Contrast Stage 1 and Stage 2 of the natural history of Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus based on glycemic status.
back:
• Stage 1: Multiple autoantibodies present but patient is normoglycemic.
• Stage 2: Autoantibodies present with demonstrable dysglycemia but no clinical symptoms.

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: Name two chromosomal genetic syndromes associated with an increased etiological risk of developing Diabetes Mellitus.
back:
• Down Syndrome
• Turner Syndrome
• Klinefelter Syndrome
• Prader-Willi Syndrome.

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus is characterized by an absolute deficiency of insulin resulting from the autoimmune destruction of pancreatic [___] cells.
back:
• Beta (β) cells
• Results in failure of insulin synthesis
• Leads to a catabolic state and ketoacidosis if untreated

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: A 45-year-old obese male presents with asymptomatic hyperglycemia but no ketonuria. The underlying etiological category of his diabetes is [___].
back:
• Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus
• Characterized by peripheral insulin resistance
• Accompanied by relative (not absolute) insulin deficiency

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: Explain the two essential metabolic defects required to produce the clinical phenotype of Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus.
back:
• Insulin resistance: Failure of target tissues (liver, muscle, fat) to respond to insulin
• β-cell dysfunction: Secretory exhaustion where insulin levels become inadequate for the blood glucose level

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: Contrast the characteristic islet histopathology of long-standing Type 1 vs Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus.
back:
• Type 1: Insulitis (lymphocytic infiltrate), β-cell depletion, and islet atrophy
• Type 2: Islet amyloid deposition (amylin) and mild β-cell mass reduction

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: List four specific endocrinopathies that can induce secondary Diabetes Mellitus by antagonizing insulin action.
back:
• Acromegaly (Excess GH)
• Cushing syndrome (Excess Cortisol)
• Pheochromocytoma (Excess Catecholamines)
• Hyperthyroidism (Excess Thyroid Hormone)

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: Autosomal dominant genetic defects of β-cell function that present before age 25 and mimic T2DM are collectively termed [___].
back:
• MODY (Maturity-Onset Diabetes of the Young)
• Caused by single-gene mutations (e.g., GCK, HNF1A)
• Lacks β-cell autoantibodies

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: A 22-year-old non-obese female with a strong family history of early-onset diabetes is found to have a mutation in the Glucokinase (GCK) gene. This specific form is [___].
back:
• MODY2
• Glucokinase acts as the β-cell glucose sensor
• Mutations raise the threshold for glucose-stimulated insulin release

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: Describe the mechanism by which exogenous drugs such as glucocorticoids or protease inhibitors lead to clinical Diabetes Mellitus.
back:
• Induce peripheral insulin resistance
• Stimulate hepatic gluconeogenesis
• Mimic the metabolic profile of Type 2 DM

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: Distinguish between Type 1A and Type 1B Diabetes Mellitus based on their causative factors.
back:
• Type 1A: Immune-mediated destruction (islet autoantibodies present)
• Type 1B: Idiopathic (insulin deficiency without evidence of autoimmunity or HLA linkage)

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: Identify four conditions classified as 'Exocrine Pancreatic Defects' that cause secondary pancreatogenic diabetes.
back:
• Chronic pancreatitis
• Cystic fibrosis
• Hemochromatosis (Iron overload)
• Pancreatectomy or trauma

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: The most frequent cause of endogenous hypercortisolism (Cushing syndrome) is a(n) [___] pituitary adenoma.
back:
• ACTH-secreting microadenoma
• Clinically termed Cushing Disease
• Accounts for 60%–70% of endogenous cases

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: A 55-year-old male smoker with a lung mass presents with truncal obesity and severe hypercortisolism. Lab shows high ACTH. Identify the mechanism.
back:
• Ectopic ACTH secretion
• Most commonly caused by small-cell lung carcinoma
• Results in bilateral adrenal cortical hyperplasia

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: Explain the role of the high-dose dexamethasone suppression test in distinguishing pituitary vs. ectopic ACTH sources.
back:
• Pituitary adenomas: ACTH levels are reduced (suppressed) by high-dose steroids
• Ectopic sources: ACTH secretion is insensitive/autonomous and fails to suppress

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: Contrast the biochemical findings of ACTH-dependent versus ACTH-independent Cushing syndrome.
back:
• ACTH-dependent: Elevated serum ACTH (Pituitary/Ectopic sources)
• ACTH-independent: Low/suppressed serum ACTH (Adrenal adenoma/carcinoma or exogenous steroids)

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: List the three standard laboratory screening tests for the initial diagnosis of Cushing syndrome.
back:
• 24-hour urinary free cortisol (increased)
• Loss of normal diurnal cortisol rhythm
• Late-night salivary cortisol or low-dose dexamethasone suppression test

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: In ACTH-independent Cushing syndrome caused by primary adrenal neoplasms, the [___] gene is frequently mutated in both adenomas and carcinomas.
back:
• PRKAR1A
• Leads to increased intracellular cAMP levels
• Also associated with Carney complex/micronodular hyperplasia

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: A patient on long-term prednisone therapy for SLE presents with a 'buffalo hump' and thin skin. Identify the expected state of the adrenal cortex.
back:
• Bilateral cortical atrophy
• Affects zona fasciculata and reticularis
• Due to lack of endogenous ACTH stimulation

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: Explain why ACTH-secreting pituitary tumors can be associated with hyperpigmentation (Nelson Syndrome).
back:
• ACTH is derived from pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC)
• POMC processing also generates melanocyte-stimulating hormone (MSH)
• High ACTH/MSH stimulates dermal melanocytes

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: Contrast the gross appearance of the adrenal glands in Pituitary Cushing Disease versus Bilateral Macronodular Adrenal Hyperplasia (BMAH).
back:
• Cushing Disease: Diffuse, subtle nodular thickening (yellow due to lipid)
• BMAH: Large prominent nodules (>10 mm) replacing the entire gland

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: Identify the primary hormone responsible for the 'moon facies' and 'abdominal striae' seen in Cushing syndrome.
back:
• Cortisol (Glucocorticoid)
• Striae result from catabolic loss of collagen
• Facies from centripetal fat redistribution

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: The most frequent cause of endogenous hypercortisolism, accounting for nearly 70% of cases, is a(n) [___] microadenoma.
back:
• ACTH-secreting pituitary adenoma (Cushing disease)
• Results in bilateral nodular cortical hyperplasia
• Characterized by high serum ACTH levels.

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: A 35-year-old female presents with moon facies, truncal obesity, and purple striae. Labs show elevated cortisol, high ACTH, and cortisol suppression with high-dose dexamethasone. Identify the diagnosis.
back:
• Cushing Disease (Pituitary adenoma)
• Elevated ACTH confirms ACTH-dependence
• Suppression by high-dose dexamethasone distinguishes pituitary sources from ectopic ACTH production.

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: Explain the role of the high-dose dexamethasone suppression test in distinguishing pituitary versus ectopic sources of ACTH.
back:
• Pituitary adenomas: Retain some sensitivity to glucocorticoid feedback; ACTH/cortisol levels drop significantly.
• Ectopic ACTH: Secretion is autonomous; ACTH/cortisol levels remain elevated despite high-dose dexamethasone.

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: Contrast ACTH-dependent Cushing syndrome with ACTH-independent forms regarding serum ACTH levels and adrenal morphology.
back:
• ACTH-dependent: High ACTH; bilateral diffuse or nodular adrenal hyperplasia.
• ACTH-independent: Low (suppressed) ACTH; unilateral adrenal neoplasm (adenoma/carcinoma) or rare primary hyperplasia.

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: List three specific malignant neoplasms classically associated with paraneoplastic ectopic ACTH secretion.
back:
• Small-cell carcinoma of the lung (most common)
• Carcinoid tumors
• Medullary carcinoma of the thyroid
• Pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors (PanNETs).

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: Initial screening for Cushing syndrome often utilizes the measurement of [___] in a 24-hour urine sample.
back:
• 24-hour urine free cortisol
• Provides a measure of total daily cortisol production
• Bypasses the diagnostic limitations of diurnal variation.

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: A patient presents with clinical Cushing syndrome, low serum ACTH, and no suppression on high-dose dexamethasone. Adrenal imaging shows a single 2cm yellow nodule. What is the diagnosis?
back:
• Adrenocortical adenoma
• Functionally autonomous cortisol secretion
• Leads to atrophy of the contralateral adrenal gland.

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: Describe the biochemical hallmark used to differentiate Cushing syndrome from primary adrenal insufficiency regarding pituitary feedback.
back:
• Cushing Syndrome: Excessive cortisol leads to ACTH suppression (if adrenal-primary) or high ACTH (if pituitary-primary).
• Adrenal Insufficiency: Low cortisol always leads to high ACTH (primary Addison).

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: Contrast the underlying drivers of bilateral macronodular adrenal hyperplasia (BMAH) versus micronodular hyperplasia in the Carney complex.
back:
• BMAH: Ectopic expression of non-ACTH receptors (e.g., GIP, LH) on adrenocortical cells.
• Micronodular: Mutations in the PRKAR1A gene causing constitutive cAMP pathway activation.

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: Identify the most common overall cause of Cushing syndrome symptoms in clinical practice.
back:
• Exogenous (Iatrogenic) administration of glucocorticoids
• Results in suppressed ACTH and bilateral cortical atrophy
• Affects the zonae fasciculata and reticularis primarily.

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
coreConcept: Most Common Cause of Cushing Syndrome
front: The most frequent etiological factor leading to Cushing syndrome in clinical practice is the [___] administration of glucocorticoids.
back:
• Exogenous (Iatrogenic)
• Results in bilateral cortical atrophy of zona fasciculata and reticularis due to suppression of endogenous ACTH
• Zona glomerulosa is typically spared.

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: A 35-year-old female presents with moon facies, truncal obesity, and proximal muscle weakness. Lab findings show elevated ACTH and suppression of cortisol by high-dose dexamethasone. Identify the specific diagnosis.
back:
• Cushing Disease
• Caused by an ACTH-secreting pituitary microadenoma (60-70% of endogenous cases)
• Characterized by bilateral nodular cortical hyperplasia.

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: Explain why high-dose dexamethasone suppresses cortisol in pituitary-driven Cushing but fails in ectopic ACTH syndromes.
back:
• Pituitary adenomas retain partial sensitivity to negative feedback inhibition by high-dose steroids.
• Ectopic tumors (e.g., small-cell lung cancer) are completely autonomous and insensitive to feedback loops.

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: Contrast the expected serum ACTH levels and adrenal morphology in a patient with a functional adrenal adenoma versus one with an ACTH-secreting bronchial carcinoid.
back:
• Adrenal Adenoma: Low (suppressed) ACTH; atrophy of contralateral/adjacent cortex.
• Bronchial Carcinoid (Ectopic): High serum ACTH; bilateral diffuse or nodular adrenal hyperplasia.

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: List two initial first-line screening tests used to biochemically confirm hypercortisolism before localizing the etiology.
back:
• 24-hour urinary free cortisol (increased)
• Late-night salivary cortisol or loss of diurnal cortisol rhythm
• Low-dose dexamethasone suppression test (LDDST).

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: In patients with ACTH-dependent Cushing syndrome who show no suppression on high-dose dexamethasone, the most common non-pituitary source of hormone is [___].
back:
• Small-cell carcinoma of the lung (Ectopic ACTH Syndrome)
• Presents with rapid onset and very high ACTH levels
• Adrenals show bilateral cortical hyperplasia.

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: A patient with severe virilization and rapidly progressing Cushing symptoms presents with a 12cm adrenal mass with necrosis. Identify the most likely cause and its effect on serum ACTH.
back:
• Adrenocortical Carcinoma
• Low (suppressed) serum ACTH
• Frequently secretes multiple steroid lineages (cortisol + androgens).

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: Describe the effect of chronic exogenous Prednisone use on the morphology of the adrenal cortex zones, stating which zone remains functional.
back:
• Bilateral atrophy of zona fasciculata and reticularis.
• Zona glomerulosa is spared/functions normally.
• Glomerulosa is regulated by the Renin-Angiotensin system, not ACTH.

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: Distinguish Cushing Disease from Ectopic ACTH Syndrome based on the response to a CRH (Corticotropin-Releasing Hormone) stimulation test.
back:
• Cushing Disease (Pituitary): ACTH and cortisol levels increase further.
• Ectopic ACTH: No response (ACTH and cortisol remain unchanged as tumor is autonomous).

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: Identify the condition characterized by rapid pituitary adenoma enlargement and skin hyperpigmentation occurring after bilateral adrenalectomy for Cushing syndrome.
back:
• Nelson Syndrome
• Caused by loss of cortisol feedback on a pre-existing corticotroph microadenoma
• High POMC/ACTH levels stimulate melanocytes.

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: The most common cause of Cushing syndrome overall is the [___] administration of glucocorticoids.
back:
• Exogenous (Iatrogenic)
• Causes bilateral adrenocortical atrophy
• Suppresses endogenous ACTH production

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: A 55-year-old smoker presents with weight loss, muscle weakness, and hyperpigmentation. Labs show elevated cortisol and very high ACTH. Identify the likely source of hypercortisolism.
back:
• Ectopic ACTH secretion
• Most commonly Small-Cell Carcinoma of the lung
• Results in bilateral adrenal cortical hyperplasia

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: Explain the physiological principle behind the overnight low-dose dexamethasone suppression test (LDDST) in Cushing screening.
back:
• Provides negative feedback to the pituitary gland
• Healthy individuals suppress ACTH and lower cortisol (<1.8 μg/dL)
• Cushing patients fail to suppress due to autonomous production

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: Contrast the serum ACTH levels and adrenal morphology in Cushing disease versus a functioning primary adrenocortical adenoma.
back:
• Cushing Disease: High/Normal ACTH; Bilateral adrenal hyperplasia
• Adrenal Adenoma: Low (suppressed) ACTH; Unilateral mass with contralateral cortical atrophy

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: Specify the expected cortisol response to a High-Dose Dexamethasone Suppression Test (HDDST) in a patient with a pituitary microadenoma.
back:
• Significant suppression (>50% reduction from baseline)
• Pituitary tumors retain partial sensitivity to high-level feedback
• Contrast: Ectopic and adrenal sources show no suppression

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: A primary screening test for hypercortisolism that measures the integrated cumulative hormone excretion over a 24-hour period is [___].
back:
• 24-hour urine free cortisol
• Values >3 times the upper limit confirm hypercortisolism
• Bypasses the variability of episodic secretion

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: A patient who underwent bilateral adrenalectomy for Cushing disease now presents with intense hyperpigmentation and an enlarging pituitary mass. Identify this condition.
back:
• Nelson Syndrome
• Loss of cortisol negative feedback on pre-existing microadenoma
• Leads to aggressive pituitary expansion and high POMC levels

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: Explain the mechanism through which hyperpigmentation occurs in endogenous ACTH-dependent Cushing syndrome.
back:
• High ACTH is derived from the precursor POMC
• POMC cleavage also produces α-MSH (Melanocyte-Stimulating Hormone)
• Increased α-MSH stimulates skin melanocytes directly

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: Contrast Bilateral Macronodular Adrenal Hyperplasia (BMAH) with Primary Pigmented Nodular Adrenocortical Disease (PPNAD) regarding morphology.
back:
• BMAH: Large nodules (usually >10 mm); may involve aberrant G-protein receptors
• PPNAD: Small brown/black micronodules (<10 mm); associated with Carney Complex and PRKAR1A mutations

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: Identify the rationale for using late-night salivary cortisol as an initial screening investigation for Cushing syndrome.
back:
• Detects loss of normal diurnal cortisol rhythm
• Cortisol should be at its nadir (lowest) around midnight
• High midnight levels indicate autonomous, non-rhythmic production

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: The most common cause of Cushing syndrome overall is the [___] administration of glucocorticoids.
back:
- Exogenous (iatrogenic) origin.
- Results in bilateral cortical atrophy due to suppressed endogenous ACTH.
- Zona glomerulosa remains normal thickness.

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: A 35-year-old female presents with moon facies, truncal obesity, and striae. Labs show elevated ACTH that suppresses with high-dose dexamethasone. Identify the specific diagnosis.
back:
- Cushing disease.
- Specifically caused by an ACTH-secreting pituitary microadenoma.
- Accounts for 60-70% of endogenous cases.

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: Explain the role of serum ACTH measurement in differentiating the causes of endogenous hypercortisolism.
back:
- High ACTH: Indicates ACTH-dependent causes (Pituitary adenoma or Ectopic source).
- Low/Undetectable ACTH: Indicates ACTH-independent causes (Primary adrenal adenoma, carcinoma, or hyperplasia).

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: Contrast the response to high-dose dexamethasone suppression testing in Cushing disease versus ectopic ACTH syndrome.
back:
- Cushing Disease: High doses partially suppress ACTH secretion and reduce urinary steroid levels.
- Ectopic ACTH: Cortisol secretion is completely insensitive to suppression by even high-dose dexamethasone.

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: Enumerate the non-pituitary neoplasms most frequently responsible for ectopic ACTH secretion.
back:
- Small-cell carcinoma of the lung (most common).
- Carcinoid tumors.
- Medullary thyroid carcinoma.
- Pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors (PanNETs).

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: In the laboratory diagnosis of Cushing syndrome, a definitive finding is the loss of the normal [___] of cortisol secretion.
back:
- Diurnal pattern (rhythm).
- Normally, cortisol is highest in the morning and lowest at night; this variation is lost in Cushing syndrome.

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: A patient with clinical Cushing syndrome has elevated 24-hour urine free cortisol, low serum ACTH, and no suppression with high-dose dexamethasone. Name the most likely underlying lesion.
back:
- Adrenocortical neoplasm.
- Either a functional adrenal adenoma or adrenal carcinoma.
- Leads to atrophy of the contralateral adrenal gland.

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: Analyze why hyperpigmentation occurs in Cushing disease but not in Cushing syndrome caused by adrenal tumors.
back:
- Cushing Disease: High ACTH is derived from pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC), which also produces melanocyte-stimulating hormone (MSH).
- Adrenal Tumors: High cortisol provides negative feedback, lowering pituitary ACTH/POMC production.

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: Contrast the typical morphology of Bilateral Macronodular Adrenal Hyperplasia (BMAH) with Primary Pigmented Nodular Adrenocortical Disease (PPNAD).
back:
- BMAH: Large nodules (>10mm); often associated with ARMC5 mutations.
- PPNAD: Darkly pigmented micronodules (<10mm); associated with PRKAR1A mutations and Carney complex.

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: Identify the two most useful initial biochemical screening tests used to confirm suspected hypercortisolism.
back:
- 24-hour urinary free-cortisol concentration (increased).
- Assessment of the loss of normal diurnal pattern of cortisol secretion.

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: The most frequent underlying cause of primary chronic adrenocortical insufficiency in high-income countries is [___].
back:
• Autoimmune adrenalitis (80-90% of cases).
• Often occurs in Autoimmune Polyendocrine Syndromes (APS-1 or APS-2).
• Characterized by autoimmune destruction of steroidogenic cells.

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: A 40-year-old female presents with progressive weakness, weight loss, and hyperpigmentation of the palmar creases and oral mucosa. Labs reveal hyponatremia and hyperkalemia. Identify the diagnosis.
back:
• Addison disease (Primary Chronic Adrenocortical Insufficiency).
• Symptoms appear only after >90% of the cortex is destroyed.
• Hyperpigmentation is due to elevated ACTH/POMC levels.

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: Explain the biochemical mechanism causing skin hyperpigmentation specifically in primary Addison disease.
back:
• Loss of cortisol feedback leads to high Pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC) levels.
• POMC is the precursor for both ACTH and Melanocyte-Stimulating Hormone (MSH).
• High ACTH/MSH stimulates dermal melanocytes.

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: Contrast the electrolyte and mineralocorticoid profiles of primary versus secondary adrenocortical insufficiency.
back:
• Primary: Low aldosterone leads to severe hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, and volume depletion.
• Secondary: Normal/near-normal aldosterone; hyperkalemia and hyponatremia are typically absent (zona glomerulosa is largely ACTH-independent).

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: Identify the four classic components of Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome associated with acute adrenal failure.
back:
• Overwhelming bacterial infection (classically Neisseria meningitidis).
• Rapidly progressive hypotension leading to shock.
• Disseminated Intravascular Coagulation (DIC) with widespread purpura.
• Massive bilateral adrenal hemorrhage.

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: In the pathogenesis of chronic adrenocortical insufficiency, symptoms typically do not manifest until [___]% of the adrenal cortex is compromised.
back:
• 90%.
• Insidious onset prevents early detection until significant functional reserve is lost.
• Stress can precipitate acute crisis before this threshold.

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: A patient with long-standing steroid use for rheumatoid arthritis undergoes major surgery without adjusting their dosage. Postoperatively, they develop intractable vomiting and vascular collapse. Identify the underlying complication.
back:
• Acute Adrenocortical Insufficiency (Adrenal Crisis).
• Caused by inability of atrophic adrenals to increase cortisol output during stress.
• Results from rapid steroid withdrawal or inadequate stress-dosing.

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: Analyze how mutations in the AIRE gene result in the autoimmune destruction seen in Autoimmune Polyendocrine Syndrome Type 1 (APS-1).
back:
• AIRE normally facilitates thymic expression of peripheral tissue antigens.
• Mutation leads to failure of central T-cell tolerance.
• Results in autoreactive T-cell attack on the adrenal cortex.

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: Contrast the typical infectious causes of Addison disease seen in low-income regions versus patients with AIDS.
back:
• Low-income: Tuberculous adrenalitis (historically the most common).
• AIDS: Cytomegalovirus (CMV), Mycobacterium avium-intracellulare, and fungal infections (Histoplasma).

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: List three characteristic physical sites for hyperpigmentation in primary adrenocortical insufficiency.
back:
• Skin creases (palmar).
• Pressure points (elbows, knees, knuckles).
• Recent scars, oral mucosa, and sun-exposed areas.

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: The most frequent cause of Cushing syndrome overall is the administration of [___].
back:
• Exogenous glucocorticoids (iatrogenic).
• It results in bilateral cortical atrophy of the adrenal glands due to ACTH suppression.

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: A 35-year-old female presents with truncal obesity and high ACTH levels. High-dose dexamethasone suppresses her cortisol by 60%. The most likely cause is [___].
back:
• Cushing Disease.
• Caused by an ACTH-secreting pituitary adenoma (usually a microadenoma).
• It is the most common endogenous cause.

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: Explain the response of cortisol and ACTH levels in ectopic ACTH syndrome to a High-Dose Dexamethasone Suppression Test (HDDST).
back:
• ACTH and Cortisol both remain high (no suppression).
• Neoplasms (e.g., small-cell lung cancer) lack the feedback receptors present in pituitary adenomas.

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: Contrast Pituitary Cushing (Cushing Disease) and Primary Adrenal Cushing regarding their effect on the non-neoplastic portion of the adrenal cortex.
back:
• Pituitary: Bilateral diffuse or nodular hyperplasia due to excess ACTH.
• Adrenal: Atrophy of the contralateral gland and adjacent cortex due to ACTH suppression.

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: Identify the most common paraneoplastic source of ACTH leading to Cushing syndrome.
back:
• Small-cell carcinoma of the lung.
• Other sources include bronchial carcinoids, medullary thyroid carcinoma, and pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors.

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: In patients with Cushing syndrome, the high levels of glucocorticoids induce the replacement of granular basophilic cytoplasm in pituitary corticotrophs by pale keratin filaments, a process termed [___].
back:
• Crooke hyaline change.
• This is a reactive morphological feature found regardless of the cause of hypercortisolism.

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: A patient presents with rapid virilization, a 250g suprarenal mass, and severe hypercortisolism that is not suppressed by high-dose dexamethasone. Plasma ACTH is undetectable. Identify the diagnosis.
back:
• Adrenocortical Carcinoma.
• These are more likely to be functional and virilizing than adenomas.
• Characterized by low ACTH and lack of feedback.

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: Describe the physiological mechanism behind the hyperpigmentation seen in primary ACTH-dependent Cushing syndromes.
back:
• Excessive ACTH precursors (POMC) are cleaved into Melanocyte-Stimulating Hormone (MSH).
• High ACTH/MSH levels stimulate melanin production in skin.

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: Contrast Bilateral Macronodular Adrenal Hyperplasia (BMAH) and Primary Pigmented Nodular Adrenocortical Disease (PPNAD) regarding nodule size and typical mutation association.
back:
• BMAH: Large nodules (>10mm); often ARMC5 mutations or ectopic G-protein receptors.
• PPNAD: Small (<10mm) dark pigmented nodules; associated with PRKAR1A mutations (Carney complex).

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: List the three initial screening tests used to confirm hypercortisolism in a suspected patient.
back:
1. 24-hour urinary free cortisol (increased).
2. Late-night salivary cortisol (loss of diurnal rhythm).
3. Low-dose dexamethasone suppression test (failure to suppress).

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: The most common cause of Cushing syndrome overall is the administration of exogenous [___].
back:
• Glucocorticoids
• This leads to bilateral adrenocortical atrophy due to ACTH suppression
• The zona glomerulosa is typically spared as it is ACTH-independent

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: A patient with central obesity and striae has elevated 24-hour urine free cortisol and very low serum ACTH levels. Identify the most likely underlying pathology.
back:
• ACTH-independent Cushing syndrome
• Primary adrenal neoplasm (adenoma or carcinoma)
• High autonomous cortisol suppresses pituitary ACTH release via negative feedback

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: Explain the role of serum ACTH measurement in the initial diagnostic algorithm of Cushing syndrome.
back:
• Distinguishes ACTH-dependent (Pituitary/Ectopic) from ACTH-independent (Adrenal) causes
• Low ACTH: Indicates primary adrenal tumor or exogenous steroids
• High/Normal ACTH: Indicates pituitary adenoma or paraneoplastic ACTH production

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: Contrast the responses to High-Dose Dexamethasone Suppression Testing in Cushing Disease versus Ectopic ACTH Syndrome.
back:
• Cushing Disease (Pituitary): Cortisol levels are suppressed as adenomas retain partial feedback sensitivity
• Ectopic ACTH: Cortisol levels remain elevated as non-pituitary tumors (e.g., small-cell lung cancer) secrete ACTH autonomously

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: List the three biochemical investigations used to confirm the presence of hypercortisolism (screening).
back:
• 24-hour urinary free cortisol (increased)
• Late-night salivary cortisol or loss of normal diurnal cortisol rhythm
• Low-dose dexamethasone suppression test (fails to suppress cortisol)

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: In patients with ACTH-dependent Cushing syndrome, the adrenal glands typically exhibit bilateral [___] hyperplasia.
back:
• Diffuse or nodular cortical hyperplasia
• This is caused by chronic trophic stimulation by excessive ACTH
• Adrenals can weigh up to 30g each

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: A 50-year-old male smoker with a lung mass presents with rapid-onset hypertension, hypokalemia, and hyperpigmentation. Identify the cause of his hypercortisolism.
back:
• Ectopic ACTH secretion (Paraneoplastic Syndrome)
• Most commonly caused by small-cell lung carcinoma
• Hyperpigmentation results from MSH-activity within the ACTH/POMC precursor

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: Describe the physiological mechanism causing ‘Crooke Hyaline Change’ in the pituitary gland.
back:
• High levels of glucocorticoids (endogenous or exogenous)
• Causes accumulation of intermediate keratin filaments in the cytoplasm of ACTH-producing cells
• The normally granular basophilic cytoplasm becomes homogeneous and pale

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: Contrast the morphological findings of the contralateral adrenal gland in a patient with a functional adrenocortical adenoma versus Cushing disease.
back:
• Functional Adenoma: Contralateral gland is atrophic due to suppressed ACTH
• Cushing Disease: Both glands show bilateral diffuse or nodular hyperplasia due to excess trophic ACTH stimulation

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: Identify the genetic mutation most commonly associated with primary pigmented nodular adrenocortical disease (micronodular hyperplasia).
back:
• PRKAR1A mutation
• Often occurs as part of the Carney Complex
• Results in increased cAMP-dependent signaling and autonomous cortisol production

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
coreConcept: Pathogenesis of hyperpigmentation in Addison disease
front: In primary chronic adrenocortical insufficiency, hyperpigmentation of the skin is caused by elevated levels of [___], which is a precursor to both ACTH and melanocyte-stimulating hormone.
back:
• Pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC)
• Elevated due to loss of negative feedback
• Higher in sun-exposed areas and pressure points

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: A 45-year-old female presents with progressive weakness, weight loss, and darkening of her skin creases. Labs show high ACTH and low cortisol. Identify the most common etiology in high-income countries.
back:
• Autoimmune adrenalitis
• Responsible for 80-90% of cases in developed nations
• Often associated with autoantibodies to 21-hydroxylase

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: Explain why primary adrenocortical insufficiency causes hyponatremia and hyperkalemia.
back:
• Deficiency of mineralocorticoids (Aldosterone)
• Results in renal sodium wasting (hyponatremia)
• Leads to impaired renal potassium excretion (hyperkalemia)

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: Contrast the effects on skin pigmentation and mineralocorticoid function between primary and secondary adrenocortical insufficiency.
back:
• Pigmentation: Hyperpigmented in primary (high ACTH); normal in secondary
• Mineralocorticoids: Deficient in primary; near-normal in secondary (regulated by renin-angiotensin system)

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: Describe the clinical triad defining Autoimmune Polyendocrine Syndrome Type 1 (APS-1).
back:
• Chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis
• Autoimmune hypoparathyroidism
• Addison disease
• Caused by mutations in AIRE gene

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
coreConcept: Functional reserve of the adrenal cortex
front: Clinical manifestations of chronic adrenocortical insufficiency typically do not appear until at least [___]% of the adrenal cortex has been compromised.
back:
• 90%
• Onset is typically insidious
• Reserves must be significantly depleted before crisis occurs

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: A patient with long-standing tuberculosis presents with hypotension and hyperkalemia. Imaging shows enlarged, calcified adrenal glands. Identify the specific pathological process.
back:
• Tuberculous adrenalitis
• Granulomatous inflammation replaces normal architecture
• A major cause of Addison disease in developing countries

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: How does the rapid withdrawal of long-term exogenous corticosteroid therapy trigger an acute adrenal crisis?
back:
• Exogenous steroids suppress the HPA axis
• Causes bilateral adrenocortical atrophy
• Atrophic glands cannot produce cortisol during acute stress

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: Contrast the macroscopic appearance of the adrenal glands in autoimmune adrenalitis vs. metastatic carcinoma.
back:
• Autoimmune: Irregularly shrunken, thin, and lipid-depleted
• Metastatic: Enlarged, nodular, and architecture obscured by infiltrating tumor

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: Enlist the cardinal clinical features of an acute adrenal crisis.
back:
• Intractable vomiting and abdominal pain
• Hypotension and vascular collapse
• Rapidly developing shock and depressed consciousness

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: Hyperpigmentation in Addison disease is primarily caused by elevated levels of [___], which is a common precursor for both ACTH and melanocyte-stimulating hormone.
back:
- Pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC)
- POMC cleavage increases levels of ACTH and melanotropins
- Causes tanning of sun-exposed areas and pressure points.

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: A 40-year-old female presents with progressive fatigue, weight loss, and bronze skin in her palm creases. Lab tests show hyponatremia and hyperkalemia. Identify the underlying diagnosis.
back:
- Primary Chronic Adrenocortical Insufficiency (Addison Disease)
- Key cause: Autoimmune adrenalitis
- Associated with mineralocorticoid and glucocorticoid deficiency.

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: Explain the role of the pituitary-adrenal feedback loop in the development of hyperpigmentation seen in primary adrenal failure.
back:
- Low cortisol removes negative feedback on the pituitary
- Causes compensatory hypersecretion of POMC/ACTH
- POMC-derived melanotropins stimulate epidermal melanocytes.

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
coreConcept: Acute Adrenal Crisis vs Chronic Addison
front: A 35-year-old male with long-standing steroid use for asthma suddenly develops shock, abdominal pain, and intractable vomiting after stopping his medication. Distinguish this acute event from the chronic presentation of Addison disease.
back:
- Acute Adrenal Crisis: Rapid hypotension, abdominal emergency, vascular collapse
- Chronic Addison: Insidious fatigue, weight loss, hyperpigmentation, electrolyte disturbances.

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: Enlist the three cardinal components of Waterhouse-Friderichsen Syndrome resulting in acute adrenocortical insufficiency.
back:
- Overwhelming bacterial infection (e.g., Neisseria meningitidis)
- Rapidly progressive hypotension leading to shock
- Massive bilateral adrenal hemorrhage.

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: Autoimmune Polyendocrine Syndrome Type 1 (APS-1), which includes Addison disease as a component, is caused by mutations in the [___] gene.
back:
- Autoimmune Regulator (AIRE)
- Characterized by chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis and ectodermal dystrophy
- Impairs central T-cell tolerance.

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: A patient presents with symptoms of Addison disease but exhibits significant skin pallor and has normal serum potassium levels. Identify the likely site of pathology.
back:
- Secondary Adrenocortical Insufficiency (Hypothalamic/Pituitary)
- Lack of hyperpigmentation (low ACTH/MSH)
- Intact Renin-Angiotensin system preserves aldosterone levels.

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: Explain how mineralocorticoid deficiency in primary adrenal insufficiency leads to metabolic acidosis and hyperkalemia.
back:
- Loss of aldosterone reduces sodium reabsorption
- Impairs secretion of potassium and hydrogen ions in renal tubules
- Leads to potassium retention and metabolic acidosis.

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: Contrast the gross morphology of the adrenal glands in autoimmune adrenalitis versus chronic tuberculous adrenalitis.
back:
- Autoimmune: Irregularly shrunken glands; thin cortex with lymphoid infiltrates
- Tuberculous: Enlarged glands with granulomatous inflammation or caseous necrosis.

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: Enlist the four most common global causes of primary chronic adrenocortical insufficiency.
back:
- Autoimmune adrenalitis (most common in high-income regions)
- Tuberculosis (common in low-income regions)
- AIDS (CMV/MAI infections)
- Metastatic carcinoma (Lung/Breast).

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: The most frequent cause of Cushing syndrome encountered in clinical practice is the exogenous administration of [___].
back:
* Glucocorticoids (steroids).
* This leads to bilateral cortical atrophy of the adrenal glands due to ACTH suppression.

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: A 35-year-old female presents with truncal obesity, moon facies, and purple abdominal striae. Labs reveal elevated ACTH and suppression of cortisol following high-dose dexamethasone. Identify the most likely cause.
back:
* Cushing Disease.
* Specifically caused by an ACTH-secreting pituitary microadenoma.

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: Explain the role of autonomous cortisol production by an adrenal adenoma in the suppression of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis.
back:
* High cortisol levels exert negative feedback on the anterior pituitary.
* This results in markedly decreased ACTH secretion and atrophy of the non-neoplastic adrenal cortex.

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: Contrast the expected laboratory findings for high-dose dexamethasone suppression and plasma ACTH levels in Ectopic ACTH Syndrome versus Cushing Disease.
back:
* Ectopic ACTH: Markedly high ACTH; No cortisol suppression.
* Cushing Disease: Elevated ACTH; Cortisol suppression occurs.

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: Identify three specific non-pituitary neoplasms that frequently cause hypercortisolism through ectopic hormone secretion.
back:
* Small cell carcinoma of the lung (most common).
* Medullary thyroid carcinoma.
* Pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors (PanNETs) or Bronchial carcinoids.

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: An initial screening test to confirm hypercortisolism by measuring the integrated hormonal production over 24 hours is the [___].
back:
* 24-hour urinary free cortisol test.
* Measures unbound cortisol excreted in the urine.

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: A patient presents with virilization and hypercortisolism. Imaging reveals a 15-cm variegated adrenal mass with areas of necrosis. State the likely cause and its typical biochemical profile.
back:
* Adrenocortical Carcinoma.
* Profile: ACTH-independent; very high cortisol/androgens; low plasma ACTH.

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: Explain the molecular mechanism of micronodular adrenal hyperplasia in patients with Carney Complex.
back:
* Inactivating mutations in the PRKAR1A gene.
* Leads to constitutive activation of protein kinase A and autonomous cAMP signaling, stimulating cortisol release.

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: Contrast the morphological appearance of the non-neoplastic adrenal cortex in iatrogenic Cushing syndrome versus Cushing disease.
back:
* Iatrogenic: Bilateral cortical atrophy (zona fasciculata and reticularis).
* Cushing Disease: Bilateral diffuse or nodular hyperplasia.

category: Enumerate causes of Cushing syndrome with lab investigations
front: Distinguish between the terms 'Cushing Syndrome' and 'Cushing Disease'.
back:
* Cushing Syndrome: Any condition causing hypercortisolism.
* Cushing Disease: Hypercortisolism specifically due to a pituitary ACTH-secreting adenoma.

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: Primary chronic adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease) typically remains clinically silent until approximately [___]% of the adrenal cortex has been destroyed.
back:
• 90%
• Symptoms arise only when metabolic demands exceed the remaining functional capacity.

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: A 35-year-old female presents with progressive fatigue, vomiting, and new dark pigmentation on her palmar creases and buccal mucosa. Lab results show hyperkalemia and hyponatremia. Identify the most common cause of this condition in high-income countries.
back:
• Autoimmune Adrenalitis
• Associated with autoantibodies against steroidogenic enzymes (e.g., 21-hydroxylase).

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: Explain the biochemical mechanism responsible for the diffuse hyperpigmentation observed in primary adrenocortical insufficiency.
back:
• Low cortisol increases Pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC) production via loss of feedback.
• POMC is cleaved into ACTH and Melanocyte-Stimulating Hormone (MSH).
• Elevated MSH stimulates melanin synthesis in skin.

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: Contrast primary adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison's) with secondary adrenocortical insufficiency regarding skin color and mineralocorticoid status.
back:
• Skin: Pigmentation in Primary (high ACTH); no pigmentation in Secondary (low ACTH).
• Mineralocorticoids: Deficient in Primary; near-normal in Secondary (aldosterone is largely ACTH-independent).

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: Enlist the triad of clinical and pathological findings characteristic of Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome.
back:
• Overwhelming bacterial infection (classically Neisseria meningitidis).
• Rapidly progressive hypotension/shock and DIC.
• Massive bilateral adrenal hemorrhage leading to acute insufficiency.

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: The genetic basis for Autoimmune Polyendocrinopathy Syndrome Type 1 (APS-1), which includes Addison disease, is a mutation in the [___] gene.
back:
• AIRE (Autoimmune Regulator)
• Results in failure of central T-cell tolerance to peripheral tissue antigens.

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: A patient on chronic glucocorticoid therapy for asthma suddenly stops their medication and presents with abdominal pain, intractable vomiting, and vascular collapse. Identify the underlying clinical crisis.
back:
• Primary Acute Adrenocortical Insufficiency (Adrenal Crisis).
• Caused by the inability of atrophic adrenals to produce necessary steroids upon sudden withdrawal.

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: Describe the mechanism by which disseminated tuberculosis causes chronic adrenocortical insufficiency.
back:
• Hematogenous spread of M. tuberculosis to the adrenal glands.
• Formation of granulomatous inflammation and caseous necrosis.
• Progressive destruction of cortical parenchyma and subsequent fibrosis.

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: Contrast the electrolyte imbalances expected in primary chronic adrenocortical insufficiency with those of secondary disease.
back:
• Primary: Significant hyponatremia and hyperkalemia (due to aldosterone deficiency).
• Secondary: Minimal electrolyte disturbance (aldosterone synthesis via renin-angiotensin is preserved).

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: Identify the two most common metastatic malignancies that involve the adrenal glands and potentially cause insufficiency.
back:
• Lung carcinoma.
• Breast carcinoma.
• (Also gastrointestinal carcinomas and melanoma).

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: The most common cause of primary chronic adrenocortical insufficiency in high-income countries is [___].
back:
• Autoimmune adrenalitis
• Accounts for 80% to 90% of cases
• Involves autoimmune destruction of steroidogenic cells

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: A 45-year-old female presents with progressive weakness, weight loss, and hyperpigmentation of the knuckles and elbows. Serum labs reveal hyponatremia and hyperkalemia. Name the most likely diagnosis.
back:
• Addison Disease (Primary Chronic Adrenocortical Insufficiency)
• Characterized by high ACTH and low corticosteroids

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: Explain the mechanism behind the diffuse hyperpigmentation seen in patients with primary adrenocortical insufficiency.
back:
• Low cortisol reduces feedback inhibition on the pituitary
• Increased Pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC) secretion
• POMC is a precursor to both ACTH and Melanocyte-Stimulating Hormone (MSH)

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: Contrast the status of the adrenal medulla in autoimmune adrenalitis versus tuberculous adrenalitis.
back:
• Autoimmune: Medulla is typically preserved despite cortical shrinkage
• Tuberculosis: Entire adrenal architecture is effaced by granulomatous inflammation

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: Identify the genetic mutation and the associated triad of Autoimmune Polyendocrine Syndrome Type 1 (APS-1).
back:
• Mutation: AIRE (Autoimmune Regulator) gene
• Triad: Chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis, autoimmune hypoparathyroidism, and Addison disease

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: Clinical manifestations of chronic adrenocortical insufficiency typically do not manifest until [___]% of the adrenal cortex has been compromised.
back:
• 90%
• Reflects the significant functional reserve of the adrenal gland

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: A patient with long-standing Addison disease undergoes major surgery and postoperatively develops intractable vomiting, severe abdominal pain, and hypotension. Name the acute complication.
back:
• Adrenal Crisis (Primary Acute Adrenocortical Insufficiency)
• Precipitated by acute stress requiring immediate steroid increase

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: Explain why secondary adrenocortical insufficiency, unlike Addison disease, is not associated with hyperkalemia or hyponatremia.
back:
• Secondary insufficiency stems from low ACTH
• Aldosterone synthesis is preserved
• Aldosterone is regulated by renin-angiotensin, not the pituitary

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: Contrast the circulating levels of ACTH in primary versus secondary adrenocortical insufficiency.
back:
• Primary (Addison): High ACTH (due to loss of feedback inhibition)
• Secondary: Low or undetectable ACTH (due to pituitary/hypothalamic failure)

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: Identify the three infectious pathogens most commonly associated with chronic adrenocortical insufficiency in patients with AIDS.
back:
• Cytomegalovirus (CMV)
• Mycobacterium avium-intracellulare
• Fungi (e.g., Histoplasma capsulatum)

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: Clinical manifestations of chronic adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease) typically do not appear until at least [___]% of the adrenal cortex has been compromised.
back:
• 90%.
• Destruction must be progressive and near-total before metabolic reserves are exhausted.

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: A 40-year-old female presents with progressive fatigue, vomiting, and dark pigmentation on her knuckles and oral mucosa. Labs reveal Na+ 128 mEq/L and K+ 5.8 mEq/L. Identify the most likely diagnosis.
back:
• Addison disease (Primary chronic adrenocortical insufficiency).
• Characterized by glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid deficiency.

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: Explain the mechanism behind the characteristic hyperpigmentation seen in Addison disease.
back:
• Low cortisol removes feedback inhibition on the pituitary.
• Increased pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC) production occurs.
• POMC is cleaved into ACTH and melanocyte-stimulating hormone (MSH), which stimulates melanocytes.

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: Contrast the mineralocorticoid function in primary versus secondary (pituitary) adrenocortical insufficiency.
back:
• Primary: Deficient aldosterone (zona glomerulosa destroyed); causes hyponatremia and hyperkalemia.
• Secondary: Near-normal aldosterone levels; secretion is regulated by renin-angiotensin rather than ACTH.
