category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: List the most common cause of Addison disease in high-income countries versus its historically most common global cause.
back:
• High-income: Autoimmune adrenalitis (80-90% of cases).
• Historically/Global: Tuberculous adrenalitis.

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: Autoimmune Polyendocrine Syndrome Type 1 (APS-1), which includes adrenalitis and hypoparathyroidism, is caused by mutations in the [___] gene.
back:
• AIRE (Autoimmune Regulator).
• Results in defective central T-cell tolerance to peripheral tissue antigens.

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: A patient with established Addison disease undergoes an emergency appendectomy and post-operatively develops profound hypotension and intractable vomiting. Identify the acute complication.
back:
• Adrenal Crisis (Primary Acute Adrenocortical Insufficiency).
• Triggered by stress requiring immediate steroid output the atrophic glands cannot provide.

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: How does the deficiency of aldosterone specifically carry out its effect on serum electrolyte levels in Addison disease?
back:
• Impairs renal tubular sodium reabsorption.
• Reduces potassium and hydrogen ion excretion.
• Results in hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, and metabolic acidosis.

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: Distinguish between Autoimmune Polyendocrine Syndrome Type 1 (APS-1) and Type 2 (APS-2) based on non-adrenal features.
back:
• APS-1: Chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis, ectodermal dystrophy, and hypoparathyroidism.
• APS-2: Autoimmune thyroiditis and Type 1 Diabetes; lacks candidiasis.

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: Identify the three primary malignancies most frequently associated with metastatic destruction of the adrenal cortex.
back:
• Lung carcinoma.
• Breast carcinoma.
• Melanoma.

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
coreConcept: Most common cause of Addison Disease
front: In high-income countries, the vast majority of primary chronic adrenocortical insufficiency cases are caused by [___].
back:
* Autoimmune adrenalitis
* Involves immune-mediated destruction of steroidogenic cells
* Frequently associated with 21-hydroxylase autoantibodies

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: A 40-year-old female presents with weakness and hyperpigmentation of the palmar creases and gums. This cutaneous finding is driven by the excess production of [___].
back:
* Pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC)
* Precursor to both ACTH and melanocyte-stimulating hormone (MSH)
* Elevated due to loss of cortisol-mediated negative feedback

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: Explain how the ACTH stimulation test distinguishes primary from secondary adrenocortical insufficiency.
back:
* Primary: No increase in cortisol (damaged adrenal cortex)
* Secondary: Significant rise in cortisol (atrophied but functional cortex)
* Assesses the functional integrity of the adrenal gland

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: A patient presents with hypotension, vomiting, and skin darkening. Contrast the electrolyte findings expected in this primary insufficiency compared to a patient with secondary pituitary failure.
back:
* Primary: Hyponatremia and hyperkalemia (loss of aldosterone)
* Secondary: Normal electrolytes (aldosterone usually preserved by Renin-Angiotensin)
* Primary also presents with hyperpigmentation, secondary does not

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: Provide the physiological rationale for why rapid withdrawal of long-term glucocorticoid treatment results in an acute adrenal crisis.
back:
* Exogenous steroids cause HPA-axis suppression
* Leads to bilateral adrenocortical atrophy
* Atrophied adrenals cannot resume cortisol production immediately upon stimulant withdrawal

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: The acute, life-threatening form of adrenocortical insufficiency associated with *Neisseria meningitidis* septicemia and massive bilateral adrenal hemorrhage is [___].
back:
* Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome
* Characterized by shock and disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC)
* Presents with a distinctive widespread purpuric rash

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: A patient with a history of chronic cough presents with hypotension, weight loss, and adrenal calcifications. Name the most likely infectious cause and its morphologic hallmark.
back:
* Tuberculous adrenalitis
* Morphology: Granulomatous inflammation with caseous necrosis
* Architecture is typically effaced by granulomas and fibrosis

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: Describe the mechanistic role of the AIRE gene mutation in the development of Autoimmune Polyendocrine Syndrome Type 1 (APS-1).
back:
* AIRE normally promotes thymic expression of peripheral self-antigens
* Mutation causes failure of central T-cell tolerance
* Results in autoimmune attack against adrenals, parathyroids, and skin

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: Contrast the metabolic consequences of cortisol deficiency versus aldosterone deficiency in the context of Addison disease.
back:
* Cortisol: Hypoglycemia (impaired gluconeogenesis) and poor stress tolerance
* Aldosterone: Sodium wasting, hyperkalemia, and hypotension
* Combined loss leads to fatal cardiovascular collapse if untreated

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: Identify the two specific primary malignancies that most frequently seed the adrenal glands to cause cortical destruction.
back:
* Lung carcinoma
* Breast carcinoma
* Adrenals are a favored site for hematogenous metastatic spread

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
coreConcept: Mechanism of Hyperpigmentation in Addison Disease
front: In primary chronic adrenocortical insufficiency, the diffuse darkening of the skin and mucous membranes is primarily caused by elevated levels of [___], a precursor to both ACTH and melanocyte-stimulating hormone.
back:
• Pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC)
• POMC is processed into ACTH and MSH
• Elevation results from loss of cortisol-mediated feedback inhibition on the pituitary.

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: A 35-year-old female with vitiligo presents with progressive fatigue, salt cravings, and vomiting. Lab tests show hyponatremia and hyperkalemia. Identify the most likely underlying pathology in high-income countries.
back:
• Autoimmune adrenalitis
• Destroys steroidogenic cells via autoreactive T-cells
• Often associated with autoantibodies to 21-hydroxylase enzyme.

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: Explain the physiological mechanism behind the development of hyperkalemia and hyponatremia in patients with Addison disease.
back:
• Mineralocorticoid (Aldosterone) deficiency
• Results in decreased renal sodium reabsorption
• Impairs potassium excretion in the distal tubules, leading to hyperkalemia.

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: Contrast primary chronic adrenocortical insufficiency with secondary insufficiency regarding hyperpigmentation and aldosterone production.
back:
• Hyperpigmentation: Present in primary (high ACTH/POMC); absent in secondary (low ACTH).
• Aldosterone: Deficient in primary; near-normal in secondary (regulated by renin-angiotensin).

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: Identify the four most frequent etiologies of primary chronic adrenocortical insufficiency worldwide.
back:
• Autoimmune adrenalitis
• Infections (Tuberculosis, HIV/AIDS, Fungal)
• Metastatic neoplasms (Lung or breast carcinoma)
• Systemic diseases (Amyloidosis, Sarcoidosis).

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: Autoimmune polyendocrinopathy syndrome type 1 (APS-1), which includes Addison disease and chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis, is caused by mutations in the [___] gene.
back:
• AIRE (Autoimmune Regulator) gene
• Located on chromosome 21q22
• Mutation disrupts central T-cell tolerance in the thymus.

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: A patient on long-term prednisolone for rheumatoid arthritis abruptly stops medication. They present with intractable vomiting, abdominal pain, and cardiovascular collapse. State the most likely diagnosis.
back:
• Primary acute adrenocortical insufficiency (Adrenal Crisis)
• Caused by inability of atrophic adrenals to respond to stress
• Precipitated by sudden withdrawal of exogenous steroids.

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: Describe the morphologic features of the adrenal glands in Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome.
back:
• Massive bilateral adrenal hemorrhage
• Glands converted into sacs of clotted blood
• Associated with N. meningitidis sepsis and DIC.

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: Contrast the microscopic adrenal findings in autoimmune adrenalitis versus tuberculous adrenalitis.
back:
• Autoimmune: Irregularly shrunken glands with lymphoid infiltrates and cortical cell depletion.
• Tuberculous: Enlarged glands with effaced architecture by granulomatous inflammation and caseous necrosis.

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: List three classic clinical features of chronic adrenocortical insufficiency related to glucocorticoid deficiency.
back:
• Progressive weakness and easy fatigability
• Gastrointestinal symptoms (anorexia, nausea, weight loss)
• Hypoglycemia due to impaired gluconeogenesis.

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: A common form of monogenic diabetes characterized by primary genetic defects in ̢-cell function, occurring in younger patients and mimicking Type 2 DM, is [___].
back:
- Maturity-Onset Diabetes of the Young (MODY)
- Caused by germline loss-of-function mutations in specific genes
- Most common subtypes involve Glucokinase (GCK) or Hepatocyte Nuclear Factors (HNF).

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: A 12-year-old child presents with polyuria, polydipsia, and weight loss. Labs reveal hyperglycemia and positive autoantibodies against glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD). State the specific etiological category.
back:
- Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus (Immune-mediated)
- Characterized by autoimmune pancreatic ̢-cell destruction
- Results in an absolute deficiency of insulin and a high risk of ketoacidosis.

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: Explain the biological mechanism by which endocrinopathies such as Cushing syndrome or Acromegaly result in secondary Diabetes Mellitus.
back:
- Excess counter-regulatory hormones (Cortisol or Growth Hormone) act as insulin antagonists
- These stimulate hepatic gluconeogenesis and inhibit peripheral glucose utilization
- This results in secondary hyperglycemia categorized under Other Specific Types.

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: Contrast the primary pathophysiology and typical patient habitus of Type 1 versus Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus.
back:
- Type 1: Autoimmune ̢-cell destruction; absolute insulin deficiency; usually normal weight or recent weight loss
- Type 2: Peripheral insulin resistance with relative insulin deficiency; strongly associated with obesity and visceral adiposity.

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: Define Gestational Diabetes Mellitus (GDM) and mention its typical clinical course following parturition.
back:
- Glucose intolerance with onset or first recognition during pregnancy
- Induced by hormonal changes that increase insulin resistance
- Usually resolves after delivery, though it indicates increased risk for future Type 2 DM.

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: Diabetes Mellitus resulting from chronic pancreatitis, cystic fibrosis, or hemochromatosis is etiologically classified under the category of [___].
back:
- Exocrine Pancreatic Defects (Type 3c or Pancreatogenic Diabetes)
- Caused by direct inflammation, fibrosis, or tissue destruction of pancreatic islets
- Represents a secondary form of insulin deficiency.

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: A patient on long-term high-dose prednisolone for an autoimmune disorder develops a fasting blood glucose of 145 mg/dL. Identify the etiological classification for this condition.
back:
- Drug-induced Diabetes Mellitus
- Classified under "Other Specific Types" of Diabetes
- Glucocorticoids increase insulin resistance, stimulate gluconeogenesis, and promote protein catabolism.

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: Explain the biological defect found in Type A Insulin Resistance and name a classic cutaneous clinical finding associated with it.
back:
- Defect: Germline mutations in the insulin receptor affecting binding or signaling activity
- Finding: Acanthosis nigricans (velvety hyperpigmentation of skin folds)
- Results in severe insulin resistance and hyperinsulinemia.

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: Distinguish between Maturity-Onset Diabetes of the Young (MODY) and Type 1 Diabetes regarding their immunologic features.
back:
- MODY: A non-autoimmune monogenic defect; islet autoantibodies are absent
- Type 1 DM: An autoimmune disorder; positive for autoantibodies like Anti-GAD, Anti-Insulin, or Anti-IA2.

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: Identify the specific etiological category for neonatal diabetes appearing within the first 6 months of life due to KCNJ11 or ABCC8 mutations.
back:
- Genetic defects of ̢-cell function
- Involves ATP-sensitive potassium channel subunits (Kir6.2 or SUR1)
- Mutations prevent the channel from closing, inhibiting insulin secretion despite high glucose.

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: In developed nations, primary chronic adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease) is most commonly caused by [___].
back:
• Autoimmune adrenalitis (80–90% of cases).
• Autoimmune destruction of steroidogenic cells.
• Often involves autoantibodies against 21-hydroxylase.

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: A 45-year-old female presents with progressive fatigue, weight loss, and darkening of the skin in her palmar creases. Lab results show Na+ 128 mEq/L and K+ 5.8 mEq/L. Identify the likely diagnosis.
back:
• Chronic Adrenocortical Insufficiency (Addison Disease).
• Manifests with systemic metabolic failure.
• Characterized by volume depletion and hyperpigmentation.

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: Explain the role of the mineralocorticoid deficiency in causing the electrolyte abnormalities seen in Addison disease.
back:
• Aldosterone deficiency impairs renal sodium reabsorption.
• Results in excessive urinary sodium loss (hyponatremia).
• Causes decreased potassium excretion (hyperkalemia) and metabolic acidosis.

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: Contrast primary and secondary adrenocortical insufficiency regarding the presence of hyperpigmentation and mineralocorticoid levels.
back:
• Primary (Addison): Hyperpigmentation present (high ACTH/POMC); mineralocorticoids deficient.
• Secondary: Hyperpigmentation absent (low ACTH); mineralocorticoids usually normal (regulated by RAAS).

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: Enumerate three major infectious causes of chronic adrenocortical insufficiency globally, particularly in developing countries.
back:
• Tuberculosis (tuberculous adrenalitis).
• AIDS-associated infections (CMV, Mycobacterium avium-intracellulare).
• Disseminated fungal infections (Histoplasma capsulatum, Coccidioides immitis).

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: Clinical manifestations of adrenocortical insufficiency typically do not appear until at least [___]% of the adrenal cortex has been compromised.
back:
• 90%.
• Reflects the significant functional reserve of the adrenal glands.

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: A pediatric patient with Neisseria meningitidis septicemia develops rapidly progressive hypotension, shock, and widespread purpura. Identify the acute adrenal complication.
back:
• Waterhouse-Friderichsen Syndrome.
• Characterized by massive bilateral adrenal hemorrhage.
• Leads to primary acute adrenocortical insufficiency.

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: Describe the biochemical mechanism behind the hyperpigmentation observed in primary Addison disease.
back:
• Low cortisol triggers a compensatory increase in Pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC).
• POMC is a precursor to both ACTH and Melanocyte-Stimulating Hormone (MSH).
• High levels stimulate melanocytes directly.

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: Distinguish between Autoimmune Polyendocrine Syndrome Type 1 (APS-1) and Type 2 (APS-2) regarding their associated clinical features.
back:
• APS-1: Adrenalitis, hypoparathyroidism, and chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis (AIRE gene mutation).
• APS-2: Adrenalitis and autoimmune thyroiditis or Type 1 Diabetes.

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: Enlist the gastrointestinal clinical features commonly associated with Addison disease.
back:
• Anorexia and weight loss.
• Nausea and vomiting.
• Diarrhea.
• Abdominal pain.

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: The characteristic skin hyperpigmentation seen in primary chronic adrenocortical insufficiency is caused by the compensatory elevation of [___].
back: • POMC (pro-opiomelanocortin) • It is the common precursor molecule shared by ACTH and MSH • High levels directly stimulate melanocytes in pressure points and sun-exposed areas.

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: A 35-year-old female presents with extreme fatigue, weight loss, and low blood pressure. Labs reveal hyponatremia and hyperkalemia. Physical exam shows dark pigmentation of the palmar creases. Identify the most likely diagnosis.
back: • Addison Disease • Primary Chronic Adrenocortical Insufficiency • Characterized by the progressive destruction of the adrenal cortex and absolute hormone deficiency.

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: Explain the role of aldosterone deficiency in the electrolyte disturbances observed in Addison disease.
back: • Reduced renal tubular sodium reabsorption leading to hyponatremia • Impaired potassium excretion resulting in hyperkalemia • Volume depletion and hypotension follow urinary salt wasting.

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: Contrast the clinical presentation of primary versus secondary adrenocortical insufficiency regarding skin changes and mineralocorticoid function.
back: • Primary: Hyperpigmentation and hyperkalemia/hyponatremia are present • Secondary: Skin pallor occurs and electrolytes are typically normal • Secondary results from ACTH deficiency without affecting the zona glomerulosa.

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: Identify the specific gene mutation and clinical features that define Autoimmune Polyendocrine Syndrome Type 1 (APS-1).
back: • AIRE gene mutation causing defective central tolerance • Triad: Chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis, autoimmune hypoparathyroidism, and adrenalitis • Often presents during early childhood.

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: In patients with Addison disease caused by [___], the adrenal architecture is typically effaced by caseating granulomatous inflammation.
back: • Tuberculosis (Tuberculous adrenalitis) • Represents a major infectious cause in lower-income countries • Often associated with active infection in lungs or the genitourinary tract.

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: A patient with known Addison disease undergoes major surgery without dose adjustment of corticosteroids. They develop intractable vomiting, abdominal pain, and sudden vascular collapse. Name this condition.
back: • Adrenal Crisis (Primary Acute Adrenocortical Insufficiency) • Caused by an immediate physiological need for steroids exceeding atrophic adrenal capacity • Represents a life-threatening medical emergency.

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: Describe the microscopic changes found in the adrenal glands of a patient with primary autoimmune adrenalitis.
back: • Irregularly shrunken glands with cortical collapse and fibrosis • Extensive mononuclear lymphocytic infiltrate in the residual cortex • Relative preservation of the adrenal medulla.

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: Contrast Autoimmune Polyendocrine Syndrome Type 1 (APS-1) and Type 2 (APS-2) regarding typical associated diseases.
back: • APS-1: Candidiasis and hypoparathyroidism are hallmark features • APS-2: Adrenalitis with autoimmune thyroiditis or Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus • APS-2 is more prevalent than APS-1.

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: Enlist the classic gastrointestinal manifestations that herald the insidious onset of Addison disease.
back: • Anorexia and progressive weight loss • Nausea and recurrent vomiting • Chronic diarrhea and abdominal pain • Symptoms appear after 90 percent cortical loss.

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: In developed nations, 80% to 90% of primary chronic adrenocortical insufficiency cases are attributed to [___].
back: • Autoimmune adrenalitis. • Often associated with autoantibodies against 21-hydroxylase or 17-hydroxylase. • Results in progressive destruction of steroidogenic cells.

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: A 40-year-old female with a history of hypothyroidism presents with chronic fatigue, hypotension, and darkening of the skin on her palms and knuckles. Laboratory tests show high ACTH and low cortisol. Identify the most likely diagnosis.
back: • Addison Disease (Primary Chronic Adrenocortical Insufficiency). • Characterized by high ACTH due to loss of feedback. • Skin hyperpigmentation is a hallmark finding in primary cases.

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: Explain the role of Pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC) in the development of hyperpigmentation in patients with primary adrenal failure.
back: • Cortisol deficiency triggers increased pituitary POMC production. • POMC is a precursor to both ACTH and Melanocyte-Stimulating Hormone (MSH). • High levels of MSH-active peptides stimulate cutaneous melanocytes.

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: Contrast the mineralocorticoid-related electrolyte abnormalities in primary versus secondary adrenocortical insufficiency.
back: • Primary: Hyponatremia and hyperkalemia occur due to aldosterone deficiency. • Secondary: Aldosterone levels are near-normal (regulated by RAAS, not ACTH). • Volume depletion and hypotension are more severe in primary disease.

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: Identify the four most common pathological processes responsible for over 90% of all cases of Addison disease.
back: • Autoimmune adrenalitis (most common in developed countries). • Infections (Tuberculosis, Fungal, HIV/AIDS). • Metastatic neoplasms (Lung and Breast cancer). • Massive adrenal hemorrhage.

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: Clinical manifestations of Addison disease typically do not appear until at least [___] percent of the adrenal cortex has been compromised.
back: • 90 percent. • The disease has an insidious onset. • Significant reserve capacity delays clinical detection until destruction is near-complete.

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: A patient with a history of pulmonary disease presents with abdominal pain, weakness, and skin bronzing. Imaging reveals enlarged, calcified adrenal glands. What is the most likely infectious cause?
back: • Tuberculous adrenalitis. • Historically the leading cause of Addison disease worldwide. • Typically associated with active infection in lungs or genitourinary tract.

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: Describe the mechanism by which Autoimmune Regulator (AIRE) gene mutations lead to Addison disease in Autoimmune Polyendocrine Syndrome type 1 (APS-1).
back: • AIRE deficiency impairs central T-cell tolerance in the thymus. • Self-reactive T cells against adrenal antigens (like 21-hydroxylase) survive. • Leads to autoimmune destruction of multiple endocrine organs.

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: Contrast the presentation of Autoimmune Polyendocrine Syndrome type 1 (APS-1) and type 2 (APS-2) regarding their component conditions.
back: • APS-1: Addison disease, hypoparathyroidism, and chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis. • APS-2: Addison disease and autoimmune thyroiditis (with/without Type 1 Diabetes). • APS-1 typically presents in childhood; APS-2 in adulthood.

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: List the most frequent gastrointestinal symptoms that accompany the insidious onset of chronic adrenocortical insufficiency.
back: • Anorexia and weight loss. • Nausea and vomiting. • Abdominal pain and diarrhea. • These are often the first complaints before hypotension develops.

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: Within the etiological classification of Maturity-Onset Diabetes of the Young (MODY), the MODY2 subtype results from germline mutations in the enzyme [___].
back:
• Glucokinase (GCK)
• Function: Acts as the pancreatic glucose sensor
• Effect: Mutations raise the threshold for glucose-stimulated insulin release.

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: A 50-year-old male with chronic calcific pancreatitis and multiple hospitalizations for abdominal pain develops fasting hyperglycemia. Identify the etiological category for his diabetes.
back:
• Exocrine pancreatic defect
• Also known as Pancreatogenic or Type 3C Diabetes
• Caused by structural destruction of the entire islet cell mass.

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: Explain the immunological mechanism that initiates the destruction of pancreatic beta cells in immune-mediated Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus.
back:
• Breakdown in self-tolerance to islet autoantigens (e.g., GAD, insulin)
• Activation of CD4+ Th1 cells and CD8+ cytotoxic T cells
• Resultant insulitis and absolute insulin deficiency.

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: A 10-year-old presents with ketoacidosis and islet autoantibodies, while a 45-year-old obese male presents with acanthosis nigricans and hyperinsulinemia. Contrast their etiological drivers.
back:
• 10-year-old: Autoimmune T-cell mediated destruction (Type 1 DM)
• 45-year-old: Peripheral insulin resistance with relative insulin deficiency (Type 2 DM).

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: List three specific endocrinopathies that can etiologically cause secondary diabetes by antagonizing insulin action.
back:
• Cushing Syndrome (excess cortisol)
• Acromegaly (excess growth hormone)
• Pheochromocytoma (excess catecholamines)
• Hyperthyroidism (excess thyroid hormone).

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: Hyperglycemia that is first recognized during pregnancy and typically increases the risk for future overt Type 2 DM is classified as [___].
back:
• Gestational Diabetes Mellitus (GDM)
• Driven by pregnancy-associated hormonal shifts favoring insulin resistance
• Usually resolves post-delivery but indicates underlying metabolic susceptibility.

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: A patient with a history of HIV on Protease Inhibitor therapy develops persistent hyperglycemia. This condition is categorized under which etiological group?
back:
• Drug-induced diabetes
• Protease inhibitors interfere with insulin signaling and glucose transport
• Other triggers include glucocorticoids and thiazide diuretics.

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: Explain the divergent etiological mechanisms of beta-cell loss in Type 1 DM versus the chronic phase of Type 2 DM.
back:
• Type 1 DM: Primary autoimmune T-cell attack (insulitis) leading to rapid cell death
• Type 2 DM: Secondary "burnout" due to chronic insulin resistance, lipotoxicity (FFAs), and amyloid deposition.

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: Contrast the metabolic loop defects in MODY2 (Glucokinase) with those found in MODY3 (HNF1A).
back:
• MODY2: Defective glucose sensing; higher threshold for insulin release (stable hyperglycemia)
• MODY3: Failure of transcription factors regulating beta-cell function; progressive decline in insulin secretion.

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: Which specific genetic syndrome is commonly associated with an increased etiological risk of developing diabetes mellitus during childhood?
back:
• Down Syndrome
• Other associated syndromes include Turner Syndrome, Klinefelter Syndrome, and Prader-Willi Syndrome.

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
coreConcept: Most Common Cause of Addison Disease
front: In developed nations, 80% to 90% of cases of Addison disease are caused by [___], often associated with antibodies against 21-hydroxylase.
back:
• Autoimmune adrenalitis
• Destroys steroidogenic cells
• Can be isolated or part of Autoimmune Polyendocrinopathy Syndromes (APS)

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: A 45-year-old male presents with chronic malaise, anorexia, and hyperpigmentation of the palmar creases. Laboratory findings show serum Na+ 128 mEq/L and K+ 5.8 mEq/L. Identify the most likely condition.
back:
• Addison disease (Primary Chronic Adrenocortical Insufficiency)
• Key findings: Hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, and volume depletion
• Pigmentation is a cardinal diagnostic feature

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: Explain the biochemical mechanism leading to skin hyperpigmentation in patients with primary chronic adrenocortical insufficiency.
back:
• Low cortisol triggers elevated pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC)
• POMC is a precursor to both ACTH and MSH
• High MSH stimulates melanin production in melanocytes

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: Contrast the expected serum ACTH levels between primary and secondary adrenocortical insufficiency.
back:
• Primary (Addison): High ACTH due to loss of negative feedback
• Secondary (Pituitary): Low or inappropriately normal ACTH levels

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: List three specific components of Autoimmune Polyendocrinopathy Syndrome Type 1 (APS-1) besides adrenal insufficiency.
back:
• Chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis
• Ectodermal dystrophy (skin, enamel, nails)
• Autoimmune hypoparathyroidism
• Linked to AIRE gene mutations

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: Clinical manifestations of adrenocortical insufficiency typically do not appear until at least [___]% of the adrenal cortex has been compromised.
back:
• 90%
• Reflects the significant functional reserve of the gland
• Onset is typically insidious until this threshold is crossed

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: A newborn female presents with ambiguous genitalia and severe vomiting. Labs show hyponatremia and hyperkalemia. Identify the most likely underlying enzymatic defect.
back:
• 21-hydroxylase deficiency (Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia)
• Causes cortisol and aldosterone deficiency
• Diverts precursors to androgen synthesis pathways

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: Describe the physiological events that precipitate an 'Adrenal Crisis' in a patient with stabilized Addison disease.
back:
• Acute stress (infection, trauma, surgery) increases steroid demand
• Atrophic adrenals cannot increase cortisol output
• Results in hypotension, vascular collapse, and intractable vomiting

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: Contrast the status of the zona glomerulosa and mineralocorticoid secretion in primary versus secondary adrenocortical insufficiency.
back:
• Primary: Zona glomerulosa destroyed; causes salt-wasting and hyperkalemia
• Secondary: Zona glomerulosa spared; mineralocorticoid secretion remains near-normal (independent of ACTH)

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: Identify the gross morphologic difference in the adrenal glands between Addison disease caused by autoimmunity versus that caused by tuberculosis.
back:
• Autoimmune: Irregularly shrunken, atrophic glands
• Tuberculosis: Enlarged glands with architecture effaced by granulomatous inflammation

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: In primary adrenocortical insufficiency, hyperpigmentation of the skin occurs because of elevated levels of [___], a precursor molecule shared by ACTH and melanocyte-stimulating hormone.
back:
* Pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC)
* Increased POMC results from loss of cortisol feedback inhibition
* High levels directly stimulate melanocytes in skin and mucosa.

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: A 35-year-old female with progressive fatigue and skin darkening presents with serum sodium of 128 mEq/L and potassium of 5.8 mEq/L. Identify the primary hormone deficiency responsible for these electrolyte abnormalities.
back:
* Mineralocorticoids (Aldosterone)
* Deficiency causes renal sodium wasting (hyponatremia)
* Reduced potassium excretion leads to hyperkalemia
* Often results in volume depletion and hypotension.

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: Explain the role of ACTH in the development of hyperpigmentation seen in Addison disease.
back:
* Low cortisol triggers compensatory pituitary ACTH overproduction
* ACTH is synthesized from Pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC)
* POMC cleavage produces melanocyte-stimulating hormone (MSH)
* Elevated MSH/ACTH stimulates melanin synthesis in sun-exposed and pressure areas.

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: Contrast the clinical presentation of primary adrenocortical insufficiency with secondary adrenocortical insufficiency regarding skin color and electrolyte status.
back:
* Skin: Primary shows hyperpigmentation; Secondary shows pallor (low ACTH)
* Electrolytes: Primary has hyponatremia/hyperkalemia; Secondary has near-normal electrolytes
* Mineralocorticoids: Intact in secondary disease (regulated by Renin-Angiotensin).

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: Enlist the four most common causes of primary chronic adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease) worldwide.
back:
* Autoimmune adrenalitis (most common in developed countries)
* Infections (Tuberculosis, HIV/AIDS, Histoplasmosis)
* Metastatic neoplasms (Lung, Breast, GI tract)
* Systemic diseases (Amyloidosis, Sarcoidosis).

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: Autoimmune adrenalitis occurring in the context of Autoimmune Polyendocrine Syndrome Type 1 (APS-1) is caused by mutations in the [___] gene.
back:
* Autoimmune regulator (AIRE)
* Mutations impair central T-cell tolerance
* Characterized by adrenalitis, hypoparathyroidism, and mucocutaneous candidiasis.

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: A child presents with high fever, rapid-onset shock, and widespread purpuric skin lesions. Autopsy reveals massive bilateral adrenal hemorrhage. Identify the likely diagnosis and the classic causative organism.
back:
* Waterhouse-Friderichsen Syndrome
* Neisseria meningitidis septicemia
* Characterized by overwhelming sepsis and acute adrenal crisis.

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: Describe the cellular immune mechanisms that lead to adrenal cortex destruction in autoimmune adrenalitis.
back:
* Breakdown of self-tolerance to steroidogenic enzymes (21-hydroxylase)
* Cytotoxic T-lymphocyte (CD8+) mediated cell death
* Th1 cytokine release leading to macrophage activation
* Resulting in shrunken, lipid-depleted, lymphocytic-infiltrated glands.

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: Contrast the presentation of an acute adrenal crisis with the chronic features of Addison disease.
back:
* Acute: Intractable vomiting, severe abdominal pain, sudden hypotension, and coma
* Chronic: Insidious weakness, anorexia, weight loss, and progressive hyperpigmentation
* Acute crisis is often precipitated by stress or trauma.

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: Enlist the gastrointestinal manifestations typically observed in a patient with progressing Addison disease.
back:
* Anorexia and unexplained weight loss
* Nausea and persistent vomiting
* Abdominal pain
* Chronic diarrhea.

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: The progressive destruction of the adrenal cortex, resulting in clinical symptoms once approximately 90% of the gland is compromised, is termed [___].
back: Addison Disease (Primary chronic adrenocortical insufficiency).

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: A 40-year-old female with a history of vitiligo presents with progressive fatigue, vomiting, and new-onset hyperpigmentation at her knuckles and surgical scars. Labs show hyperkalemia and hyponatremia. Identify the likely diagnosis.
back: Addison Disease (Primary chronic adrenocortical insufficiency).

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: Explain the role of Pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC) in the development of hyperpigmentation in primary adrenal insufficiency.
back:
• Low cortisol triggers high ACTH production.
• ACTH is derived from POMC, a precursor shared with melanocyte-stimulating hormone (MSH).
• High POMC/MSH levels directly stimulate skin melanocytes.

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: Contrast the clinical findings of primary versus secondary adrenocortical insufficiency regarding skin pigmentation and electrolyte levels.
back:
• Primary: Hyperpigmentation (high ACTH) and hyperkalemia (low aldosterone).
• Secondary: Pallor/no pigmentation (low ACTH) and near-normal electrolytes (intact aldosterone).

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: Enlist the three cardinal components of Autoimmune Polyendocrine Syndrome Type 1 (APS-1).
back:
• Chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis.
• Ectodermal dystrophy (skin, nails, teeth).
• Organ-specific autoimmunity (hypoparathyroidism and adrenalitis).

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: In the developed world, the most frequent cause of primary chronic adrenocortical insufficiency is [___].
back: Autoimmune adrenalitis (80% to 90% of cases).

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: A pediatric patient with Neisseria meningitidis septicemia develops sudden cardiovascular collapse and widespread purpura. Autopsy reveals massive bilateral adrenal hemorrhage. Identify the syndrome.
back: Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome (Acute adrenocortical insufficiency).

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: How does a mutation in the AIRE (Autoimmune Regulator) gene lead to the development of autoimmune adrenalitis?
back:
• Impairs thymic expression of self-antigens.
• Leads to failure of negative selection (deletion) of autoreactive T-cells.
• Results in breakdown of central tolerance to adrenal tissues.

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: Distinguish the adrenal morphology in primary autoimmune adrenalitis from that seen in metastatic carcinoma involvement.
back:
• Autoimmune: Irregularly shrunken, small glands with lymphocytic infiltrates.
• Metastatic: Enlarged glands with normal architecture obscured by infiltrating tumor nests.

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: Identify the classic triad of symptoms that characterizes the initial metabolic onset of Addison disease.
back:
• Progressive weakness/fatigability.
• Gastrointestinal disturbances (anorexia, nausea, weight loss).
• Hyperpigmentation of the skin.

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
coreConcept: Epidemiology and Etiology of Addison Disease
front: In high-income countries, approximately 80% to 90% of chronic primary adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease) cases are caused by [___].
back:
• Autoimmune adrenalitis
  • Often associated with autoantibodies against 21-hydroxylase or 17-hydroxylase enzymes

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: A 38-year-old female presents with insidious onset of progressive weakness, weight loss, and darkening of the skin over her surgical scars and elbows. Laboratory results show low serum sodium and high potassium. Identify the most likely diagnosis.
back:
• Primary Chronic Adrenocortical Insufficiency (Addison disease)
  • Clinical features include hyperpigmentation, hypotension, and GI disturbances

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: Explain the role of Pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC) in the development of hyperpigmentation seen in primary adrenocortical insufficiency.
back:
• Low cortisol triggers high pituitary POMC production
  • POMC is the shared precursor for ACTH and Melanocyte-Stimulating Hormone (MSH)
  • Increased MSH directly stimulates skin pigmentation

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: Patient A presents with fatigue, normal potassium levels, and pale skin. Patient B presents with fatigue, hyperkalemia, and hyperpigmentation of the buccal mucosa. Contrast the likely anatomical levels of their endocrine lesions.
back:
• Patient A: Secondary insufficiency (Pituitary/Hypothalamic level); lacks ACTH elevation and mineralocorticoid deficiency
  • Patient B: Primary insufficiency (Adrenal cortex level); features both cortisol and aldosterone deficiency

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: Enlist the triad of clinical findings that characterize Autoimmune Polyendocrine Syndrome Type 1 (APS-1) caused by AIRE gene mutations.
back:
• Chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis
  • Autoimmune hypoparathyroidism
  • Autoimmune adrenalitis (Addison disease)
  • Also includes ectodermal dystrophy (skin, nails, enamel)

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: The mineralocorticoid deficiency in Addison disease leads to the hallmark electrolyte abnormalities of hyponatremia and [___].
back:
• Hyperkalemia
  • Caused by decreased renal potassium excretion and impaired sodium reabsorption

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: A 10-year-old child presents with high fever, rapidly progressing purpura, and sudden hypotension following a Neisseria meningitidis infection. Post-mortem examination reveals the adrenals as 'sacs of clotted blood.' Identify the syndrome.
back:
• Waterhouse-Friderichsen Syndrome
  • An acute primary adrenocortical insufficiency caused by massive bilateral adrenal hemorrhage

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: A patient with known Addison disease presents with intractable vomiting, abdominal pain, and vascular collapse following an acute respiratory infection. Explain the physiologic failure occurring in this 'Adrenal Crisis.'
back:
• Acute stress increases metabolic demand for glucocorticoids
  • The atrophic/damaged adrenal cortex fails to provide a compensatory steroid surge
  • Leads to rapid circulatory collapse and potential death

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: Contrast the macroscopic and microscopic appearance of the adrenal glands in tuberculous adrenalitis versus autoimmune adrenalitis.
back:
• Tuberculous: Enlarged glands with granulomatous inflammation and caseous necrosis
  • Autoimmune: Irregularly shrunken glands with loss of cortical cells and lymphoid infiltrates

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: Enlist the three most common extra-adrenal primary malignancies that metastasize to the adrenal glands, potentially causing insufficiency.
back:
• Lung carcinoma
  • Breast carcinoma
  • Gastrointestinal carcinomas
  • (Malignant melanoma is also a frequent source)

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: Primary chronic adrenocortical insufficiency, also known as Addison disease, typically does not manifest clinically until at least [___]% of the adrenal cortex has been compromised.
back:
• 90%
• Destruction must be progressive and extensive before metabolic reserves are exhausted.
• Clinical features appear insidiously once this threshold is crossed.

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
coreConcept: Epidemiology and Presentation of Addison Disease
front: A 40-year-old female presents with progressive fatigue, nausea, and weight loss. Physical exam reveals darkening of the skin at the elbows and knuckles. Identify the most likely diagnosis and its primary cause in high-income countries.
back:
• Diagnosis: Addison Disease (Primary Chronic Adrenocortical Insufficiency).
• Primary Cause: Autoimmune Adrenalitis.
• This accounts for 80% to 90% of cases in developed nations.

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: Explain the role of Pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC) in the development of hyperpigmentation specifically in primary adrenocortical insufficiency.
back:
• Low cortisol triggers a compensatory rise in pituitary POMC.
• POMC is a precursor to both ACTH and Melanocyte-Stimulating Hormone (MSH).
• Elevated MSH stimulates melanocytes, producing skin darkening at pressure points.

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: A patient with long-standing Addison disease undergoes major surgery and postoperatively develops intractable vomiting, hypotension, and vascular collapse. Identify the most likely acute complication.
back:
• Adrenal Crisis (Primary Acute Adrenocortical Insufficiency).
• Precipitated by stress (infection, surgery) that requires an immediate increase in steroid output that the atrophic adrenals cannot provide.

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: Enlist the specific electrolyte and glucose abnormalities typically encountered in primary chronic adrenocortical insufficiency.
back:
• Hyponatremia (Sodium loss due to mineralocorticoid deficiency).
• Hyperkalemia (Potassium retention).
• Hypoglycemia (Impaired gluconeogenesis due to glucocorticoid deficiency).
• Volume depletion and hypotension.

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: Autoimmune Polyendocrinopathy Syndrome Type 1 (APS-1) is caused by mutations in the [___] gene, leading to central T-cell tolerance failure.
back:
• AIRE (Autoimmune Regulator) gene.
• Characterized by a triad of chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis, ectodermal dystrophy (skin/nails), and organ-specific autoimmune destruction.

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: A 50-year-old male with chronic cough and weight loss presents with weakness and hyperpigmentation. Imaging reveals bilateral adrenal enlargement. What is the most likely infectious cause in low-income countries?
back:
• Tuberculous Adrenalitis.
• Effaces adrenal architecture with granulomatous inflammation.
• Usually associated with active infection in the lungs or genitourinary tract.

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: How does secondary adrenocortical insufficiency differ from primary Addison disease regarding hyperpigmentation and electrolyte balance?
back:
• No Hyperpigmentation: Low ACTH means MSH levels are not elevated.
• Normal Electrolytes: Aldosterone synthesis is usually preserved because it is regulated by the renin-angiotensin system, not pituitary ACTH.

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: Contrast the typical clinical findings of Autoimmune Polyendocrine Syndrome Type 1 (APS-1) with Type 2 (APS-2).
back:
• APS-1: Childhood onset; candidiasis, ectodermal dystrophy, and hypoparathyroidism.
• APS-2: Adult onset; combination of adrenal insufficiency and autoimmune thyroiditis or type 1 diabetes.

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: Identify the four most frequent disorders responsible for 90% of all Addison disease cases.
back:
• Autoimmune Adrenalitis (most common in high-income countries).
• Tuberculosis (common in endemic regions).
• AIDS (CMV, MAC infections).
• Metastatic Neoplasms (Lung and breast carcinoma).

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: Chronic adrenocortical insufficiency, also known as Addison disease, typically remains clinically silent until at least [___] of the adrenal cortex has been compromised or destroyed.
back:
* 90% (threshold for clinical manifestation).
* Symptoms appear earlier during periods of acute metabolic stress.
* Results in combined mineralocorticoid and glucocorticoid deficiency.

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: A 35-year-old female presents with progressive fatigue, nausea, and weight loss. Physical examination reveals bronze-like pigmentation on the knuckles, elbows, and buccal mucosa. Identify the most likely underlying pathophysiology for her skin changes.
back:
* Primary Adrenocortical Insufficiency (Addison disease).
* Loss of cortisol feedback leads to elevated Pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC) levels.
* POMC is a precursor to ACTH and Melanocyte-Stimulating Hormone (MSH).

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: Explain the role of aldosterone deficiency in the electrolyte disturbances seen in primary adrenocortical insufficiency.
back:
* Failure of sodium reabsorption in the distal renal tubules.
* Results in hyponatremia and volume depletion.
* Impaired excretion of potassium and hydrogen ions leads to hyperkalemia and metabolic acidosis.

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: Contrast primary versus secondary adrenocortical insufficiency regarding skin pigmentation and mineralocorticoid secretion.
back:
* Primary: Hyperpigmentation (high ACTH/MSH) and salt wasting (low aldosterone).
* Secondary: Skin pallor (low ACTH/MSH) and near-normal aldosterone levels (regulated by Renin-Angiotensin system).

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: Enlist the four most common causes of primary chronic adrenocortical insufficiency globally.
back:
* Autoimmune Adrenalitis (most common in developed nations).
* Tuberculosis (significant cause in Pakistan/developing nations).
* AIDS (associated with CMV or Kaposi sarcoma).
* Metastatic Neoplasms (chiefly Lung and Breast carcinoma).

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: Autoimmune polyendocrinopathy syndrome type 1 (APS-1) is caused by a mutation in the [___] gene, which normally facilitates central T-cell tolerance in the thymus.
back:
* AIRE (Autoimmune Regulator) gene.
* Characterized by Addison disease, hypoparathyroidism, and chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis.
* Results from failure to eliminate self-reactive T-cells.

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: A patient on long-term corticosteroid therapy suddenly stops their medication. They present to the ER with intractable vomiting, abdominal pain, and profound hypotension. Identify the diagnosis.
back:
* Acute Adrenocortical Insufficiency (Adrenal Crisis).
* Caused by rapid steroid withdrawal in the setting of atrophic adrenals.
* Represents a medical emergency requiring immediate IV saline and glucocorticoids.

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: Describe the morphologic changes in the adrenal glands during autoimmune adrenalitis versus tuberculous adrenalitis.
back:
* Autoimmune: Irregularly shrunken glands with thinned cortex and lymphocytic infiltrates.
* Tuberculous: Enlarged glands with architecture effaced by granulomatous inflammation and caseous necrosis.

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: Contrast the diagnostic response to exogenous ACTH administration in primary versus secondary adrenocortical insufficiency.
back:
* Primary: No increase in plasma cortisol (adrenal glands are destroyed).
* Secondary: Prompt rise in plasma cortisol (adrenal cortex remains functional and responsive).

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: List the classic triad of metabolic laboratory findings in an Addisonian patient.
back:
* Hyponatremia (Sodium < 135 mEq/L).
* Hyperkalemia (Potassium > 5.0 mEq/L).
* Hypoglycemia (due to glucocorticoid deficiency/impaired gluconeogenesis).

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
coreConcept: POMC as the mediator of Addisonian hyperpigmentation
front: In Primary Adrenocortical Insufficiency, hyperpigmentation occurs due to the elevation of [___], which is a precursor to both ACTH and melanocyte-stimulating hormone.
back:
• Pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC)
• Loss of feedback inhibition increases precursor synthesis
• High levels lead to direct stimulation of melanocytes

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: A 35-year-old female presents with progressive fatigue, nausea, and weight loss. Physical exam reveals darkening of the skin at the knuckles and elbows. Lab results show potassium of 5.8 mEq/L and sodium of 128 mEq/L. Identify the most likely diagnosis.
back:
• Addison Disease (Primary Chronic Adrenocortical Insufficiency)
• Characterized by electrolyte imbalances (hyperkalemia, hyponatremia)
• Hyperpigmentation confirms primary rather than secondary failure

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: Explain the role of the AIRE gene mutation in the pathogenesis of Autoimmune Polyendocrine Syndrome type 1 (APS-1).
back:
• AIRE normally promotes expression of peripheral antigens in the thymus
• Mutation causes failure of central T-cell tolerance
• Leads to autoimmune destruction of adrenal and parathyroid glands

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
coreConcept: Primary vs Secondary Adrenal Insufficiency Differential
front: Contrast the electrolyte disturbances and pigmentary changes seen in Primary vs. Secondary Adrenocortical Insufficiency.
back:
• Primary: Hyperpigmentation present; Hyponatremia/hyperkalemia common (aldosterone deficiency)
• Secondary: No hyperpigmentation; Normal electrolytes (aldosterone preserved via Renin-Angiotensin axis)
• Secondary failure lacks ACTH/POMC elevation

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: Enlist the three most common causes of primary chronic adrenocortical insufficiency globally, noting regional variation.
back:
• Autoimmune adrenalitis (most common in high-income regions)
• Tuberculosis (significant cause in lower-income regions)
• AIDS-associated infections (CMV, MAC)
• Metastatic carcinoma (Lung/Breast)

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: Acute adrenocortical insufficiency characterized by overwhelming bacterial sepsis (typically N. meningitidis) and massive bilateral adrenal hemorrhage is known as [___].
back:
• Waterhouse-Friderichsen Syndrome
• Presents with rapidly progressive hypotension and shock
• Associated with widespread purpura and DIC

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: A patient with long-standing rheumatoid arthritis suddenly stops taking high-dose prednisone. Within 24 hours, they present with intractable vomiting, abdominal pain, and vascular collapse. Identify the underlying pathophysiological event.
back:
• Acute Adrenal Crisis (Primary Acute Insufficiency)
• Chronic steroids cause bilateral adrenocortical atrophy
• Atrophic glands cannot meet homeostatic needs during stress/withdrawal

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: Describe how the mutation in Autoimmune Polyendocrine Syndrome type 1 (APS-1) results specifically in chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis.
back:
• Autoantibodies are generated against IL-17 and IL-22
• These cytokines are essential for Th17 T-cell function
• Loss of Th17 immunity prevents effective defense against fungal infections

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: Contrast the expected serum ACTH levels and the cortisol response to exogenous ACTH administration in Primary versus Secondary Adrenocortical Insufficiency.
back:
• Primary: Elevated ACTH; No cortisol rise (gland is non-functional)
• Secondary: Low/Normal ACTH; Prompt cortisol rise (gland responds to stimulus)
• Helps differentiate pituitary vs. adrenal pathology

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: Name the classic "90% rule" regarding the progression and manifestation of symptoms in Addison disease.
back:
• Clinical manifestations only appear after 90% of the cortex is destroyed
• Early stages are typically asymptomatic or vague
• Symptoms often manifest only during periods of physiologic stress

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: In Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus, the strongest genetic association is with the [___] gene cluster, specifically the DR3 and DR4 haplotypes.
back:
• HLA (Human Leukocyte Antigen) class II
• Specifically involves HLA-DR and HLA-DQ loci
• Contributes approximately 50% of the total genetic susceptibility.

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: A 10-year-old boy presents with sudden onset polyuria, polydipsia, and significant weight loss despite an increased appetite. Lab results show ketonuria. Identify the most likely underlying pathophysiology.
back:
• Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus
• T-cell mediated autoimmune destruction of pancreatic β-cells
• Results in an absolute insulin deficiency.

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: Explain the role of central (visceral) obesity in the development of insulin resistance in Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus.
back:
• Excess Free Fatty Acids (FFAs) overwhelm oxidation pathways, interfering with insulin signaling
• Pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-1β) released via inflammasome activation
• Reduced levels of the insulin-sensitizing hormone Adiponectin.

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: Contrast the primary acute metabolic complications typically seen in Type 1 versus Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus.
back:
• DM-1: Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA) due to absolute insulin lack and excessive ketone body formation
• DM-2: Hyperosmolar Hyperglycemic State (HHS) due to severe dehydration from sustained osmotic diuresis without significant ketosis.

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: Explain why serum C-peptide levels are useful in differentiating between Type 1 and Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus.
back:
• C-peptide is co-secreted with insulin
• Levels are low/absent in DM-1 (absolute deficiency)
• Levels are often normal or elevated in early DM-2 (reflecting insulin resistance and hyperinsulinemia).

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: According to World Health Organization criteria, a fasting plasma glucose level of [___] mg/dL or higher on two separate occasions is diagnostic for Diabetes Mellitus.
back:
• 126 mg/dL
• Alternatives: HbA1c ≥ 6.5% or random glucose ≥ 200 mg/dL with symptoms.

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: A long-standing diabetic patient's renal biopsy shows PAS-positive, ovoid, laminated hyaline masses in the glomerular periphery. Identify this pathognomonic lesion.
back:
• Nodular Glomerulosclerosis
• Also known as Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules
• Pathognomonic for Diabetic Nephropathy.

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: Explain how the interaction between Advanced Glycation End products (AGEs) and their receptor (RAGE) promotes vascular damage.
back:
• Induces reactive oxygen species (ROS) in endothelial cells
• Stimulates release of pro-inflammatory cytokines and growth factors (VEGF, TGF-β)
• Enhances procoagulant activity and vascular smooth muscle proliferation.

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: Contrast the classic histological findings within the pancreatic islets of Type 1 versus Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus.
back:
• DM-1: Insulitis (lymphocytic infiltration) and marked β-cell depletion
• DM-2: Amyloid deposition (amylin) within islets and subtle/mild β-cell reduction.

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: State the clinical advantage of using Glycated Hemoglobin (HbA1c) over random blood glucose for monitoring long-term diabetic control.
back:
• Reflects average blood glucose levels over the preceding 2–3 months
• Not affected by acute day-to-day fluctuations or recent meal intake
• Correlates strongly with the risk of chronic microvascular complications.

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: In Type 1 Diabetes, the primary genetic susceptibility is linked to the [___] gene cluster, specifically the DR3 and DR4 haplotypes.
back:
• HLA (Human Leukocyte Antigen) class II
• Contributes approximately 50% of genetic susceptibility
• Polymorphisms affect peptide-binding pockets during T-cell selection.

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: A 12-year-old child presents with rapid weight loss, extreme thirst, and frequent urination. Laboratory testing reveals ketones in the urine. Name the underlying mechanism of cell destruction.
back:
• Autoimmune destruction of pancreatic β-cells
• Mediated by T-lymphocytes (CD8+ CTLs and Th1 cells)
• Results in an absolute deficiency of insulin.

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: Explain the role of visceral adipose tissue in the development of insulin resistance in Type 2 Diabetes.
back:
• Releases excess Free Fatty Acids (FFAs) that overwhelm oxidation pathways
• Secretes pro-inflammatory adipokines (e.g., IL-1β)
• Reduces levels of insulin-sensitizing adiponectin.

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: Contrast the characteristic islet morphology seen in chronic Type 1 Diabetes versus Type 2 Diabetes.
back:
• DM-I: Insulitis (lymphocytic T-cell infiltrate) and severe β-cell depletion
• DM-II: Amyloid (amylin) deposition within islets and mild β-cell mass reduction.

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: Identify the biochemical byproduct measured to distinguish endogenous insulin production from exogenous administration in diabetic patients.
back:
• C-peptide
• Secreted in equimolar amounts with insulin from the Golgi complex
• Absent or low in DM-I; elevated or normal in early DM-II.

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: The 'gold standard' laboratory test for monitoring long-term glycemic control over the past 120 days is [___].
back:
• HbA1c (Glycated Hemoglobin)
• Reflects non-enzymatic addition of glucose to hemoglobin
• Diagnostic threshold for Diabetes is ≥ 6.5%.

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: A 65-year-old obese male with long-standing Type 2 Diabetes presents with severe dehydration and a plasma glucose of 800 mg/dL. He has no fruity breath or Kussmaul breathing. Diagnosis?
back:
• Hyperosmolar Hyperglycemic State (HHS)
• Characterized by extreme osmotic diuresis without significant ketosis
• Residual insulin prevents hepatic fatty acid oxidation/ketone formation.

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: Explain the role of the AGE-RAGE axis in the pathogenesis of diabetic vascular complications.
back:
• Hyperglycemia accelerates Advanced Glycation End product (AGE) formation
• AGEs bind RAGE receptors on endothelium/macrophages
• Induces ROS, pro-coagulant activity, and cross-links Type IV collagen.

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: Contrast the glomerular lesions of Diabetic Nephropathy: Diffuse Mesangial Sclerosis versus Nodular Glomerulosclerosis.
back:
• Diffuse: Generalized increase in PAS-positive mesangial matrix
• Nodular (Kimmelstiel-Wilson): Ovoid, laminated PAS+ matrix nodules in glomerular periphery.

category: Give differentiating features of DM-I and DM-II on the basis of pathogenesis, clinical features, diagnosis and complications
front: List the three classic clinical signs of newly onset Diabetes Mellitus (The Triad).
back:
• Polyuria (osmotic diuresis from glycosuria)
• Polydipsia (intracellular dehydration)
• Polyphagia (catabolic state and negative energy balance).

category: Describe the morphological features of inflammatory disorders of breast
front: The primary organism responsible for the formation of localized abscesses in the breast during the first month of breastfeeding is [___].
back:
• Staphylococcus aureus
• Streptococcus species (typically cause spreading cellulitis rather than localized abscesses).

category: Describe the morphological features of inflammatory disorders of breast
front: A 32-year-old female smoker presents with a painful subareolar mass and nipple inversion. Histology shows keratinizing squamous metaplasia of the duct lining. Identify the diagnosis.
back:
• Squamous Metaplasia of Lactiferous Ducts (Zuska disease)
• Key features: Keratin plugs, periductal granulomatous inflammation, and strong association with cigarette smoking.

category: Describe the morphological features of inflammatory disorders of breast
front: Explain the role of Vitamin A in the pathogenesis of squamous metaplasia of lactiferous ducts in smokers.
back:
• Smoking-induced Vitamin A deficiency or toxins alter ductal epithelial differentiation.
• This leads to keratinizing squamous metaplasia, which plugs the ductal system, causing rupture and granulomatous inflammation.

category: Describe the morphological features of inflammatory disorders of breast
front: Contrast the microscopic features of Fat Necrosis in the acute stage versus the chronic reparative stage.
back:
• Acute: Liquefactive fat necrosis, hemorrhage, and neutrophilic infiltrate.
• Chronic: Foamy macrophages, multinucleated giant cells, hemosiderin, and eventual replacement by scar tissue or calcified cysts.

category: Describe the morphological features of inflammatory disorders of breast
front: Describe the characteristic histopathological triad associated with Lymphocytic Mastopathy.
back:
• Densely collagenized (sclerotic) stroma.
• Atrophic ducts and lobules with thickened basement membranes.
• Prominent perivascular and periductal lymphocytic infiltrates.

category: Describe the morphological features of inflammatory disorders of breast
front: In the morphological presentation of Duct Ectasia, the dilated ducts are classically filled with [___] and numerous lipid-laden macrophages.
back:
• Inspissated (thickened) secretions
• Grossly appearing as a greenish-brown, cheesy discharge.

category: Describe the morphological features of inflammatory disorders of breast
front: A 55-year-old multiparous woman presents with a firm periareolar mass and skin retraction. Histology shows ductal dilation and a plasma cell-rich infiltrate. What is the diagnosis?
back:
• Mammary Duct Ectasia
• Clinically mimics carcinoma due to fibrosis and skin retraction; pathologically distinct by periductal chronic inflammation.

category: Describe the morphological features of inflammatory disorders of breast
front: Describe the mechanism by which Granulomatous Lobular Mastitis is distinguished from systemic granulomatous diseases.
back:
• The granulomatous inflammatory response is strictly restricted to the breast lobules.
• It typically occurs only in parous women and may show associated lipid vacuoles.

category: Describe the morphological features of inflammatory disorders of breast
front: Contrast the typical clinical presentation and patient profile of Lymphocytic Mastopathy with that of Acute Mastitis.
back:
• Lymphocytic Mastopathy: Hard palpable masses in women with Type 1 Diabetes or autoimmune thyroiditis.
• Acute Mastitis: Erythematous, painful breast with fever, exclusively during lactation/nursing.

category: Describe the morphological features of inflammatory disorders of breast
front: List the three components of the morphological reaction seen in Duct Ectasia once a duct ruptures.
back:
• Periductal/interstitial chronic inflammation (lymphocytes/plasma cells).
• Granuloma formation around cholesterol deposits.
• Extensive fibrosis producing an irregular mass.

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: Chronic adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease) typically remains clinically silent until at least [___]% of the adrenal cortex has been compromised.
back:
90%.
- Symptoms appear insidiously once this threshold of parenchymal destruction is reached.
- Primary destruction occurs due to intrinsic adrenal disease.

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
coreConcept: Epidemiology and Cause of Addison Disease
front: A 35-year-old female presents with persistent fatigue, nausea, and weight loss. Physical examination reveals bronze-like pigmentation on the palmar creases and knuckles. Laboratory tests show high ACTH and low serum cortisol. Identify the most likely cause in high-income countries.
back:
Autoimmune Adrenalitis.
- Accounts for 80-90% of primary cases in developed nations.
- Involves autoantibodies against steroidogenic enzymes like 21-hydroxylase.
- Often associated with Autoimmune Polyendocrine Syndromes (APS).

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: Explain the biochemical mechanism responsible for the skin hyperpigmentation observed in primary adrenocortical insufficiency but not in secondary disease.
back:
Elevated POMC levels.
- Low cortisol triggers high pituitary production of pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC).
- POMC is a precursor to both ACTH and melanocyte-stimulating hormone (MSH).
- Elevated levels stimulate melanocytes to increase melanin production.

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
coreConcept: Primary vs. Secondary Adrenal Insufficiency Differentiators
front: Contrast the serum electrolyte profile and serum ACTH levels between primary adrenocortical insufficiency and secondary adrenocortical insufficiency.
back:
- Primary: High ACTH; Hyponatremia and Hyperkalemia (due to mineralocorticoid deficiency).
- Secondary: Low/Normal ACTH; Normal potassium and sodium (near-normal aldosterone synthesis).

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: Identify the genetic mutation and the clinical triad associated with Autoimmune Polyendocrine Syndrome Type 1 (APS-1).
back:
AIRE gene mutation.
- Triad: Chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis.
- Ectodermal dystrophy (skin, nails, dental enamel).
- Autoimmune organ destruction (Adrenalitis, hypoparathyroidism, etc.).

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: Mineralocorticoid deficiency in Addison disease results in potassium [___] and sodium [___], eventually leading to hypotension and volume depletion.
back:
Retention; Loss.
- Leads to hyperkalemia and hyponatremia.
- Results in the characteristic 'salt-craving' and orthostatic hypotension seen in primary insufficiency.

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: A child presents with a high-grade fever, rapidly progressive purpura, and sudden cardiovascular collapse following a Neisseria meningitidis infection. Identify the syndrome and the underlying adrenal pathology.
back:
Waterhouse-Friderichsen Syndrome.
- Pathophysiology: Massive bilateral adrenal hemorrhage.
- Results in acute primary adrenocortical insufficiency and DIC-mediated shock.

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
front: Explain why a patient on long-term high-dose prednisolone is at risk of an 'adrenal crisis' if they abruptly stop the medication before a major surgery.
back:
Iatrogenic Adrenocortical Atrophy.
- Exogenous steroids suppress pituitary ACTH via negative feedback.
- Sustained low ACTH causes atrophy of the zona fasciculata and reticularis.
- The atrophic cortex cannot produce sufficient cortisol to meet surgical stress.

category: Enlist causes and clinical features of adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison disease)
