* Ectasia lacks the 'blue-dome' gross appearance of simple cysts.

category: Describe the morphological features of inflammatory disorders of breast
front: What is the primary significance of identifying fat necrosis or duct ectasia during a clinical breast examination?
back:
Mimicking Breast Cancer.
* Both produce firm, irregular palpable masses.
* Both can show mammographic calcifications or densities.
* Both can cause skin or nipple retraction.

category: Enumerate the infectious agents that cause the lower genital tract infections and PIDs along with lab investigations
front: The characteristic cytologic finding of Bacterial Vaginosis in a Papanicolaou smear is the presence of [___], which are squamous cells covered by a shaggy coat of coccobacilli.
back:
• Clue cells
• Caused by Gardnerella vaginalis
• Associated with thin, green-gray, malodorous (fishy) discharge.

category: Enumerate the infectious agents that cause the lower genital tract infections and PIDs along with lab investigations
front: A 24-year-old female presents with yellow, frothy vaginal discharge and a "strawberry cervix" visible on colposcopy. Identify the causative agent and the diagnostic finding on a wet mount.
back:
• Agent: Trichomonas vaginalis
• Diagnosis: Motile, large, flagellated ovoid protozoan on wet mount.

category: Enumerate the infectious agents that cause the lower genital tract infections and PIDs along with lab investigations
front: Explain the role of the Papanicolaou (Pap) smear and KOH mounts in the laboratory diagnosis of symptomatic Candidiasis.
back:
• Pap smear: Identifies pseudospores or filamentous fungal hyphae
• KOH mount: Dissolves cellular debris to highlight fungal elements
• Key signs: Pruritus and curdlike discharge.

category: Enumerate the infectious agents that cause the lower genital tract infections and PIDs along with lab investigations
front: Contrast the typical histological features of Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV) seen in a Tzanck smear compared to Molluscum Contagiosum in a biopsy.
back:
• HSV: Multinucleated cells with "ground-glass" intranuclear viral inclusions
• Molluscum Contagiosum: Pearly papules with large intracytoplasmic viral inclusions (Henderson-Paterson bodies).

category: Enumerate the infectious agents that cause the lower genital tract infections and PIDs along with lab investigations
front: Enumerate the common infectious agents responsible for non-gonococcal Pelvic Inflammatory Disease (PID) following a spontaneous or induced abortion.
back:
• Staphylococci
• Streptococci
• Coliforms (e.g., E. coli)
• Clostridium perfringens

category: Enumerate the infectious agents that cause the lower genital tract infections and PIDs along with lab investigations
front: In the laboratory diagnosis of acute gonorrhea from inflammatory exudates, a presumptive finding is the presence of phagocytosed [___] within neutrophils.
back:
• Gram-negative diplococci
• Definitive diagnosis requires culture or NAAT (DNA/RNA detection).

category: Enumerate the infectious agents that cause the lower genital tract infections and PIDs along with lab investigations
front: A 30-year-old patient presents with pelvic pain and adnexal tenderness. Biopsy reveals scarring and fusion of the tubal plicae forming gland-like spaces. Identify the chronic complication of PID described.
back:
• Chronic Salpingitis
• Leads to tubal obstruction, infertility, and high risk of ectopic pregnancy.

category: Enumerate the infectious agents that cause the lower genital tract infections and PIDs along with lab investigations
front: Describe the mechanism by which gonococcal PID leads to the formation of a "Tubo-ovarian abscess" (TOA).
back:
• Ascending endocervical infection spreads to fallopian tubes
• Induces acute suppurative salpingitis and purulent exudate
• Infection breaches fimbriated ends to involve the ovary, walling off pus.

category: Enumerate the infectious agents that cause the lower genital tract infections and PIDs along with lab investigations
front: Contrast the route of infection spread between gonococcal PID and staphylococcal puerperal PID.
back:
• Gonococcal: Spreads primarily along mucosal surfaces (lumen-limited initially)
• Puerperal (Staph/Strep): Spreads via deep lymphatics and venous channels, involving deeper tissue layers and broad ligaments.

category: Enumerate the infectious agents that cause the lower genital tract infections and PIDs along with lab investigations
front: Identify the two most frequent sexually transmitted pathogens causing Pelvic Inflammatory Disease in females younger than 35 years.
back:
• Chlamydia trachomatis
• Neisseria gonorrhoeae

category: Describe the morphological features of inflammatory disorders of breast
coreConcept: Squamous Metaplasia of Lactiferous Ducts (Zuska Disease)
front: In Squamous Metaplasia of Lactiferous Ducts (Zuska disease), the primary inciting event is the extension of [___] deep into the nipple duct, leading to keratin trapping and rupture.
back:
Keratinizing squamous metaplasia

* Extends past the usual transition point.
* Keratin debris causes intense granulomatous inflammation.
* Highly associated with cigarette smoking.

category: Describe the morphological features of inflammatory disorders of breast
front: A 45-year-old female presents with a firm, painless breast mass. Grossly, the lesion shows gray-white nodules with small chalky-white foci. Histology reveals multinucleated giant cells and lipid-laden macrophages. Diagnosis?
back:
Fat Necrosis

* Triggers: Prior trauma or surgery in ~50% of cases.
* Early stage: Liquefactive fat necrosis and hemorrhage.
* Late stage: Fibrosis, calcifications, and giant cell reaction.

category: Describe the morphological features of inflammatory disorders of breast
front: Explain the role of Staphylococcus aureus versus Streptococcus in the morphological presentation of acute lactational mastitis.
back:
* Staphylococcus aureus: Typically localized; tends to form single or multiple abscess cavities.
* Streptococcus: Characterized by diffuse, spreading infection in the form of cellulitis.

category: Describe the morphological features of inflammatory disorders of breast
front: Contrast the stromal findings and clinical associations of Lymphocytic Mastopathy with those of Duct Ectasia.
back:
* Lymphocytic Mastopathy: Dense collagenized stroma and atrophic ducts; linked to Type 1 Diabetes and autoimmune thyroiditis.
* Duct Ectasia: Periductal chronic inflammation and fibrosis; linked to multiparity and 5th-6th decade of life.

category: Describe the morphological features of inflammatory disorders of breast
front: Identify the defining histological feature and specific patient population associated with idiopathic Granulomatous Lobular Mastitis.
back:
* Histology: Granulomatous inflammation strictly limited to the breast lobules.
* Population: Occurs only in parous women.
* Pathogenesis: Possible hypersensitivity to antigens expressed during lactation.

category: Describe the morphological features of inflammatory disorders of breast
front: The hallmark of [___] is the presence of dilated ducts filled with inspissated secretions and numerous lipid-laden macrophages, often presenting as a palpable periareolar mass.
back:
Duct Ectasia

* Clinical: Thick, white nipple secretions and skin retraction.
* Gross: Dilated ducts with 'cheesy' material.
* Histology: Granulomatous response to ruptured secretions.

category: Describe the morphological features of inflammatory disorders of breast
front: A 35-year-old female smoker presents with a painful subareolar mass and an associated fistula tract opening at the edge of the areola. The nipple is inverted. Name this condition.
back:
Squamous Metaplasia of Lactiferous Ducts

* Also known as recurrent subareolar abscess or periductal mastitis.
* Caused by Vitamin A deficiency in smokers altering epithelium.
* Fistula develops under the nipple's smooth muscle.

category: Describe the morphological features of inflammatory disorders of breast
front: How does the 'swollen, erythematous breast' in Inflammatory Carcinoma differ microscopically from Acute Mastitis?
back:
* Inflammatory Carcinoma: Malignant emboli obstruct dermal lymphatics; peau d’orange appearance; usually lacks true inflammatory cells.
* Acute Mastitis: True infection with neutrophilic infiltration, edema, and tissue necrosis.

category: Describe the morphological features of inflammatory disorders of breast
front: Distinguish between 'classic' Hashimoto thyroiditis and Riedel thyroiditis regarding the extent of fibrosis.
back:
* Hashimoto: Fibrosis is limited to the thyroid gland parenchyma.
* Riedel: Extensive, woody fibrosis that extends beyond the thyroid capsule into contiguous neck structures; mimics malignancy.

category: Describe the morphological features of inflammatory disorders of breast
front: Identify the primary morphological feature of Riedel thyroiditis that distinguishes it from other forms of thyroid inflammation.
back:
Extensive, dense fibrosis

* Hard, 'woody' thyroid mass.
* Extends beyond the capsule to neck structures.
* Part of the IgG4-related disease spectrum.

category: Enumerate the infectious agents that cause the lower genital tract infections and PIDs along with lab investigations
coreConcept: Herpes Simplex Virus Morphologic Cytopathic Effects
front: In cervical smears, squamous cells containing multiple nuclei and intranuclear viral inclusions with a characteristic "ground-glass" appearance are diagnostic of [___].
back:
• Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV)
• Most commonly HSV-2 in the genital tract
• Accompanied by epithelial desquamation and acute inflammation

category: Enumerate the infectious agents that cause the lower genital tract infections and PIDs along with lab investigations
front: A 26-year-old female presents with a thin, malodorous, green-gray vaginal discharge. Microscopy reveals squamous cells with a "shaggy" appearance due to adherent organisms. Identify the causative agent.
back:
• Gardnerella vaginalis (Bacterial Vaginosis)
• Characterized by "clue cells" on Pap smear
• Associated with a positive "fishy" Whiff test

category: Enumerate the infectious agents that cause the lower genital tract infections and PIDs along with lab investigations
front: Explain how the depletion of vaginal Lactobacilli leads to lower genital tract infections like cervicitis.
back:
• Loss of lactic acid production increases vaginal pH (>4.5)
• Decreased bacteriotoxic hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) production
• Promotes overgrowth of anaerobes and Gardnerella

category: Enumerate the infectious agents that cause the lower genital tract infections and PIDs along with lab investigations
front: Contrast the route of infection and tissue depth typically seen in Gonococcal Pelvic Inflammatory Disease (PID) versus puerperal PID (post-abortion).
back:
• Gonococcal: Spreads via mucosal surfaces; primary involvement of the tube lumen (suppurative salpingitis)
• Puerperal: Spreads through lymphatics or veins; involves deeper layers/walls of the organs
• Higher bacteremia risk in puerperal infections

category: Enumerate the infectious agents that cause the lower genital tract infections and PIDs along with lab investigations
front: Enumerate the significant chronic sequelae resulting from untreated Pelvic Inflammatory Disease (PID).
back:
• Infertility and tubal obstruction
• Increased risk of ectopic pregnancy
• Chronic pelvic pain and intestinal obstruction (adhesions)

category: Enumerate the infectious agents that cause the lower genital tract infections and PIDs along with lab investigations
front: The characteristic colposcopic appearance of a "strawberry cervix" is produced by mucosal vessel dilation due to infection with [___].
back:
• Trichomonas vaginalis
• Large, flagellated ovoid protozoan
• Presents with yellow, frothy discharge and dysuria

category: Enumerate the infectious agents that cause the lower genital tract infections and PIDs along with lab investigations
front: A patient presents with multiple pearly, dome-shaped papules with a dimpled center on the vulva. Histology shows intracytoplasmic viral inclusions. Identify the pathogen.
back:
• Molluscum Contagiosum virus (MCV)
• A member of the poxvirus family
• MCV-2 is most commonly sexually transmitted in adults

category: Enumerate the infectious agents that cause the lower genital tract infections and PIDs along with lab investigations
coreConcept: Evolution of Tubal Pathology in PID
front: Outline the morphologic transition of the fallopian tubes from acute suppurative salpingitis to chronic hydrosalpinx.
back:
• Acute: Neutrophils infiltrate plicae; lumen fills with pus (pyosalpinx)
• Chronic: Plicae fuse and denude; fimbriae seal
• Result: Clear fluid distends the scarred tube (hydrosalpinx)

category: Enumerate the infectious agents that cause the lower genital tract infections and PIDs along with lab investigations
front: Distinguish between the microscopic findings of a Candida albicans wet mount compared to a Gardnerella vaginalis smear.
back:
• Candida: Pseudospores and filamentous fungal hyphae in KOH mount
• Gardnerella: Squamous "clue cells" covered in a shaggy coat of coccobacilli

category: Enumerate the infectious agents that cause the lower genital tract infections and PIDs along with lab investigations
front: Identify the two most definitive laboratory methods for confirming a Neisseria gonorrhoeae infection in suspected PID.
back:
• Bacterial culture (e.g., Thayer-Martin media)
• Nucleic Acid Amplification Test (NAAT) to detect gonococcal DNA/RNA

category: Enumerate the infectious agents that cause the lower genital tract infections and PIDs along with lab investigations
front: The hallmark histologic feature of a Human Papillomavirus (HPV) infection in the lower genital tract, characterized by perinuclear cytoplasmic vacuolization and nuclear enlargement, is [___].
back:
• Koilocytosis (or koilocytic atypia)
• Indicates viral cytopathic effect
• Commonly seen in condyloma acuminatum and squamous intraepithelial lesions

category: Enumerate the infectious agents that cause the lower genital tract infections and PIDs along with lab investigations
front: A 24-year-old female presents with a malodorous "fishy" vaginal discharge. A saline wet mount reveals squamous epithelial cells covered by a dense "shaggy coat" of coccobacilli. Identify the likely causative agent and the diagnostic cell name.
back:
• Agent: Gardnerella vaginalis
• Diagnosis: Bacterial vaginosis
• Cell: Clue cells (epithelial cells with blurred borders due to adherent bacteria)

category: Enumerate the infectious agents that cause the lower genital tract infections and PIDs along with lab investigations
front: Explain the role of vaginal Lactobacilli in preventing lower genital tract infections and how their depletion leads to disease.
back:
• Lactobacilli maintain vaginal pH < 4.5 via lactic acid production
• They produce bacteriotoxic hydrogen peroxide (H2O2)
• Depletion (by antibiotics/douching) allows overgrowth of anaerobes or Candida

category: Enumerate the infectious agents that cause the lower genital tract infections and PIDs along with lab investigations
front: Contrast the typical morphologic spread and tissue involvement of Neisseria gonorrhoeae with staphylococcal or streptococcal Pelvic Inflammatory Disease (PID).
back:
• N. gonorrhoeae: Spreads via mucosal surfaces; primary involvement of tube lumen (acute suppurative salpingitis)
• Staphylococci/Streptococci: Spread via lymphatics/veins; causes deeper inflammation within tube walls and broad ligaments

category: Enumerate the infectious agents that cause the lower genital tract infections and PIDs along with lab investigations
front: Identify the primary infectious agent associated with a "strawberry cervix" appearance and the motility characteristics used for its lab identification.
back:
• Agent: Trichomonas vaginalis
• Appearance: Fiery-red mucosa due to marked vessel dilation
• Lab: Saline wet mount shows large, flagellated ovoid protozoa with characteristic twitching motility

category: Enumerate the infectious agents that cause the lower genital tract infections and PIDs along with lab investigations
front: In suspected cases of genital herpes, smears from active lesions show multinucleated squamous cells containing [___] intranuclear viral inclusions.
back:
• "Ground-glass" inclusions
• Represents Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV) cytopathic effect
• Confirmed by NAAT/PCR or tissue culture

category: Enumerate the infectious agents that cause the lower genital tract infections and PIDs along with lab investigations
front: Following an induced abortion, a patient develops high fever and adnexal tenderness. Evaluation reveals extensive pelvic adhesions and a distended, fluid-filled fallopian tube. Name the complication and a common polymicrobial cause.
back:
• Complication: Hydrosalpinx (secondary to chronic salpingitis)
• Cause: Puerperal infection (Staphylococci, Streptococci, or Clostridium perfringens)
• Risk: Increases likelihood of ectopic pregnancy

category: Enumerate the infectious agents that cause the lower genital tract infections and PIDs along with lab investigations
front: Describe the mechanism of fallopian tube damage in Pelvic Inflammatory Disease (PID) that leads to permanent infertility.
back:
• Acute suppurative inflammation causes epithelial sloughing
• Denuded plicae adhere to one another during repair
• Resultant scarring/fusion forms blind pouches and luminal obstruction

category: Enumerate the infectious agents that cause the lower genital tract infections and PIDs along with lab investigations
front: Contrast the typical clinical findings and discharge characteristics of Candida albicans with Gardnerella vaginalis.
back:
• C. albicans: Thick, curd-like white discharge; marked pruritus and erythema; pH < 4.5
• G. vaginalis: Thin, green-gray malodorous discharge; Clue cells; pH > 4.5

category: Enumerate the infectious agents that cause the lower genital tract infections and PIDs along with lab investigations
front: Enumerate three primary laboratory investigations used to diagnose Chlamydia trachomatis cervicitis and its subsequent PID complications.
back:
• NAAT/PCR (Gold standard for detection)
• Identification of chronic endometritis via plasma cells in biopsy
• Culture or direct immunofluorescent antibody tests

category: Enumerate the infectious agents that cause the lower genital tract infections and PIDs along with lab investigations
front: In the diagnosis of bacterial vaginosis caused by Gardnerella vaginalis, Papanicolaou smears typically reveal superficial squamous cells covered with a shaggy coat of coccobacilli, known as [___].
back: - Clue cells. - Indicates a disturbance in vaginal microbial ecosystem. - Associated with thin, malodorous (fishy) discharge.

category: Enumerate the infectious agents that cause the lower genital tract infections and PIDs along with lab investigations
front: A 28-year-old female presents with yellow, frothy vaginal discharge and intense vulvovaginal discomfort. Colposcopy reveals marked dilation of mucosal vessels, termed a 'strawberry cervix.' The likely diagnosis is [___].
back: - Trichomoniasis (Trichomonas vaginalis). - Pathogen is a large, flagellated ovoid protozoan. - Usually transmitted via sexual contact.

category: Enumerate the infectious agents that cause the lower genital tract infections and PIDs along with lab investigations
front: Describe the characteristic microscopic cytopathic changes observed in a Tzanck smear or cervical biopsy of an active Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV) lesion.
back: - Multinucleated squamous cells. - Eosinophilic to basophilic intranuclear viral inclusions. - 'Ground-glass' chromatin appearance.

category: Enumerate the infectious agents that cause the lower genital tract infections and PIDs along with lab investigations
front: Contrast the typical pathways of spread and tissue involvement between PID caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae versus non-gonococcal puerperal infections (e.g., Staphylococci).
back: - Gonococcus: Spreads via mucosal surfaces; involves endosalpinx and tube lumen. - Puerperal: Spreads via lymphatics and veins; involves deeper layers, serosa, and broad ligaments.

category: Enumerate the infectious agents that cause the lower genital tract infections and PIDs along with lab investigations
front: Identify the primary morphologic features of chronic salpingitis and its most serious clinical consequences.
back: - Features: Fusion of tubal plicae and formation of gland-like blind pouches. - Consequences: Tubal infertility and increased risk of ectopic pregnancy.

category: Enumerate the infectious agents that cause the lower genital tract infections and PIDs along with lab investigations
front: Molluscum contagiosum, a lower genital tract infection characterized by pearly, dome-shaped papules with a dimpled center, is caused by a [___].
back: - Poxvirus. - Contains diagnostic intracytoplasmic viral inclusions. - Transmitted by direct contact or shared articles.

category: Enumerate the infectious agents that cause the lower genital tract infections and PIDs along with lab investigations
front: A diabetic patient presents with vulvovaginal pruritus and curd-like discharge. Identify the standard rapid laboratory investigation and the specific findings that confirm the diagnosis.
back: - Wet KOH mount of discharge. - Findings: Pseudospores or filamentous fungal hyphae. - Diagnosis: Candidiasis (Candida albicans).

category: Enumerate the infectious agents that cause the lower genital tract infections and PIDs along with lab investigations
front: Explain the physiological mechanism by which Lactobacilli maintain a protective environment against lower genital tract infections.
back: - Produce lactic acid to maintain vaginal pH below 4.5. - Synthesize bacteriotoxic hydrogen peroxide (H2O2). - Suppresses growth of saprophytic and pathogenic organisms.

category: Enumerate the infectious agents that cause the lower genital tract infections and PIDs along with lab investigations
front: Contrast the macroscopic and microscopic appearance of the fallopian tube in acute versus chronic salpingitis.
back: - Acute: Dilated lumen filled with pus; edematous, congested plicae with neutrophils. - Chronic: Fimbriae fusion (hydrosalpinx); scarred, adherent plicae forming blind pouches.

category: Enumerate the infectious agents that cause the lower genital tract infections and PIDs along with lab investigations
front: Identify the two most frequent sexually transmitted bacterial pathogens responsible for Pelvic Inflammatory Disease (PID).
back: - Neisseria gonorrhoeae. - Chlamydia trachomatis. - These are major causes of female infertility worldwide.

category: Enumerate causes of infertility in females along with hormonal investigations
front: To confirm that ovulation has occurred in an infertile female with a 28-day cycle, the most high-yield hormonal investigation is measuring serum [___] levels on Day 21.
back:
• Serum Progesterone.
• Levels >10 ng/mL indicate successful ovulation.
• Represents the mid-luteal phase activity of the corpus luteum.

category: Enumerate causes of infertility in females along with hormonal investigations
front: A 28-year-old female with primary infertility presents with hirsutism and irregular periods. Ultrasound shows a "string of pearls" appearance. Identify the primary hormonal profile associated with this diagnosis.
back:
• Polycystic Ovarian Syndrome (PCOS).
• Elevated LH:FSH ratio (>2:1 or 3:1).
• Increased serum androgens (Testosterone/DHEA).
• Results in chronic anovulation.

category: Enumerate causes of infertility in females along with hormonal investigations
front: Describe the mechanism by which Pelvic Inflammatory Disease (PID) leads to permanent mechanical infertility.
back:
• N. gonorrhoeae or Chlamydia cause acute suppurative salpingitis.
• Tubal plicae denude and fuse during the reparative scarring process.
• Leads to tubal obstruction, pyosalpinx, or hydrosalpinx, preventing oocyte passage.

category: Enumerate causes of infertility in females along with hormonal investigations
front: Contrast the FSH/LH profiles between Primary Ovarian Insufficiency (POI) and Hypogonadotropic Hypogonadism (Secondary Failure).
back:
• POI: High FSH and LH levels due to loss of negative feedback (hypergonadotropic).
• Secondary Failure: Low FSH and LH due to pituitary or hypothalamic dysfunction.
• Estrogen is low in both conditions.

category: Enumerate causes of infertility in females along with hormonal investigations
front: Enumerate three specific uterine structural causes of infertility that interfere with embryo implantation.
back:
• Submucosal Leiomyomas: Distort the endometrial cavity.
• Endometrial Polyps: Act as space-occupying lesions.
• Asherman Syndrome: Intrauterine synechiae (scarring) following over-vigorous curettage.

category: Enumerate causes of infertility in females along with hormonal investigations
front: In the hormonal evaluation of anovulation, elevated serum [___] suggests a diagnosis that inhibits GnRH pulsatility and causes secondary amenorrhea.
back:
• Prolactin.
• Inhibits FSH and LH secretion at the pituitary level.
• Often caused by lactotroph adenomas or dopamine-antagonist drugs.

category: Enumerate causes of infertility in females along with hormonal investigations
front: A 31-year-old female with severe cyclical pelvic pain and infertility undergoes laparoscopy, revealing "powder-burn" lesions and ovarian "chocolate cysts." What is the likely cause of her infertility?
back:
• Endometriosis.
• Ectopic endometrial tissue leads to extensive pelvic adhesions.
• Adhesions distort pelvic anatomy and interfere with fimbrial ovum pickup.

category: Enumerate causes of infertility in females along with hormonal investigations
front: Explain how Sheehan Syndrome leads to failure of conception in the postpartum period.
back:
• Pituitary infarction due to massive obstetric hemorrhage.
• Necrosis of gonadotrophs leads to loss of FSH and LH.
• Results in secondary hypogonadism, amenorrhea, and failure of follicular development.

category: Enumerate causes of infertility in females along with hormonal investigations
front: Contrast the clinical utility of Anti-Müllerian Hormone (AMH) versus Day 3 FSH in assessing ovarian reserve.
back:
• AMH: Reflects the primordial follicle pool; remains stable throughout the cycle.
• Day 3 FSH: High levels indicate poor reserve; values vary by cycle.
• AMH is a superior predictor of ovarian response to stimulation.

category: Enumerate causes of infertility in females along with hormonal investigations
front: Identify the primary endocrine investigation used to screen for ovulatory dysfunction caused by metabolic systemic disorders.
back:
• Serum TSH (to exclude Hypothyroidism).
• Abnormal thyroid levels disrupt GnRH secretion.
• Associated with menstrual irregularities and increased risk of early pregnancy loss.

category: Enumerate causes of infertility in females along with hormonal investigations
front: Chronic [___] resulting from Neisseria gonorrhoeae or Chlamydia trachomatis infection is a major cause of female infertility due to the fusion of tubal plicae and fimbriae.
back:
• Salpingitis
• Leads to fibrous scarring and tubal obstruction
• Prevents normal oocyte uptake and transport through the fallopian tube

category: Enumerate causes of infertility in females along with hormonal investigations
front: An obese 24-year-old female presents with primary infertility, hirsutism, and oligomenorrhea. Ultrasound shows enlarged ovaries with multiple subcortical follicles. Identify the underlying endocrine derangement.
back:
• Polycystic Ovarian Syndrome (PCOS)
• Characterized by excessive ovarian androgen production
• Associated with insulin resistance and dysregulated androgen biosynthesis enzymes

category: Enumerate causes of infertility in females along with hormonal investigations
front: Explain the role of measuring serum Progesterone on Day 21 of a standard 28-day menstrual cycle in an infertility workup.
back:
• Confirms successful ovulation has occurred
• Elevated levels indicate a functioning corpus luteum
• Determines if the secretory phase of the endometrium is maintained for implantation

category: Enumerate causes of infertility in females along with hormonal investigations
front: Contrast the anatomical location of "ectopic" endometrial tissue in Endometriosis versus Adenomyosis as causes of infertility.
back:
• Endometriosis: Tissue implants outside the uterus (e.g., ovaries forming 'chocolate cysts' or pelvic peritoneum)
• Adenomyosis: Tissue is located deep within the uterine myometrium
• Both cause inflammation that impairs fertility

category: Enumerate causes of infertility in females along with hormonal investigations
front: Enlist the specific hormonal investigations used to evaluate anovulation in a patient presenting with both galactorrhea and secondary infertility.
back:
• Serum Prolactin (detects hyperprolactinemia)
• Serum TSH (hypothyroidism can secondarily elevate prolactin)
• FSH and LH levels (assess hypothalamic-pituitary axis status)

category: Enumerate causes of infertility in females along with hormonal investigations
front: To evaluate a patient's ovarian reserve, basal serum [___] levels are typically measured alongside Anti-Müllerian Hormone (AMH) on Day 2 or 3 of the cycle.
back:
• FSH (Follicle-Stimulating Hormone)
• Persistently high basal FSH indicates diminished follicle pool
• Reflects Primary Ovarian Insufficiency or advancing reproductive age

category: Enumerate causes of infertility in females along with hormonal investigations
front: A patient with a history of recurrent PID fails to conceive. Imaging reveals a distended fallopian tube filled with clear fluid and fused fimbriae. What is the diagnosis?
back:
• Hydrosalpinx
• A consequence of chronic suppurative salpingitis
• Results from the accumulation of tubal secretions following fimbrial end blockage

category: Enumerate causes of infertility in females along with hormonal investigations
front: Describe the mechanism by which central obesity contributes to anovulatory infertility in patients with PCOS.
back:
• Adipose tissue increases peripheral conversion of androgens to estrone
• Elevated estrone provides abnormal feedback to the pituitary
• Disrupts the LH/FSH ratio, preventing dominant follicle selection

category: Enumerate causes of infertility in females along with hormonal investigations
front: Contrast the expected FSH and LH findings in Primary Ovarian Insufficiency (POI) versus Hypogonadotropic Hypogonadism (Secondary Failure).
back:
• POI: High FSH/LH (loss of negative feedback from ovarian steroids)
• Hypogonadotropic Hypogonadism: Low or inappropriately normal FSH/LH (pituitary or hypothalamic dysfunction)

category: Enumerate causes of infertility in females along with hormonal investigations
front: Identify the cause of panhypopituitarism leading to infertility in a female who fails to lactate and remains amenorrheic after a history of massive obstetric hemorrhage.
back:
• Sheehan Syndrome
• Ischemic necrosis of the anterior pituitary gland
• Results from pituitary enlargement during pregnancy combined with postpartum hypovolemic shock

category: Enumerate causes of infertility in females along with hormonal investigations
front: The most reliable serum biochemical marker for assessing ovarian reserve, which remains relatively stable throughout the menstrual cycle, is [___].
back:
• Anti-Müllerian Hormone (AMH)
• Produced by granulosa cells of preantral/small antral follicles
• Reflects the remaining primordial follicle pool
• Levels decrease significantly with advancing maternal age.

category: Enumerate causes of infertility in females along with hormonal investigations
front: A 26-year-old female presents with irregular menstrual cycles, hirsutism, and infertility for 3 years. Ultrasonography reveals 'string of pearls' ovaries. What is the expected LH to FSH ratio in this patient?
back:
• Elevated LH:FSH ratio (>2:1 or 3:1)
• Consistent with Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS)
• High LH stimulates ovarian androgen production
• Low FSH leads to impaired follicular maturation/anovulation.

category: Enumerate causes of infertility in females along with hormonal investigations
front: Explain the diagnostic mechanism of measuring serum progesterone during the mid-luteal phase (Day 21) in an infertile female.
back:
• Confirms the occurrence of ovulation
• Levels >10 ng/mL indicate successful release of an oocyte
• Reflects the secretory activity of the corpus luteum
• Low levels suggest anovulation or luteal phase deficiency.

category: Enumerate causes of infertility in females along with hormonal investigations
front: A patient with primary infertility shows FSH levels >40 IU/L on two occasions. Contrast this hormonal state with infertility caused by Hypothalamic Amenorrhea regarding gonadotropin levels.
back:
• Primary Ovarian Insufficiency (POI): Hypergonadotropic hypogonadism (High FSH/LH) due to negative feedback loss.
• Hypothalamic Amenorrhea: Hypogonadotropic hypogonadism (Low/Normal FSH/LH) due to GnRH pulsatility failure.

category: Enumerate causes of infertility in females along with hormonal investigations
front: In the hormonal workup of an infertile woman with galactorrhea, specify the necessary diagnostic step regarding the pituitary-thyroid axis.
back:
• Measure Serum Prolactin and TSH levels
• Primary hypothyroidism increases TRH
• TRH acts as a prolactin-releasing factor
• Resultant hyperprolactinemia inhibits GnRH pulsatility, causing anovulation.

category: Enumerate causes of infertility in females along with hormonal investigations
front: Chronic pelvic pain and infertility following a severe Pelvic Inflammatory Disease (PID) infection are most commonly attributed to structural damage of the [___].
back:
• Fallopian Tubes
• Mechanisms include tubal scarring, fimbrial adhesions, and hydrosalpinx
• Prevents sperm-ovum encounter or embryo transport to the uterus.

category: Enumerate causes of infertility in females along with hormonal investigations
front: A 32-year-old female presents with deep dyspareunia, cyclic pelvic pain, and inability to conceive. Laparoscopy shows 'chocolate cysts' in the ovaries. How does this condition impair fertility beyond structural adhesions?
back:
• Endometriosis
• Chronic inflammation creates a toxic peritoneal environment
• Cytokines impair sperm motility and ovum pickup
• Associated with poor oocyte quality and impaired implantation.

category: Enumerate causes of infertility in females along with hormonal investigations
front: Describe the physiological pathway by which extreme physical stress or weight loss leads to infertility and explain how this differs from the mechanism in Shehan Syndrome.
back:
• Functional Hypothalamic Amenorrhea: Reversible suppression of GnRH pulsatility due to stress/leptin deficiency.
• Sheehan Syndrome: Irreversible pituitary necrosis (hypopituitarism) usually following severe postpartum hemorrhage/shock.

category: Enumerate causes of infertility in females along with hormonal investigations
front: Contrast the impact of submucosal versus subserosal leiomyomas on a patient's ability to achieve and maintain pregnancy.
back:
• Submucosal Fibroids: Distort uterine cavity and impair implantation/blood supply (Significant infertility cause).
• Subserosal Fibroids: Located on the outer uterine surface; rarely interfere with fertility or cavity geometry.

category: Enumerate causes of infertility in females along with hormonal investigations
front: Identify the uterine condition characterized by intrauterine adhesions and amenorrhea following aggressive dilation and curettage (D&C).
back:
• Asherman Syndrome
• Destruction of the stratum basalis layer of the endometrium
• Leads to cavity obliteration and implantation failure
• Diagnosed via Hysterosalpingography (HSG) or Hysteroscopy.

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: Diabetes mellitus caused by the destruction of exocrine pancreatic tissue, such as in chronic pancreatitis or cystic fibrosis, is etiologically classified as [___].
back:
• Type 3c Diabetes (Pancreatogenic DM)
• Results from generalized loss of islet cell mass and exocrine function
• Often associated with malabsorption and nutrient deficiencies

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: A 15-year-old male with a BMI of 22 presents with new-onset hyperglycemia. Genetic testing reveals a mutation in the Glucokinase (GCK) gene. Identify the specific etiological diagnosis.
back:
• MODY2 (Maturity-Onset Diabetes of the Young, Type 2)
• A monogenic form of DM characterized by a primary defect in beta-cell glucose sensing and function.

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: Explain the primary pathophysiologic triad defining the etiological classification of Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus.
back:
• Genetic susceptibility (primarily HLA-DR3/DR4 linkage)
• Autoimmune destruction of pancreatic beta cells
• Absolute insulin deficiency requiring exogenous replacement

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: Contrast the etiological basis of hyperglycemia in Cushing Syndrome versus Acromegaly.
back:
• Cushing Syndrome: Excess glucocorticoids induce gluconeogenesis and inhibit peripheral glucose uptake.
• Acromegaly: Growth Hormone excess antagonizes insulin's metabolic actions and stimulates hepatic glucose production.

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: List three specific drugs or chemical agents that can etiologically cause secondary Diabetes Mellitus.
back:
• Glucocorticoids (Steroids)
• Thiazide diuretics
• Protease inhibitors (HIV therapy)
• Phenytoin (Dilantin)

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: The etiological sub-classification of Type 1 Diabetes that results in absolute insulin deficiency but lacks detectable islet autoantibodies is [___].
back:
• Idiopathic Type 1 Diabetes (Type 1B)
• Most common in individuals of African or Asian descent
• Pathogenesis is non-immune-mediated beta-cell loss.

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: A 32-year-old pregnant female at 26 weeks gestation has an abnormal Oral Glucose Tolerance Test (OGTT). Identify the specific etiological classification of her condition.
back:
• Gestational Diabetes Mellitus (GDM)
• Glucose intolerance first recognized during pregnancy
• Usually resolves postpartum but increases future Type 2 DM risk.

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: Detail how specific genetic defects in insulin action (Type A Insulin Resistance) differ from Type 2 DM in etiological classification.
back:
• Type A: Direct monogenic mutations in the insulin receptor gene (binding or kinase defects).
• Type 2 DM: Polygenic disorder involving post-receptor signaling defects, obesity, and insulin resistance.

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: Contrast the etiologies of Neonatal Diabetes versus Maturity-Onset Diabetes of the Young (MODY).
back:
• Neonatal DM: Onset <6 months; often due to activating mutations in K-ATP channel subunits (KCNJ11/ABCC8).
• MODY: Onset usually <25 years; involves mutations in transcription factors (HNF1A) or Glucokinase.

category: Give etiological Classification of DM (Diabetes Mellitus)
front: Identify the primary etiological defect shared by all forms of Maturity-Onset Diabetes of the Young (MODY).
back:
• Genetic defects of beta-cell function
• Autosomal dominant inheritance of single-gene mutations (monogenic diabetes)
• Impaired insulin secretion without autoimmune destruction.

category: Enumerate the infectious agents that cause the lower genital tract infections and PIDs along with lab investigations
front: In a female patient presenting with a "fishy" malodorous vaginal discharge, the Papanicolaou (Pap) smear typically reveals superficial squamous cells covered with a shaggy coat of coccobacilli, commonly referred to as [___].
back:
• Clue cells
• Diagnostic for Bacterial Vaginosis
• Caused by the overgrowth of *Gardnerella vaginalis*

category: Enumerate the infectious agents that cause the lower genital tract infections and PIDs along with lab investigations
front: A 24-year-old female presents with yellow, frothy vaginal discharge and intense vulvovaginal pruritus. Colposcopy reveals a "strawberry cervix." Identify the most likely infectious agent and the specific diagnostic finding on a wet mount.
back:
• Agent: *Trichomonas vaginalis*
• Lab finding: Motile, flagellated ovoid protozoans
• Morphology: Marked dilation of cervical mucosal vessels

category: Enumerate the infectious agents that cause the lower genital tract infections and PIDs along with lab investigations
front: Explain the role of the E6 and E7 oncoproteins encoded by high-risk Human Papillomavirus (HPV) serotypes 16 and 18 in cervical carcinogenesis.
back:
• E6 protein: Binds and degrades p53 tumor suppressor
• E7 protein: Inactivates RB protein and inhibits p21/p27
• Result: Genomic instability and cellular immortalization

category: Enumerate the infectious agents that cause the lower genital tract infections and PIDs along with lab investigations
front: Contrast the characteristic microscopic viral inclusions seen in Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV) with those seen in *Molluscum contagiosum*.
back:
• HSV: Multinucleated squamous cells with "ground-glass" intranuclear inclusions
• Molluscum: Pearly papules with large, eosinophilic intracytoplasmic inclusions (Henderson-Paterson bodies)

category: Enumerate the infectious agents that cause the lower genital tract infections and PIDs along with lab investigations
front: Enumerate the three most common categories of microbial agents responsible for Pelvic Inflammatory Disease (PID) and identify the specific site where gonococcal infection typically starts.
back:
• Agents: *N. gonorrhoeae*, *C. trachomatis*, and polymicrobial anaerobes
• Initial site: Endocervical mucosa
• Complications: Tubo-ovarian abscess and infertility

category: Enumerate the infectious agents that cause the lower genital tract infections and PIDs along with lab investigations
front: The definitive laboratory diagnosis of a suspected *Neisseria gonorrhoeae* infection in a patient with suppurative salpingitis requires either a bacterial culture or the detection of [___].
back:
• Gonococcal RNA or DNA (NAAT)
• Morphology: Phagocytosed Gram-negative diplococci within neutrophils

category: Enumerate the infectious agents that cause the lower genital tract infections and PIDs along with lab investigations
front: A patient presents with painful vulvar vesicles that progress to coalescent ulcers. A biopsy shows multinucleated giant cells. Which laboratory test is most useful for distinguishing between a primary acute infection and a recurrent/latent phase?
back:
• Serum anti-HSV antibodies
• Primary: Absence of specific anti-HSV antibodies
• Recurrent/Latent: Detection of anti-HSV antibodies in serum

category: Enumerate the infectious agents that cause the lower genital tract infections and PIDs along with lab investigations
front: Analyze how chronic salpingitis following an acute episode of Pelvic Inflammatory Disease (PID) results in structural tubal changes and subsequent ectopic pregnancy.
back:
• Denuded tubal plicae adhere and fuse (scarring)
• Formation of gland-like spaces and blind pouches
• Obstructs oocyte passage while allowing sperm entry

category: Enumerate the infectious agents that cause the lower genital tract infections and PIDs along with lab investigations
front: Contrast the lab findings and vaginal pH disturbances seen in symptomatic Candidal Vulvovaginitis versus *Gardnerella vaginalis* infections.
back:
• Candida: Normal pH (<4.5); KOH mount shows pseudospores or hyphae
• Gardnerella: Alkaline pH (>4.5); Pap smear shows "shaggy" clue cells

category: Enumerate the infectious agents that cause the lower genital tract infections and PIDs along with lab investigations
front: List three laboratory molecular or immunological methods, apart from tissue culture, used for the detection of Herpes Simplex Virus in genital secretions.
back:
• Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR)
• Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA)
• Direct immunofluorescent antibody tests

category: Enumerate causes of infertility in females along with hormonal investigations
front: A major cause of female infertility resulting from the upward spread of Neisseria gonorrhoeae or Chlamydia trachomatis is [___].
back:
Pelvic Inflammatory Disease (PID).
• Leads to acute suppurative salpingitis and tubal scarring.
• Causes fimbrial fusion and chronic tubal obstruction.
• Increases the risk of ectopic pregnancy.

category: Enumerate causes of infertility in females along with hormonal investigations
front: A 28-year-old female with obesity and hirsutism presents with primary infertility. Labs reveal hyperandrogenism and elevated serum estrone. Identify the underlying ovarian condition.
back:
Polycystic Ovarian Syndrome (PCOS).
• Characterized by chronic anovulation and decreased fertility.
• Associated with insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes.
• Morphologically shows numerous subcortical cystic follicles.

category: Enumerate causes of infertility in females along with hormonal investigations
front: Explain the role of chronic salpingitis in the mechanism of female infertility.
back:
Permanent tubal dysfunction.
• Adhesion and fusion of tubal plicae create blind pouches.
• Fibrous scarring narrows or obliterates the tubal lumen.
• Prevents the necessary uptake and passage of oocytes.

category: Enumerate causes of infertility in females along with hormonal investigations
front: Contrast the clinical impact of submucosal leiomyomas versus subserosal leiomyomas on female reproductive success.
back:
Submucosal: Impairs fertility by distorting the endometrial cavity and preventing implantation.
• Subserosal: Primarily asymptomatic regarding fertility; causes pressure on the bladder or bowel.

category: Enumerate causes of infertility in females along with hormonal investigations
front: Identify the primary hormonal investigation used to screen for infertility in a patient presenting with spontaneous galactorrhea and amenorrhea.
back:
Serum Prolactin levels.
• Elevated prolactin inhibits GnRH release from the hypothalamus.
• Results in secondary failure of ovulation.
• Most commonly caused by a lactotroph adenoma.

category: Enumerate causes of infertility in females along with hormonal investigations
front: Infertility associated with 'chocolate cysts' of the ovary and extensive pelvic adhesions is diagnostic of [___].
back:
Endometriosis.
• Defined as ectopic endometrial glands and stroma outside the uterus.
• Causes periodic bleeding leading to organizing hemorrhage and fibrosis.
• Distorts pelvic anatomy, preventing normal oocyte capture.

category: Enumerate causes of infertility in females along with hormonal investigations
front: A woman experiences massive obstetric hemorrhage during delivery and subsequently fails to lactate or resume menses. Identify the underlying pituitary cause of her infertility.
back:
Sheehan Syndrome (Postpartum Necrosis).
• Ischemic infarction of the anterior pituitary during hemorrhage.
• Leads to panhypopituitarism and loss of gonadotropins (LH/FSH).
• Results in permanent amenorrhea and infertility if untreated.

category: Enumerate causes of infertility in females along with hormonal investigations
front: Describe how 21-hydroxylase deficiency in congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH) results in female reproductive dysfunction.
back:
Androgen Excess Pathway.
• Blocked cortisol synthesis triggers compensatory ACTH elevation.
• Adrenal androgens overproduce, leading to virilization.
• High androgens disrupt the hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis, causing oligomenorrhea.

category: Enumerate causes of infertility in females along with hormonal investigations
front: Contrast the diagnostic utility of early follicular phase FSH versus mid-luteal phase Progesterone in infertility workups.
back:
Early FSH (Day 2/3): Assesses ovarian reserve and screens for primary ovarian insufficiency.
• Mid-luteal Progesterone (Day 21): Confirms that ovulation has successfully occurred during that cycle.

category: Enumerate causes of infertility in females along with hormonal investigations
front: Enumerate three structural uterine causes of female infertility and their hormonal status.
back:
Causes:
• Chronic Endometritis (e.g., Chlamydia or Tuberculosis).
• Submucosal Leiomyomas or Endometrial Polyps.
• Hormonal Status: Usually euthyroid/eumenorrheic, as these are anatomic defects.

category: Enlist causes of dysfunctional uterine bleeding with histopathological features
front: The most frequent underlying cause of dysfunctional uterine bleeding (DUB) is [___].
back: Anovulation (failure to ovulate), leading to hormonal imbalances that disrupt the regular cycle.

category: Enlist causes of dysfunctional uterine bleeding with histopathological features
front: A 46-year-old female presents with irregular menses. Endometrial biopsy shows stromal condensation, eosinophilic epithelial metaplasia, and cystic glandular dilation without subnuclear vacuoles. Identify the diagnosis.
back:
Anovulatory cycle (Dysfunctional Uterine Bleeding).
* Key features: Estrogen-driven proliferative glands without progesterone-induced secretory changes.

category: Enlist causes of dysfunctional uterine bleeding with histopathological features
front: Explain why progesterone-dependent morphologic features are absent in the histopathology of anovulatory dysfunctional uterine bleeding.
back: Without ovulation, the corpus luteum fails to develop; consequently, there is no source of progesterone to induce glandular differentiation or stromal predecidualization.

category: Enlist causes of dysfunctional uterine bleeding with histopathological features
front: Contrast the endometrial breakdown seen in anovulatory dysfunctional uterine bleeding with that of a normal menstrual cycle.
back: Anovulatory breakdown occurs in proliferative-type glands under unopposed estrogen; normal menstrual breakdown occurs after secretory exhaustion and a drop in progesterone levels.

category: Enlist causes of dysfunctional uterine bleeding with histopathological features
front: Enlist three non-gonadal systemic causes that can result in anovulatory dysfunctional uterine bleeding.
back:
1. Thyroid disease
2. Adrenal disease
3. Pituitary tumors (e.g., Prolactinoma)

category: Enlist causes of dysfunctional uterine bleeding with histopathological features
front: Dysfunctional uterine bleeding is clinically defined as uterine bleeding that lacks an underlying [___].
back: Structural (organic) abnormality (e.g., no leiomyomas, polyps, or carcinomas).

category: Enlist causes of dysfunctional uterine bleeding with histopathological features
front: A 52-year-old obese female presents with heavy bleeding. Histology shows an increased gland-to-stroma ratio with back-to-back glands. Identify the condition resulting from her prolonged unopposed estrogenic state.
back:
Endometrial Hyperplasia.
* This represents an exaggerated response to the same hormonal stimulus that causes basic DUB.

category: Enlist causes of dysfunctional uterine bleeding with histopathological features
front: How does obesity specifically carry out its effect on the pathogenesis of chronic anovulatory cycles?
back: Adipose tissue contains aromatase, which converts adrenal androgens into estrogens, maintaining a high circulating level of estrogen that suppresses the regular hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis.

category: Enlist causes of dysfunctional uterine bleeding with histopathological features
front: Distinguish between the histopathological appearance of early secretory phase DUB (luteal phase defect) and anovulatory DUB.
back:
* Luteal phase defect: Delayed secretory vacuoles (relative to cycle day).
* Anovulatory DUB: Complete absence of secretory vacuoles; only proliferative/cystic glands.

category: Enlist causes of dysfunctional uterine bleeding with histopathological features
front: Name the specific hormone responsible for the 'sawtooth' appearance of glands in the late phase of a functional menstrual cycle.
back:
Progesterone.
* It causes glandular tortuosity and secretory exhaustion, which is lacking in patients with anovulatory DUB.

category: Enlist causes of dysfunctional uterine bleeding with histopathological features
coreConcept: Primary Etiology of Dysfunctional Uterine Bleeding
front: The most common underlying hormonal disturbance leading to dysfunctional uterine bleeding is [___].
back:
• Anovulation (failure to ovulate)
• Results in excessive, unopposed estrogenic stimulation
• Histology shows persistent proliferative phase without secretory changes

category: Enlist causes of dysfunctional uterine bleeding with histopathological features
front: A 14-year-old girl recently reached menarche and presents with irregular, heavy periods. Endometrial biopsy shows proliferative-type glands and stromal condensation without subnuclear vacuoles. Identify the diagnosis.
back:
• Anovulatory cycle
• Most common at the extremes of reproductive life (menarche and perimenopause)
• Characterized by a lack of progesterone effect

category: Enlist causes of dysfunctional uterine bleeding with histopathological features
front: Explain the role of the corpus luteum absence in the histopathology of anovulatory dysfunctional uterine bleeding.
back:
• No corpus luteum formation means no progesterone production
• Prevents secretory differentiation (no subnuclear vacuoles or predecidualization)
• Leads to a persistent proliferative pattern with eventual stromal breakdown

category: Enlist causes of dysfunctional uterine bleeding with histopathological features
front: Contrast the microscopic appearance of anovulatory endometrium with normal menstrual endometrium.
back:
• Anovulatory: Proliferative-type glands with focal stromal condensation and breakdown
• Menstrual: "Sawtooth" glands with secretory exhaustion, predecidualized stroma, and neutrophils

category: Enlist causes of dysfunctional uterine bleeding with histopathological features
front: Enlist the conditions associated with generalized metabolic disturbances that often lead to anovulatory dysfunctional uterine bleeding.
back:
• Obesity (peripheral conversion of androgens to estrogens)
• Malnutrition and chronic systemic diseases
• Polycystic Ovarian Syndrome (PCOS)

category: Enlist causes of dysfunctional uterine bleeding with histopathological features
front: In long-standing anovulatory dysfunctional uterine bleeding, the endometrial glands frequently undergo architectural changes such as [___] and eosinophilic epithelial metaplasia.
back:
• Cystic dilation
• Caused by persistent, unopposed estrogen stimulation
• Usually resolves if a subsequent ovulatory cycle occurs

category: Enlist causes of dysfunctional uterine bleeding with histopathological features
front: A 32-year-old female presents with infertility and regular cycles but light bleeding. Biopsy performed on day 21 of the cycle reveals day 17 secretory changes. Identify the cause of this bleeding pattern.
back:
• Inadequate luteal phase (ovulatory DUB)
• Caused by low progesterone levels or poor corpus luteum function
• Histology shows secretory changes lagging by >2 days from expected date

category: Enlist causes of dysfunctional uterine bleeding with histopathological features
front: Describe the mechanism by which unopposed estrogen specifically leads to stromal breakdown and clinical bleeding in anovulation.
back:
• Continuous estrogen stimulates glandular/stromal proliferation
• The endometrium outgrows its hormonal and vascular support
• Leads to focal areas of ischemia, stromal condensation, and irregular shedding

category: Enlist causes of dysfunctional uterine bleeding with histopathological features
front: Distinguish between the stromal findings in dysfunctional uterine bleeding and chronic endometritis.
back:
• DUB: Shows stromal breakdown, condensation, or dyssynchronous maturity
• Chronic Endometritis: Characterized by the diagnostic presence of plasma cells in the stroma

category: Enlist causes of dysfunctional uterine bleeding with histopathological features
front: The clinical term used to describe uterine bleeding that lacks an underlying structural or organic abnormality is [___].
back:
• Dysfunctional Uterine Bleeding (DUB)
• Most cases stem from hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis disturbances
• Diagnosis is made by excluding polyps, fibroids, or cancer

category: Discuss pathophysiology and lab diagnosis of eclampsia and preeclampsia
front: The inciting event in the pathogenesis of preeclampsia is the failure of trophoblasts to convert decidual [___] from small-caliber resistance vessels to large-capacity vessels.
back:
• Spiral arteries
• Lack of physiological remodeling prevents adequate perfusion
• Results in placental ischemia and hypoxia

category: Discuss pathophysiology and lab diagnosis of eclampsia and preeclampsia
front: A 26-year-old primipara in her 35th week of gestation presents with a blood pressure of 165/110 mmHg, generalized edema, and 3+ proteinuria on dipstick. Identify the condition.
back:
• Preeclampsia
• Defined by hypertension, edema, and proteinuria
• Occurs typically in the last trimester

category: Discuss pathophysiology and lab diagnosis of eclampsia and preeclampsia
coreConcept: Role of sFlt1 in Endothelial Dysfunction
front: Describe the mechanism by which the placenta-derived antiangiogenic factor sFlt1 induces systemic maternal symptoms in preeclampsia.
back:
• Antagonizes VEGF and PlGF signaling
• Leads to widespread systemic endothelial dysfunction
• Reduces PGI2 production, promoting vasoconstriction and hypertension

category: Discuss pathophysiology and lab diagnosis of eclampsia and preeclampsia
front: Contrast preeclampsia and eclampsia regarding their primary clinical distinction and Central Nervous System (CNS) involvement.
back:
• Preeclampsia: Hypertension, edema, and proteinuria only
• Eclampsia: Addition of convulsions and potential coma
• Eclampsia is a severe progression of systemic endothelial dysfunction

category: Discuss pathophysiology and lab diagnosis of eclampsia and preeclampsia
front: Identify the characteristic vascular lesion seen in the decidual vessels of the placenta in patients with eclampsia.
back:
• Acute atherosis
• Features fibrinoid necrosis of the vessel wall
• Characterized by subendothelial lipid-laden macrophages

category: Discuss pathophysiology and lab diagnosis of eclampsia and preeclampsia
front: Renal involvement in preeclampsia is pathologically characterized by [___], where glomerular endothelial cells swell and fibrin is deposited on the basement membrane.
back:
• Glomerular endotheliosis
• Causes narrowed capillary lumens
• Associated with mesangial cell hyperplasia and proteinuria

category: Discuss pathophysiology and lab diagnosis of eclampsia and preeclampsia
front: A pregnant patient at 36 weeks gestation presents with hypertension, jaundice, and right upper quadrant pain. Labs reveal schistocytes on peripheral smear, low platelets, and elevated ALT. Identify the syndrome.
back:
• HELLP Syndrome
• H: Hemolysis (microangiopathic)
• EL: Elevated Liver enzymes
• LP: Low Platelets

category: Discuss pathophysiology and lab diagnosis of eclampsia and preeclampsia
front: Explain the role of soluble endoglin in the development of systemic hypertension during preeclampsia.
back:
• Released by ischemic placenta
• Antagonizes TGF-beta signaling
• Inhibits endothelial nitric oxide production, leading to vasoconstriction

category: Discuss pathophysiology and lab diagnosis of eclampsia and preeclampsia
front: Contrast the spiral arteries of a normal pregnancy with those in a preeclamptic pregnancy regarding their smooth muscle coat.
back:
• Normal: Trophoblasts replace smooth muscle, creating large-capacity vessels
• Preeclamptic: Vessels retain their smooth muscle coat
• Result: Persistent small-caliber resistance vessels cause placental ischemia

category: Discuss pathophysiology and lab diagnosis of eclampsia and preeclampsia
front: Enumerate two maternal systemic complications of preeclampsia that serve as absolute indications for immediate delivery regardless of gestational age.
back:
• Eclampsia (convulsions)
• HELLP syndrome
• Severe end-organ dysfunction (e.g., acute renal failure or pulmonary edema)

category: Enlist causes of dysfunctional uterine bleeding with histopathological features
coreConcept: Primary Cause of Dysfunctional Uterine Bleeding
front: The most frequent cause of dysfunctional uterine bleeding is the [___] cycle, resulting from hormonal imbalances most common during menarche and the perimenopausal period.
back:
Anovulatory
* Caused by unopposed estrogenic stimulation
* Leads to excessive endometrial proliferation
* Lacks the stabilizing effect of progesterone.

category: Enlist causes of dysfunctional uterine bleeding with histopathological features
front: A 48-year-old female presents with irregular, heavy menstrual bleeding. Endometrial biopsy reveals cystic dilation of glands, stromal condensation, and an absence of secretory changes. Identify the underlying pathophysiology.
back:
Anovulatory Dysfunctional Bleeding
* Excessive estrogen stimulation without ovulation
* Absence of corpus luteum and progesterone
* Leads to architectural distortion and breakthrough bleeding.

category: Enlist causes of dysfunctional uterine bleeding with histopathological features
front: Explain the role of unopposed estrogen in the mechanism of anovulatory dysfunctional uterine bleeding.
back:
* Estrogen drives continuous glandular/stromal proliferation
* No progesterone is produced to induce secretory differentiation
* Endometrium outgrows blood supply, leading to stromal breakdown and hemorrhage.

category: Enlist causes of dysfunctional uterine bleeding with histopathological features
front: Contrast the microscopic features of an anovulatory cycle with an inadequate luteal phase.
back:
Anovulatory Cycle:
* Non-secretory glands with cystic dilation and stromal condensation.
Inadequate Luteal Phase:
* Secretory features are present but lag behind the expected cycle day (e.g., >2 days behind).

category: Enlist causes of dysfunctional uterine bleeding with histopathological features
front: Identify the four major functional categories that cause abnormal uterine bleeding across different life stages.
back:
* Anovulatory cycle (most common)
* Inadequate luteal phase
* Oral contraceptive-induced changes
* Menopausal/Postmenopausal atrophy.

category: Enlist causes of dysfunctional uterine bleeding with histopathological features
front: In dysfunctional uterine bleeding due to inadequate luteal phase deficiency, the endometrial biopsy classically demonstrates [___] secretory changes.
back:
Lagging (or Delayed)
* Associated with low progesterone levels
* Morphology fails to match chronological cycle day
* Clinical presentation includes infertility or increased bleeding.

category: Enlist causes of dysfunctional uterine bleeding with histopathological features
front: A 28-year-old female presents with breakthrough bleeding while taking combined oral contraceptive pills. The endometrial biopsy is likely to show [___].
back:
Inactive glands with plump, decidualized stroma
* Discordance between glandular and stromal maturation
* Glands are small and quiescent
* Stroma appears large and eosinophilic (decidual-like).

category: Enlist causes of dysfunctional uterine bleeding with histopathological features
front: Provide the mechanistic rationale for why postmenopausal females experience abnormal uterine bleeding in the absence of structural lesions.
back:
Endometrial Atrophy
* Low estrogen levels lead to a thin, inactive endometrium
* Friable tissue and dilated cystic glands easily bleed
* Must be distinguished from endometrial carcinoma via biopsy.

category: Enlist causes of dysfunctional uterine bleeding with histopathological features
front: Contrast the stromal appearance of a normal menstrual endometrium with that of an anovulatory endometrium.
back:
Menstrual Endometrium:
* Shows stromal breakdown with mixed inflammatory infiltrates and predecidual changes.
Anovulatory Endometrium:
* Shows stromal condensation and eosinophilic epithelial metaplasia without predecidualization.

category: Enlist causes of dysfunctional uterine bleeding with histopathological features
front: Define Dysfunctional Uterine Bleeding (DUB) and its distinguishing clinical criterion.
back:
DUB is abnormal uterine bleeding lacking an underlying structural abnormality
* Diagnosis of exclusion
* No polyps, fibroids, or malignancies present
* Primarily stems from hormonal disturbances.

category: Enlist causes of dysfunctional uterine bleeding with histopathological features
front: Clinical uterine bleeding that occurs in the absence of an underlying structural or organic abnormality is termed [___].
back:
• Dysfunctional Uterine Bleeding (DUB).
• Primarily results from hormonal imbalances.
• Most commonly associated with anovulatory cycles.

category: Enlist causes of dysfunctional uterine bleeding with histopathological features
front: A 16-year-old female presents with irregular, heavy menstrual cycles. Endometrial biopsy reveals pseudostratified glands with mitoses and stromal breakdown but lacks secretory vacuoles. Identify the most likely underlying condition.
back:
• Anovulatory cycle.
• Caused by unopposed estrogen stimulation.
• Histology shows persistent proliferative features without progesterone-induced secretory changes.

category: Enlist causes of dysfunctional uterine bleeding with histopathological features
front: Explain the cellular consequence of the absence of a corpus luteum on the endometrial glands during a dysfunctional cycle.
back:
• Leads to absolute deficiency of progesterone.
• Prevents transition from proliferative to secretory phase.
• Results in excessive endometrial stimulation by estrogens, leading to architectural abnormalities.

category: Enlist causes of dysfunctional uterine bleeding with histopathological features
front: Contrast the histological features of anovulatory dysfunctional uterine bleeding with those of normal menstrual shedding.
back:
• Anovulatory DUB: Breakdown occurs in the setting of proliferative glands (pseudostratification, mitoses).
• Normal Menses: Breakdown occurs in secretory-phase endometrium (exhausted glands, predecidualized stroma).

category: Enlist causes of dysfunctional uterine bleeding with histopathological features
front: Identify the diagnostic histological finding in an endometrial biopsy taken on day 22 of a 28-day cycle in a patient with an 'inadequate luteal phase.'
back:
• Discrepancy/Lag in secretory changes.
• Histologic age lags behind clinical cycle date by >2 days.
• Caused by deficient progesterone production from the corpus luteum.

category: Enlist causes of dysfunctional uterine bleeding with histopathological features
front: The definitive histological diagnosis of chronic endometritis as a cause of abnormal bleeding requires the detection of [___] within the endometrial stroma.
back:
• Plasma cells.
• Often accompanied by lymphocytes and neutrophils.
• Frequently associated with Chlamydia or retained products of conception.

category: Enlist causes of dysfunctional uterine bleeding with histopathological features
front: A 52-year-old obese female presents with heavy postmenopausal bleeding. Biopsy shows an increased gland-to-stroma ratio with dilated acini. State the likely metabolic driver of this lesion.
back:
• Endometrial Hyperplasia.
• Driven by peripheral conversion of androgens to estrogens in adipose tissue.
• Results in prolonged, unopposed estrogenic stimulation.

category: Enlist causes of dysfunctional uterine bleeding with histopathological features
front: Explain the role of PTEN tumor suppressor gene inactivation in the development of hyperplastic endometrial lesions.
back:
• PTEN loss causes overactivation of the PI3K/AKT pathway.
• Increases endometrial cell sensitivity to estrogen.
• Drives excessive proliferation, leading to atypical hyperplasia and carcinoma.

category: Enlist causes of dysfunctional uterine bleeding with histopathological features
front: Differentiate between Typical Hyperplasia and Atypical Hyperplasia based on microscopic nuclear morphology.
back:
• Typical: Glandular crowding with normal, proliferative-type nuclei.
• Atypical: Rounder nuclei, vesicular (open) chromatin, and conspicuous nucleoli (Endometrial Intraepithelial Neoplasia).

category: Enlist causes of dysfunctional uterine bleeding with histopathological features
front: Enlist three non-neoplastic systemic conditions that result in anovulation and subsequent dysfunctional uterine bleeding.
back:
• Polycystic Ovarian Syndrome (PCOS).
• Thyroid disease (Hypo/Hyperthyroidism).
• Pituitary tumors (Prolactinomas) or adrenal disorders.

category: Enlist causes of dysfunctional uterine bleeding with histopathological features
front: The clinical term for uterine bleeding that lacks an underlying structural abnormality and most commonly stems from hormonal disturbances is [___].
back:
• Dysfunctional Uterine Bleeding (DUB).
• Most frequently caused by anovulation (failure to ovulate).
• Results in excessive endometrial stimulation by estrogens unopposed by progesterone.

category: Enlist causes of dysfunctional uterine bleeding with histopathological features
front: A 15-year-old female presents with irregular, heavy menses since menarche. Biopsy reveals stromal condensation and eosinophilic epithelial metaplasia without subnuclear vacuoles. Identify the diagnosis.
back:
• Anovulatory cycle.
• Pathophysiology: Immature hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis leads to failure of ovulation.
• Histology: Lacks progesterone-dependent features like glandular secretory changes.

category: Enlist causes of dysfunctional uterine bleeding with histopathological features
coreConcept: Corpus Luteum Function in Glucose Homeostasis
front: Explain the role of the corpus luteum in preventing the development of dysfunctional uterine bleeding.
back:
• Produces progesterone after ovulation.
• Induces endometrial differentiation and secretory phase maturation.
• Absence causes unopposed estrogen stimulation, leading to irregular stromal breakdown.

category: Enlist causes of dysfunctional uterine bleeding with histopathological features
front: Contrast the microscopic significance of stromal plasma cells in an endometrial biopsy versus their significance in the cervix.
back:
• Endometrium: Diagnostic for chronic endometritis, a potential cause of bleeding/infertility.
• Cervix: Common and clinically insignificant finding in most women due to microflora.

category: Enlist causes of dysfunctional uterine bleeding with histopathological features
front: Name the two primary age groups most frequently affected by anovulatory dysfunctional uterine bleeding.
back:
• Adolescence (menarche).
• Perimenopausal period.
• Both occur due to hormonal imbalances and fluctuations in the hypothalamic-pituitary axis.

category: Enlist causes of dysfunctional uterine bleeding with histopathological features
front: In anovulatory dysfunctional uterine bleeding, the endometrium fails to demonstrate [___] due to the lack of progesterone-induced maturation.
back:
• Secretory changes (subnuclear vacuoles).
• Stromal pre-decidualization.
• These features only occur if a functional corpus luteum develops post-ovulation.

category: Enlist causes of dysfunctional uterine bleeding with histopathological features
front: A 26-year-old female with obesity and hirsutism presents with secondary amenorrhea followed by heavy bleeding. Biopsy shows mild architectural changes and cystic dilation. Identify the underlying metabolic cause.
back:
• Polycystic Ovarian Syndrome (PCOS).
• Mechanism: Peripheral conversion of androgens to estrogens in fat tissue.
• Results in chronic anovulation and unopposed estrogenic stimulation.

category: Enlist causes of dysfunctional uterine bleeding with histopathological features
front: Explain how functioning ovarian granulosa cell tumors result in the development of dysfunctional uterine bleeding.
back:
• Tumors actively secrete high levels of estrogen.
• Persistent hormone levels drive continuous endometrial proliferation.
• Unopposed by progesterone, the tissue eventually undergoes irregular shedding.

category: Enlist causes of dysfunctional uterine bleeding with histopathological features
front: Contrast the gland morphology in the normal proliferative phase versus anovulatory dysfunctional uterine bleeding.
back:
• Proliferative: Regular, straight tubular glands lined by tall pseudostratified columnar cells.
• Anovulatory: Mild architectural changes, including cystic dilation and eosinophilic epithelial metaplasia.

category: Enlist causes of dysfunctional uterine bleeding with histopathological features
front: Identify the non-neoplastic, inflammatory cause of abnormal uterine bleeding characterized by the presence of plasma cells in the stroma.
back:
• Chronic Endometritis.
• Associated with PID, retained gestational tissue, or IUCD use.
• Histology: Essential finding is plasma cells (not seen in normal endometrium).

category: Discuss pathophysiology and lab diagnosis of eclampsia and preeclampsia
front: Preeclampsia is characterized by hypertension, edema, and proteinuria; the addition of convulsions to this clinical triad defines the condition known as [___].
back:
• Eclampsia
• A severe systemic syndrome involving maternal endothelial dysfunction
• Most commonly occurs in the last trimester, particularly in primiparas

category: Discuss pathophysiology and lab diagnosis of eclampsia and preeclampsia
front: A 36-week pregnant female presents with hypertension, proteinuria, schistocytes on a peripheral film, and a platelet count of 55,000/µL. Identify the likely diagnosis.
back:
• HELLP Syndrome
• H: Hemolysis
• EL: Elevated Liver enzymes
• LP: Low Platelets

category: Discuss pathophysiology and lab diagnosis of eclampsia and preeclampsia
front: Explain the failure of vascular remodeling in the spiral arteries that initiates the pathogenesis of preeclampsia.
back:
• Fetal trophoblasts fail to invade maternal decidual vessels correctly
• Spiral arteries remain small-caliber resistance vessels instead of large-capacity conduits
• Resultant placental ischemia triggers the release of systemic antiangiogenic factors

category: Discuss pathophysiology and lab diagnosis of eclampsia and preeclampsia
front: Contrast the roles of VEGF/TGF-β with sFlt1 and soluble endoglin in the development of maternal hypertension during pregnancy.
back:
• VEGF/TGF-β: Maintain endothelial health and stimulate nitric oxide (vasodilator) production
• sFlt1/Endoglin: Antagonize VEGF and TGF-β, leading to systemic vasoconstriction and increased vascular permeability

category: Discuss pathophysiology and lab diagnosis of eclampsia and preeclampsia
front: Enumerate the characteristic gross and microscopic findings in the liver of a patient who succumbed to eclampsia.
back:
• Gross: Irregular, focal subcapsular and intraparenchymal hemorrhages
• Microscopic: Fibrin thrombi in portal capillaries
• Foci of hemorrhagic necrosis in the parenchyma

category: Discuss pathophysiology and lab diagnosis of eclampsia and preeclampsia
front: Microscopic examination of the placenta in preeclampsia reveals larger and more numerous [___], along with increased syncytial knots and retroplacental hematomas.
back:
• Infarcts
• Caused by chronic malperfusion and uteroplacental ischemia
• Associated with abnormal decidual vessels showing fibrinoid necrosis

category: Discuss pathophysiology and lab diagnosis of eclampsia and preeclampsia
front: A postpartum renal biopsy from an eclamptic patient shows marked swelling of endothelial cells and amorphous fibrin deposits on the endothelial side of the basement membrane. Identify this lesion.
back:
• Glomerular Endotheliosis
• Pathognomonic renal lesion of preeclampsia
• Causes decreased GFR and resultant proteinuria/edema

category: Discuss pathophysiology and lab diagnosis of eclampsia and preeclampsia
front: How does the placental release of sFlt1 specifically contribute to the development of maternal proteinuria?
back:
• sFlt1 neutralizes circulating VEGF required for podocyte and endothelial health
• This induces systemic endothelial dysfunction and glomerular capillary injury
• Increased glomerular permeability allows protein leakage into the urine

category: Discuss pathophysiology and lab diagnosis of eclampsia and preeclampsia
coreConcept: Differential Diagnosis of Hypertensive Disorders of Pregnancy
front: Contrast preeclampsia and gestational hypertension regarding the presence of urinary protein.
back:
• Preeclampsia: Hypertension (new onset after 20 weeks) with significant proteinuria or end-organ dysfunction
• Gestational Hypertension: Isolated hypertension without proteinuria or systemic signs

category: Discuss pathophysiology and lab diagnosis of eclampsia and preeclampsia
front: Identify the definitive treatment for eclampsia that addresses the root cause of the endothelial dysfunction.
back:
• Delivery of the fetus and the placenta
• Eliminates the source of antiangiogenic factors (sFlt1/endoglin)
• Maternal symptoms usually resolve within 1–2 weeks post-delivery

category: Discuss pathophysiology and lab diagnosis of eclampsia and preeclampsia
front: The primary defect in the development of preeclampsia involves the failure of fetal [___] to adequately remodel maternal spiral arteries into large-capacity vessels.
back:
• Extravillous trophoblasts
• Normal remodeling destroys vascular smooth muscle
• Failure leads to high-resistance, small-caliber vessels and placental ischemia

category: Discuss pathophysiology and lab diagnosis of eclampsia and preeclampsia
front: A 34-week primipara presents with BP 165/115 mmHg and 4+ proteinuria. Labs show LDH 800 U/L, AST 150 U/L, and platelets 70,000/µL. Identify the specific systemic syndrome.
back:
• HELLP Syndrome
• H: Hemolysis (Microangiopathic)
• EL: Elevated Liver enzymes
• LP: Low Platelets

category: Discuss pathophysiology and lab diagnosis of eclampsia and preeclampsia
front: Explain the role of soluble FMS-like tyrosine kinase 1 (sFlt1) in the systemic manifestations of preeclampsia.
back:
• Secreted by ischemic placenta into maternal circulation
• Antagonizes VEGF and PlGF
• Leads to widespread maternal endothelial dysfunction and hypertension

category: Discuss pathophysiology and lab diagnosis of eclampsia and preeclampsia
front: Contrast the histologic appearance of placental decidual vessels in normal pregnancy versus those affected by preeclampsia.
back:
• Normal: Thin-walled, large-capacity, lack smooth muscle
• Preeclampsia: Fibrinoid necrosis, intimal lipid deposition (acute atherosis), and thrombi

category: Discuss pathophysiology and lab diagnosis of eclampsia and preeclampsia
front: Enlist the triad of clinical findings that classically define the systemic syndrome of preeclampsia.
back:
• Hypertension (new onset after 20 weeks)
• Edema
• Proteinuria

category: Discuss pathophysiology and lab diagnosis of eclampsia and preeclampsia
front: The specific maternal central nervous system event that distinguishes eclampsia from severe preeclampsia is the presence of [___].
back:
