• Convulsions (Seizures)
• Usually tonic-clonic type
• Often associated with cerebral edema and hemorrhage

category: Discuss pathophysiology and lab diagnosis of eclampsia and preeclampsia
front: A pregnant woman at 38 weeks gestation presents with sudden onset of seizures and a BP of 160/110 mmHg. Identify the immediate life-saving definitive management step.
back:
• Delivery of the placenta and fetus
• Symptoms typically disappear rapidly post-delivery
• Magnesium sulfate is used for seizure control

category: Discuss pathophysiology and lab diagnosis of eclampsia and preeclampsia
front: Describe the hepatic pathophysiology and resulting laboratory markers observed in severe eclampsia.
back:
• Portal capillary fibrin thrombi causing hemorrhagic necrosis
• Subcapsular hematoma formation
• Labs show elevated AST/ALT and hyperbilirubinemia

category: Discuss pathophysiology and lab diagnosis of eclampsia and preeclampsia
front: Distinguish between gestational hypertension and preeclampsia based on laboratory criteria.
back:
• Gestational Hypertension: Isolated high BP after 20 weeks without proteinuria
• Preeclampsia: Hypertension accompanied by proteinuria or end-organ dysfunction

category: Discuss pathophysiology and lab diagnosis of eclampsia and preeclampsia
front: Identify the characteristic renal morphologic change seen under light microscopy in patients with preeclampsia.
back:
• Glomerular capillary endotheliosis
• Marked swelling of endothelial cells
• Amorphous dense deposits on the basement membrane

category: Discuss pathophysiology and lab diagnosis of eclampsia and preeclampsia
front: In the pathogenesis of preeclampsia, the ischemic placenta releases [___], an anti-angiogenic factor that antagonizes VEGF and leads to systemic maternal endothelial dysfunction.
back:
• sFlt1 (soluble FMS-like tyrosine kinase 1)
• It works alongside soluble endoglin to cause vasoconstriction and proteinuria.

category: Discuss pathophysiology and lab diagnosis of eclampsia and preeclampsia
front: A 32-year-old primigravida at 36 weeks gestation presents with RUQ pain and BP 160/110. Labs show fragmented RBCs, elevated bilirubin, AST 250 U/L, and platelets 80,000/μL. Identify the specific diagnosis.
back:
• HELLP Syndrome
• H: Hemolysis
• EL: Elevated Liver enzymes
• LP: Low Platelets

category: Discuss pathophysiology and lab diagnosis of eclampsia and preeclampsia
front: Explain the failure of vascular remodeling that serves as the precipitating event in the development of placental ischemia during preeclampsia.
back:
• Cytotrophoblasts fail to invade maternal decidua properly.
• Decidual spiral arteries remain small-caliber resistance vessels.
• Result: The placenta cannot meet the increased blood flow demands of late gestation.

category: Discuss pathophysiology and lab diagnosis of eclampsia and preeclampsia
front: Contrast the defining clinical criteria of preeclampsia with those of eclampsia.
back:
• Preeclampsia: Hypertension, edema, and proteinuria in the third trimester.
• Eclampsia: The additional onset of grand mal seizures or coma in a preeclamptic patient.

category: Discuss pathophysiology and lab diagnosis of eclampsia and preeclampsia
front: Describe the characteristic glomerular changes (glomerular endotheliosis) found on renal histology in a patient with severe preeclampsia.
back:
• Marked swelling of endothelial cells.
• Fibrin deposition in the glomeruli.
• Mesangial cell hyperplasia and amorphous dense deposits.

category: Discuss pathophysiology and lab diagnosis of eclampsia and preeclampsia
front: The definitive clinical management to resolve systemic endothelial dysfunction and prevent fatal maternal hemorrhage in eclampsia is [___].
back:
• Delivery of the placenta and fetus.
• Symptoms typically disappear rapidly once the placental source of anti-angiogenic factors is removed.

category: Discuss pathophysiology and lab diagnosis of eclampsia and preeclampsia
front: A 24-year-old pregnant female presents with tonic-clonic convulsions and a BP of 180/115 mmHg. Histology of her liver at autopsy would most likely reveal [___].
back:
• Irregular subcapsular and intraparenchymal hemorrhages.
• Fibrin thrombi in portal capillaries.
• Foci of hemorrhagic necrosis.

category: Discuss pathophysiology and lab diagnosis of eclampsia and preeclampsia
front: How does the reduction of Prostacyclin (PGI2) production contribute to the hypercoagulable state in preeclampsia?
back:
• VEGF antagonism by sFlt1 reduces endothelial PGI2 synthesis.
• PGI2 is a potent vasodilator and antithrombotic factor.
• Loss of PGI2 favors vasoconstriction and microthrombi formation.

category: Discuss pathophysiology and lab diagnosis of eclampsia and preeclampsia
front: Contrast the vascular conversion of spiral arteries in normal pregnancy versus a preeclamptic pregnancy.
back:
• Normal: Trophoblasts replace endothelium, creating large-capacity vessels lacking smooth muscle.
• Preeclamptic: Vessels retain smooth muscle coats and remain high-resistance, low-capacity channels.

category: Discuss pathophysiology and lab diagnosis of eclampsia and preeclampsia
front: Identify the characteristic vascular lesion often found in the decidual vessels of patients with eclampsia, featuring fibrinoid necrosis.
back:
• Acute atherosis.
• It is characterized by vessel wall necrosis and the presence of subendothelial lipid-laden macrophages.

category: Discuss pathophysiology and lab diagnosis of eclampsia and preeclampsia
front: In preeclampsia, the failure of physiologic remodeling of the [___] results in small-caliber resistance vessels that cause placental ischemia.
back:
• Spiral arteries
• Normally remodeled by fetal extravillous trophoblasts
• Failure prevents conversion to large-capacity uteroplacental vessels

category: Discuss pathophysiology and lab diagnosis of eclampsia and preeclampsia
front: A 32-year-old primipara at 36 weeks gestation presents with a blood pressure of 165/110 mmHg and severe headache. While being monitored, she develops a generalized tonic-clonic seizure. Identify the diagnosis and the defining clinical differentiator.
back:
• Diagnosis: Eclampsia
• Differentiator: New-onset convulsions/seizures in a patient with preeclampsia
• Indicates severe systemic endothelial dysfunction affecting the CNS

category: Discuss pathophysiology and lab diagnosis of eclampsia and preeclampsia
front: Explain the role of soluble FMS-like tyrosine kinase (sFlt1) in the development of maternal hypertension and proteinuria.
back:
• sFlt1 is a placenta-derived antiangiogenic factor
• Antagonizes Vascular Endothelial Growth Factor (VEGF)
• Results in systemic endothelial dysfunction, vasoconstriction, and increased vascular permeability

category: Discuss pathophysiology and lab diagnosis of eclampsia and preeclampsia
front: Contrast the lab findings of HELLP syndrome with the classic diagnostic triad of preeclampsia.
back:
• Preeclampsia: Hypertension, proteinuria, and edema
• HELLP: Microangiopathic Hemolytic anemia, Elevated Liver enzymes, and Low Platelets
• HELLP represents severe endothelial injury with end-organ involvement

category: Discuss pathophysiology and lab diagnosis of eclampsia and preeclampsia
front: Identify the primary therapeutic step that definitively reverses the pathophysiology of eclampsia regardless of gestational age.
back:
• Delivery of the placenta and fetus
• Placenta is the central source of antiangiogenic factors
• Clinical symptoms typically resolve within 1–2 weeks postpartum

category: Discuss pathophysiology and lab diagnosis of eclampsia and preeclampsia
front: Preeclampsia is clinically defined by the new-onset development of hypertension and [___] after 20 weeks of gestation.
back:
• Proteinuria
• Caused by increased glomerular vascular permeability
• Associated with glomerular endotheliosis (endothelial cell swelling)

category: Discuss pathophysiology and lab diagnosis of eclampsia and preeclampsia
front: A microscopic examination of a preeclamptic placenta shows vessels with fibrinoid necrosis and subendothelial lipid-laden macrophages. Name this characteristic vascular lesion.
back:
• Acute atherosis
• Found in the decidual vessels
• Histologic marker of severe malperfusion and vessel wall injury

category: Discuss pathophysiology and lab diagnosis of eclampsia and preeclampsia
front: How does the inhibition of TGF-beta by soluble endoglin contribute to the hypertensive state in preeclampsia?
back:
• TGF-beta normally induces endothelial nitric oxide production
• Soluble endoglin antagonizes TGF-beta signaling
• Loss of nitric oxide (a vasodilator) leads to systemic vasoconstriction

category: Discuss pathophysiology and lab diagnosis of eclampsia and preeclampsia
front: Contrast the mechanism of edema in preeclampsia with its mechanism in normal pregnancy.
back:
• Normal: Physiologic increase in plasma volume
• Preeclampsia: Endothelial dysfunction and increased vascular permeability
• Leads to fluid shift into the interstitium and proteinuria

category: Discuss pathophysiology and lab diagnosis of eclampsia and preeclampsia
front: Name the specific maternal cell type that is the primary target of injury in the systemic syndrome of preeclampsia.
back:
• Vascular endothelial cells
• Dysfunction causes the core symptoms (HTN, proteinuria, edema)
• Triggered by imbalance of angiogenic and antiangiogenic factors

category: Enumerate causes of infertility in females along with hormonal investigations
front: The most common sexually transmitted bacterial pathogens leading to tubal factor infertility through chronic salpingitis are Neisseria gonorrhoeae and [___].
back:
• Chlamydia trachomatis
• Both pathogens cause pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) resulting in scarring.

category: Enumerate causes of infertility in females along with hormonal investigations
front: A 30-year-old female presents with primary infertility and cyclic pelvic pain. Laparoscopy reveals "powder-burn" peritoneal lesions and a large "chocolate cyst" in the left ovary. The likely diagnosis is [___].
back:
• Endometriosis
• Characterized by ectopic endometrial glands and stroma outside the uterus.

category: Enumerate causes of infertility in females along with hormonal investigations
front: Explain the role of chronic salpingitis in the pathogenesis of female infertility.
back:
• Inflammation causes injury and sloughing of tubal plicae
• Reparative scarring leads to fusion of plicae and blind pouches
• Prevents the uptake and passage of oocytes through the tube.

category: Enumerate causes of infertility in females along with hormonal investigations
front: A 38-year-old presents with amenorrhea and infertility. Contrast the expected FSH/LH findings and clinical significance for primary versus secondary ovarian failure.
back:
• Primary (Ovarian): Elevated FSH/LH (hypergonadotropic) due to loss of negative feedback
• Secondary (Pituitary): Low or inappropriately normal FSH/LH; indicates central axis failure.

category: Enumerate causes of infertility in females along with hormonal investigations
front: Identify three essential hormonal investigations used to evaluate a female presenting with infertility and features of androgen excess.
back:
• LH:FSH ratio (often >2:1 in PCOS)
• Total and Free Testosterone levels
• Fasting Glucose/Insulin (assess insulin resistance)
• Serum Prolactin (exclude pituitary cause).

category: Enumerate causes of infertility in females along with hormonal investigations
front: In the clinical investigation of anovulatory infertility, documenting the presence of a functional corpus luteum is traditionally achieved by measuring a mid-luteal serum [___] level.
back:
• Progesterone
• Peak levels confirm that ovulation has successfully occurred during that cycle.

category: Enumerate causes of infertility in females along with hormonal investigations
front: A 24-year-old obese female presents with irregular menses, infertility, and hirsutism. Ultrasound shows bilateral enlarged ovaries with multiple subcortical cysts. The likely underlying diagnosis is [___].
back:
• Polycystic Ovarian Syndrome (PCOS)
• Also known as Stein-Leventhal syndrome; involves chronic anovulation.

category: Enumerate causes of infertility in females along with hormonal investigations
front: Describe the "Regurgitation Theory" regarding the development of ectopic tissue in endometriosis-related infertility.
back:
• Proposes retrograde flow of menstrual endometrium through fallopian tubes
• Tissue implants on peritoneal surfaces and ovaries
• Leads to inflammation, adhesions, and structural distortion of adnexa.

category: Enumerate causes of infertility in females along with hormonal investigations
front: Contrast the effects of hyperprolactinemia versus thyroid dysfunction on the female reproductive axis in the context of infertility.
back:
• Hyperprolactinemia: Excess prolactin inhibits GnRH secretion, causing anovulation and amenorrhea
• Thyroid Dysfunction: Hypo- or hyperthyroidism disrupts the HPO axis and normal menstrual cyclicity.

category: Enumerate causes of infertility in females along with hormonal investigations
front: Enlist three specific infectious causes of infertility in females, highlighting one significant in developing countries.
back:
• Neisseria gonorrhoeae (leads to PID)
• Chlamydia trachomatis (tubal scarring)
• Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Tuberculous salpingitis; high prevalence in developing nations).

category: Enlist sites of abnormal placental implantations (ectopic pregnancy)
coreConcept: Most Common Site of Ectopic Pregnancy
front: The most frequent anatomical site for an ectopic pregnancy, accounting for approximately 90% of cases, is the [___].
back:
• Extrauterine Fallopian tube
• Most common location overall
• Often associated with prior pelvic inflammatory disease (PID)

category: Enlist sites of abnormal placental implantations (ectopic pregnancy)
front: A 28-year-old female presents with acute abdominal pain 7 weeks after her last period. Ultrasound reveals a gestational sac within the interstitial portion of the fallopian tube. Identify this specific placental implantation site.
back:
• Cornual (interstitial) pregnancy
• Located in the intrauterine portion of the tube
• High risk of severe hemorrhage upon rupture

category: Enlist sites of abnormal placental implantations (ectopic pregnancy)
front: Explain the role of chronic salpingitis in the pathogenesis of abnormal tubal placental implantation.
back:
• Causes intraluminal scarring and adhesions
• Physically obstructs the passage of the fertilized ovum
• Traps the embryo before it reaches the uterine cavity

category: Enlist sites of abnormal placental implantations (ectopic pregnancy)
front: Distinguish between the mechanisms leading to Ovarian vs. Abdominal ectopic pregnancies.
back:
• Ovarian: Fertilization and trapping of the ovum within the follicle at the time of rupture.
• Abdominal: Fertilized ovum fails to enter or drops out of the fimbriated end of the tube.

category: Enlist sites of abnormal placental implantations (ectopic pregnancy)
front: Enlist the four primary anatomical sites where an ectopic pregnancy may occur.
back:
• Fallopian tube (90%)
• Ovary
• Abdominal cavity
• Cornual (intrauterine tube portion)

category: Enlist sites of abnormal placental implantations (ectopic pregnancy)
front: In an ectopic pregnancy, the endometrial biopsy characteristically shows [___] without [___].
back:
• Decidual changes (decidua)
• Absence of chorionic villi
• Reflects hormonal response without intrauterine implantation

category: Enlist sites of abnormal placental implantations (ectopic pregnancy)
coreConcept: IUD as an Ectopic Pregnancy Risk Factor
front: A female with a history of Intrauterine Contraceptive Device (IUD) use presents with pelvic pain. This history is associated with a [___] increase in the risk of abnormal placental implantation.
back:
• Twofold (double) risk increase
• Mechanism involves potential for low-grade inflammation
• Most commonly results in tubal implantation

category: Enlist sites of abnormal placental implantations (ectopic pregnancy)
front: Explain the clinical phenomenon of 'tubal abortion' as a form of spontaneous regression in abnormal implantations.
back:
• Gestational sac separates from the tubal wall
• Extruded through the fimbriated end into the abdominal cavity
• May result in pelvic hematoma or resorption

category: Enlist sites of abnormal placental implantations (ectopic pregnancy)
front: Contrast the typical presentation of a ruptured tubal pregnancy with an unruptured one.
back:
• Unruptured: 6-8 weeks amenorrhea with moderate pain/bleeding.
• Ruptured: Sudden acute abdomen and rapid hemorrhagic shock (medical emergency).

category: Enlist sites of abnormal placental implantations (ectopic pregnancy)
front: Identify the primary source of hemorrhage in a 'hematosalpinx' caused by ectopic pregnancy.
back:
• Invasion of the fallopian tube wall by trophoblastic cells/villi
• Distension of the tube by the growing gestational sac
• Eventual wall thinning and arterial rupture

category: Enlist sites of abnormal placental implantations (ectopic pregnancy)
front: Approximately 90% of ectopic pregnancies occur when the fetus implants in the [___].
back:
• Extrauterine fallopian tube
• Most common site of abnormal placental implantation
• High risk of rupture and hematosalpinx

category: Enlist sites of abnormal placental implantations (ectopic pregnancy)
front: A 26-year-old female with a history of PID presents with sudden-onset acute abdominal pain and hemorrhagic shock. An endometrial biopsy reveals decidualization but no chorionic villi. Identify the underlying pathophysiology.
back:
• Ectopic (tubal) pregnancy rupture
• Massive intraperitoneal hemorrhage
• Predisposed by chronic salpingitis scarring

category: Enlist sites of abnormal placental implantations (ectopic pregnancy)
front: Explain the role of the decidua in the mechanism of abnormal placental attachment seen in Placenta Accreta.
back:
• Partial or complete absence of decidua
• Placental villous tissue adheres directly to myometrium
• Results in failure of placental separation at birth

category: Enlist sites of abnormal placental implantations (ectopic pregnancy)
front: Contrast the implantation site of Placenta Previa with the site of a Cornual pregnancy.
back:
• Placenta Previa: Lower uterine segment or cervix (covers internal os)
• Cornual Pregnancy: Intrauterine portion of the fallopian tube

category: Enlist sites of abnormal placental implantations (ectopic pregnancy)
front: Identify the contraceptive device associated with a twofold increased risk for abnormal ectopic implantation.
back:
• Intrauterine Contraceptive Device (IUCD)
• Interferes with normal intrauterine implantation
• Paradoxically increases ectopic risk despite overall efficacy

category: Enlist sites of abnormal placental implantations (ectopic pregnancy)
front: In an [___] pregnancy, the fertilized ovum fails to enter the tube or drops out of the fimbria to implant on the peritoneal surface.
back:
• Abdominal pregnancy
• A subtype of ectopic pregnancy
• Implants on various abdominal viscera or pelvic serosa

category: Enlist sites of abnormal placental implantations (ectopic pregnancy)
front: A patient in her third trimester presents with sudden, painless vaginal bleeding. Ultrasound shows the placenta completely covering the internal cervical os. State the diagnosis.
back:
• Complete Placenta Previa
• Implantation in the lower uterine segment
• Mandatory Cesarean delivery required to prevent rupture

category: Enlist sites of abnormal placental implantations (ectopic pregnancy)
front: Explain the specific mechanical sequence that results in an Ovarian pregnancy.
back:
• Fertilization and trapping of the ovum within the follicle
• Occurs precisely at the time of follicular rupture
• Rare site of abnormal implantation

category: Enlist sites of abnormal placental implantations (ectopic pregnancy)
front: Contrast the diagnostic findings of a normal pregnancy versus an ectopic pregnancy during histologic examination of uterine curettage.
back:
• Normal: Decidua PLUS chorionic villi/implantation site
• Ectopic: Decidua ONLY (villi are absent from the uterus)

category: Enlist sites of abnormal placental implantations (ectopic pregnancy)
front: Enlist four distinct anatomic locations where an ectopic pregnancy may occur.
back:
• Fallopian tube (extrauterine - 90%)
• Ovary
• Abdominal cavity
• Cornual (intrauterine portion of fallopian tube)

category: Enlist sites of abnormal placental implantations (ectopic pregnancy)
coreConcept: Most common site of ectopic pregnancy
front: Approximately 90% of ectopic pregnancies occur in the [___], which is the most frequent site of abnormal placental implantation.
back:
• Fallopian tube
• Most common extrauterine location
• Typically associated with chronic salpingitis or PID-related scarring

category: Enlist sites of abnormal placental implantations (ectopic pregnancy)
front: A 28-year-old female with a history of PID presents with acute abdominal pain and shock. Laparotomy reveals a blood-filled fallopian tube (hematosalpinx). Explain the pathophysiology of the resulting rupture.
back:
• Growth of the gestational sac distends the narrow tube
• Invading trophoblasts weaken the tubal wall structure
• Thinning and eventual wall breach lead to massive intraperitoneal hemorrhage

category: Enlist sites of abnormal placental implantations (ectopic pregnancy)
front: How does an endometrial biopsy assist in the diagnosis of an extrauterine ectopic pregnancy when intrauterine chorionic villi are absent?
back:
• Demonstrates decidual changes (hypertrophic stroma) from hormonal response
• Confirms a systemic pregnancy state despite empty uterus
• Absence of villi strongly suggests implantation at an extra-endometrial site

category: Enlist sites of abnormal placental implantations (ectopic pregnancy)
front: Contrast the anatomical site and clinical risk associated with a "cornual pregnancy" versus a typical "tubal pregnancy."
back:
• Site: Cornual occurs in the intrauterine portion of the tube; tubal in the extrauterine portion
• Risk: Cornual ruptures later but causes more severe, life-threatening hemorrhage due to high vascularity

category: Enlist sites of abnormal placental implantations (ectopic pregnancy)
front: Enlist the primary sites of ectopic pregnancy implantation excluding the fallopian tubes.
back:
• Ovary (trapped ovum within the follicle)
• Abdominal cavity (implanting on peritoneal surfaces)
• Cervical canal or prior cesarean section scar

category: Enlist sites of abnormal placental implantations (ectopic pregnancy)
front: In the diagnosis of abnormal placental implantation, the triad of clinical features typically includes abdominal pain, vaginal bleeding, and [___].
back:
• Amenorrhea (usually 6–8 weeks after last menstrual period)
• Accompanied by elevated hCG titers and pelvic ultrasound findings
• High clinical suspicion required to prevent catastrophic rupture

category: Enlist sites of abnormal placental implantations (ectopic pregnancy)
front: An ovum is fertilized but fails to enter the fimbriated end of the tube, implanting on the peritoneal surface. Identify this type of pregnancy and its primary risk factor.
back:
• Abdominal pregnancy
• Primary risk factor: Peritubal scarring or adhesions (e.g., from prior appendicitis or endometriosis)
• Placenta may attach to abdominal viscera, complicating removal

category: Enlist sites of abnormal placental implantations (ectopic pregnancy)
front: Explain why chronic salpingitis is the most significant predisposing factor for abnormal tubal placental implantation.
back:
• Induces intraluminal scarring and permanent mucosal adhesions
• Slows or physically blocks the passage of the fertilized ovum
• Forces the blastocyst to implant within the fallopian tube wall

category: Enlist sites of abnormal placental implantations (ectopic pregnancy)
front: Distinguish between an ovarian pregnancy and a tubal pregnancy based on the mechanism of trapping.
back:
• Ovarian: Fertilization and trapping of the ovum within the follicle immediately at the time of rupture
• Tubal: Fertilized ovum enters the tube but is hindered by anatomical barriers or scarring

category: Enlist sites of abnormal placental implantations (ectopic pregnancy)
front: Identify the most common underlying cause of hematosalpinx in the context of gestational disorders.
back:
• Tubal ectopic pregnancy
• Caused by hemorrhage from the implanting sac or wall rupture
• Often presents as a surgical emergency with signs of an acute abdomen

category: Enumerate causes of inflammation of male genital tract
front: In uncircumcised males, the accumulation of desquamated epithelial cells, sweat, and debris, termed [___], acts as a local irritant leading to chronic balanoposthitis.
back:
• Smegma
• Acts as a nidus for infection
• Common agents: C. albicans, Gardnerella, and pyogenic bacteria
• Leads to inflammatory scarring and phimosis.

category: Enumerate causes of inflammation of male genital tract
front: A 40-year-old male presents with fever, chills, dysuria, and an exquisitely tender, boggy prostate on rectal examination. The most likely infectious route is [___].
back:
• Intraprostatic reflux of contaminated urine
• Most commonly caused by E. coli, enterococci, or staphylococci
• Can also occur via lymphohematogenous seeding or surgical manipulation (catheterization).

category: Enumerate causes of inflammation of male genital tract
front: Explain how the causative agents of non-specific epididymitis vary according to the patient's age group.
back:
• Children: Gram-negative rods (associated with congenital GU anomalies)
• Men <35 years: Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae
• Men >35 years: E. coli and Pseudomonas (UTI pathogens).

category: Enumerate causes of inflammation of male genital tract
front: Contrast the histological localization and findings of Idiopathic Granulomatous Orchitis versus Tuberculous Epididymo-orchitis.
back:
• Idiopathic: Granulomas restricted to spermatic tubules; non-caseating
• Tuberculosis: Begins in epididymis; classic caseating granulomatous inflammation with acid-fast bacilli; spreads secondarily to testis.

category: Enumerate causes of inflammation of male genital tract
front: State the clinical reason why needle biopsy is strictly contraindicated in suspected cases of acute bacterial prostatitis.
back:
• High risk of inducing bacterial sepsis
• Manipulation of the acutely inflamed gland can seed bacteria into the bloodstream
• Diagnosis is established via urine culture and clinical features.

category: Enumerate causes of inflammation of male genital tract
front: The histologic hallmark of chronic syphilitic inflammation in the testis is [___] endarteritis associated with perivascular cuffs of lymphocytes and plasma cells.
back:
• Obliterative
• Can also manifest as gummas (granulomatous inflammation)
• Unlike most infections, syphilis involves the testis first, sparing the epididymis early on.

category: Enumerate causes of inflammation of male genital tract
front: A 22-year-old male presents with acute testicular swelling and pain one week after parotid gland swelling. Identify the inflammatory pattern and the potential long-term complication.
back:
• Mumps Orchitis (Acute interstitial orchitis)
• Occurs in 20-30% of postpubertal males with Mumps
• Risk: Edema and inflammation can lead to pressure-induced atrophy and permanent sterility.

category: Enumerate causes of inflammation of male genital tract
front: Describe the diagnostic criteria used to distinguish Chronic Abacterial Prostatitis (Chronic Pelvic Pain Syndrome) from Chronic Bacterial Prostatitis.
back:
• Expressed prostatic secretions: >10 leukocytes per high-power field
• Bacterial cultures: Uniformly negative
• Clinical: No history of recurrent urinary tract infections (UTIs).

category: Enumerate causes of inflammation of male genital tract
front: Contrast the role of inflammation in the development of inflammatory Phimosis versus Lichen Sclerosis (Balanitis Xerotica Obliterans).
back:
• Phimosis: Chronic balanoposthitis causes scarring of the preputial ring
• Lichen Sclerosis: Autoimmune sclerosing chronic inflammation; results in white porcelain-like plaques and urethral meatal stenosis.

category: Enumerate causes of inflammation of male genital tract
front: Identify the two primary anatomical routes through which urinary tract infections reach the epididymis and testis.
back:
• Vas deferens
• Lymphatics of the spermatic cord
• Infections typically begin in the posterior urethra, prostate, or bladder.

category: Enlist sites of abnormal placental implantations (ectopic pregnancy)
coreConcept: Most common site of ectopic pregnancy
front: Approximately 90% of ectopic pregnancies occur when placental tissue implants abnormally within the [___].
back:
● Fallopian tube (extrauterine portion)
● This is the most common site of ectopic gestation
● Often results in hematosalpinx or rupture.

category: Enlist sites of abnormal placental implantations (ectopic pregnancy)
front: A 28-year-old female presents with acute abdominal pain and vaginal spotting 7 weeks after her last menstrual period. Pelvic ultrasound reveals an empty uterus and a mass in the adnexa. Identify the most likely underlying condition.
back:
● Ectopic pregnancy
● Likely located in the fallopian tube
● Rupture poses a risk of life-threatening hemorrhage and shock.

category: Enlist sites of abnormal placental implantations (ectopic pregnancy)
coreConcept: PID as a mechanism for ectopic pregnancy
front: Explain the mechanical role of Chronic Salpingitis in the development of abnormal placental implantation.
back:
● Intraluminal scarring of the fallopian tube
● Formation of physical barriers and blind pouches
● Prevents the passage of the fertilized oocyte to the uterus.

category: Enlist sites of abnormal placental implantations (ectopic pregnancy)
front: Contrast a cornual pregnancy with a standard extrauterine tubal pregnancy regarding their anatomic site.
back:
● Cornual: Implantation in the intrauterine portion of the fallopian tube
● Tubal: Implantation in the extrauterine portion of the tube
● Both are variants of ectopic pregnancy.

category: Enlist sites of abnormal placental implantations (ectopic pregnancy)
front: Enlist the three primary extra-tubal sites for ectopic pregnancy implantation.
back:
● Ovary (follicular trapping)
● Abdominal cavity (peritoneal surface)
● Cornua (intrauterine tubal segment).

category: Enlist sites of abnormal placental implantations (ectopic pregnancy)
front: The characteristic gross morphologic finding of a blood-filled fallopian tube resulting from an ectopic pregnancy is termed [___].
back:
● Hematosalpinx
● Caused by the invasion of the tubal wall by trophoblastic cells and villi
● Often leads to tubal distention and rupture.

category: Enlist sites of abnormal placental implantations (ectopic pregnancy)
front: A patient is diagnosed with an abdominal pregnancy. By what mechanism does the fertilized ovum typically reach this abnormal implantation site?
back:
● Fertilized ovum fails to enter the fimbriated end
● Ovum drops out of the tube into the peritoneal cavity
● Tissue then implants on abdominal or pelvic serosal surfaces.

category: Enlist sites of abnormal placental implantations (ectopic pregnancy)
front: Describe how the presence of an Intrauterine Contraceptive Device (IUCD) affects the site of placental implantation.
back:
● Creates a hostile environment for normal intrauterine implantation
● Associated with a twofold increased risk of ectopic sites
● Favors implantation in the tubes or other extrauterine locations.

category: Enlist sites of abnormal placental implantations (ectopic pregnancy)
front: Contrast the pathogenesis of an Ovarian Pregnancy with that of an Abdominal Pregnancy.
back:
● Ovarian: Fertilization and trapping occurs within the follicle during rupture
● Abdominal: Fertilized ovum drops out of the fimbriated end
● Both result in extra-tubal gestations.

category: Enlist sites of abnormal placental implantations (ectopic pregnancy)
front: Identify the primary inflammatory disease responsible for approximately 35% to 50% of abnormal placental implantations in the fallopian tube.
back:
● Pelvic Inflammatory Disease (PID)
● Results in chronic salpingitis and adhesions
● Most important predisposing factor for ectopic pregnancy.

category: Enumerate causes of inflammation of male genital tract
front: In sexually active men younger than 35 years, the most common pathogens causing acute nonspecific epididymitis are [___] and Neisseria gonorrhoeae.
back:
• Chlamydia trachomatis.
• Infection typically spreads from the urethra or bladder.
• Reaches the epididymis via the vas deferens or spermatic cord lymphatics.

category: Enumerate causes of inflammation of male genital tract
front: A 22-year-old male presents with sudden, painful testicular swelling one week after recovering from parotid gland enlargement and fever. Identify the most likely diagnosis.
back:
• Mumps Orchitis.
• Occurs in 20% to 30% of postpubertal males.
• Characterized by acute interstitial inflammation.
• Rare in school-aged children.

category: Enumerate causes of inflammation of male genital tract

category: Enlist sites of abnormal placental implantations (ectopic pregnancy)

category: Enlist sites of abnormal placental implantations (ectopic pregnancy)

category: Enlist sites of abnormal placental implantations (ectopic pregnancy)

category: Enlist sites of abnormal placental implantations (ectopic pregnancy)

category: Enlist sites of abnormal placental implantations (ectopic pregnancy)

category: Enumerate causes of inflammation of male genital tract

category: Enumerate causes of inflammation of male genital tract

category: Enumerate causes of inflammation of male genital tract

category: Enumerate causes of inflammation of male genital tract

category: Enumerate causes of inflammation of male genital tract

category: Enlist causes of male infertility with semen analysis
front: The primary genetic cause of male infertility characterized by small, firm testes, gynecomastia, and a 47,XXY karyotype is [___].
back:
• Klinefelter Syndrome

• Characterized by seminiferous tubule dysgenesis
• Results in hypergonadotropic hypogonadism

category: Enlist causes of male infertility with semen analysis
front: A 28-year-old male presents with a "bag of worms" sensation in the scrotum and infertility. Semen analysis shows decreased count and motility. Identify the condition and its mechanism.
back:
• Varicocele
• Dilated veins in the pampiniform plexus
• Mechanism: Increased scrotal temperature and venous congestion
• Impairs heat-sensitive spermatogenesis

category: Enlist causes of male infertility with semen analysis
front: Explain the role of temperature in the morphological changes seen in uncorrected Cryptorchidism.
back:
• High intra-abdominal temperature causes tubular atrophy
• Histology: Thickened basement membranes and loss of spermatogonia
• Sparing of Leydig cells (androgen production remains normal)
• Scarred tubules appear as hyaline connective tissue

category: Enlist causes of male infertility with semen analysis
front: A 30-year-old male with infertility and milk-like nipple discharge has a serum prolactin of 300 ng/mL. Contrast his LH/FSH levels with a patient having primary testicular failure.
back:
• Prolactinoma (Pre-testicular): Low LH and FSH (Hypogonadotropic hypogonadism)
• Primary Testicular Failure: High LH and FSH (Hypergonadotropic hypogonadism)
• Prolactin inhibits GnRH pulses from the hypothalamus

category: Enlist causes of male infertility with semen analysis
front:

1. Complete absence of sperm
2. Sperm concentration <15 million/mL
3. <40% motile sperm
back:
• 1. Azoospermia
• 2. Oligospermia
• 3. Asthenospermia
• These are core metrics for assessing male factor infertility

category: Enlist causes of male infertility with semen analysis
front: In post-pubertal males, the viral infection most commonly responsible for acute interstitial inflammation and potential sterility is [___].
back:

• Causes edema, lymphocytic infiltration, and potential tubular atrophy

category: Enlist causes of male infertility with semen analysis
front: A male with Cystic Fibrosis presents with infertility. Semen analysis shows low volume (<1.0 mL) and azoospermia. What is the anatomic defect?
back:
• Congenital Bilateral Absence of the Vas Deferens (CBAVD)
• Post-testicular/Obstructive cause of infertility
• Spermatogenesis is usually normal within the testis

category: Enlist causes of male infertility with semen analysis
front: How does chronic bacterial epididymitis from Neisseria gonorrhoeae eventually lead to secondary infertility?
back:
• Extension of infection from posterior urethra to epididymis
• Development of epididymal abscesses and suppurative necrosis
• Results in fibrous scarring and obstruction of the duct system
• Prevents sperm transport to the ejaculatory ducts

category: Enlist causes of male infertility with semen analysis
front: Contrast the typical etiology of epididymitis in men <35 years versus men >35 years.
back:
• <35 years: Sexually transmitted pathogens (C. trachomatis, N. gonorrhoeae)
• >35 years: Urinary tract pathogens (E. coli, Pseudomonas)
• Inflammatory scarring from either leads to sterility

category: Enlist causes of male infertility with semen analysis
front: Define 'Teratospermia' and state the WHO lower limit for normal sperm morphology.
back:
• Teratospermia: Presence of sperm with abnormal morphology
• Normal morphology threshold: >4% normal forms (Kruger criteria)
• Higher abnormalities correlate with decreased fertilization potential

category: Enumerate causes of inflammation of male genital tract

back:
• Balanoposthitis (inflammation of the glans and prepuce)
• Smegma (desquamated epithelial cells, sweat, and debris)

category: Enumerate causes of inflammation of male genital tract

back:

• Also known as Chronic Pelvic Pain Syndrome; it is the most common clinicopathological form of prostatitis.

category: Enumerate causes of inflammation of male genital tract
front: Contrast the typical causative organisms of acute epididymitis in children with the organisms found in men older than 35 years.
back:
• Children: Gram-negative rods (usually associated with congenital genitourinary abnormalities).
• Men > 35: Common urinary tract pathogens, specifically E. coli and Pseudomonas.

category: Enlist causes of male infertility with semen analysis
front: Histological evaluation of a 3-year-old's undescended testis, which carries a high risk for future sterility, typically reveals scarred tubules containing only [___].
back:
- Sertoli cells
- Loss of spermatogonia
- Thickened basement membranes
- Spared (prominent) Leydig cells

category: Enlist causes of male infertility with semen analysis
front: A 24-year-old male presents with acute scrotal pain and swelling one week after recovering from parotitis. The most significant long-term risk for his fertility is [___].
back:
- Post-pubertal Mumps Orchitis
- Chronic interstitial inflammation
- Fibrous scarring
- Eventual testicular atrophy and sterility

category: Enlist causes of male infertility with semen analysis
front: Explain the biological function of Prostate-Specific Antigen (PSA) within the seminal fluid required for normal fertility.
back:
- Serine protease activity
- Cleavage of seminal proteins
- Liquefaction of the seminal coagulum
- Facilitates sperm motility and release

category: Enlist causes of male infertility with semen analysis
front: Contrast the typical semen analysis and hormonal profile of Primary Testicular Failure (e.g., Klinefelter Syndrome) with Hypopituitarism.
back:
- **Primary Failure:** Azoospermia/Oligospermia with elevated FSH/LH.
- **Hypopituitarism:** Azoospermia/Oligospermia with low/decreased FSH/LH.

category: Enlist causes of male infertility with semen analysis
front: Identify the triad of clinical findings that constitute Testicular Dysgenesis Syndrome (TDS).
back:
- Cryptorchidism
- Hypospadias
- Poor sperm quality (Infertility)

category: Enlist causes of male infertility with semen analysis
front: In the setting of male infertility, the presence of [___] results in dilated veins within the spermatic cord, which is thought to impair spermatogenesis via abnormal thermoregulation.
back:
- Varicocele
- Surgical correction can improve fertility
- Most common on the left side

category: Enlist causes of male infertility with semen analysis
front: A 30-year-old male with a history of neglected gonococcal urethritis presents for an infertility workup. Semen analysis shows azoospermia despite normal testicular size. The underlying pathophysiology is [___].
back:
- Obstructive Azoospermia
- Chronic Epididymitis
- Duct destruction and fibrous scarring
- Blockage of sperm transport to the vas deferens

category: Enlist causes of male infertility with semen analysis
front: Describe the mechanism by which high-dose pelvic irradiation produces permanent male sterility.
back:
- Direct DNA damage to germ cells
- Destruction of the germinal epithelium
- Tubular atrophy
- Sparing of relatively radioresistant Leydig cells

category: Enlist causes of male infertility with semen analysis
front: Contrast the roles of Müllerian-inhibiting substance and Androgens in the etiology of cryptorchidism-related infertility.
back:
- **MIS:** Controls the first (transabdominal) phase of descent.
- **Androgens:** Controls the second (inguinoscrotal) phase via calcitonin gene–related peptide.

category: Enlist causes of male infertility with semen analysis
front: List four non-infectious causes of testicular atrophy that result in decreased male fertility.
back:
- Cryptorchidism
- Cirrhosis (Hyperestrinism)
- Klinefelter Syndrome (XXY)
- Chronic Cachexia/Malnutrition

category: Enlist causes of male infertility with semen analysis
front: In the context of male infertility, the presence of dilated veins within the pampiniform plexus of the spermatic cord is known as [___].
back:
• Varicocele
• Most common correctable cause of male infertility
• Mechanism: Increased scrotal temperature and venous stasis impairing spermatogenesis and sperm quality
• Diagnosis: Often detected as a "bag of worms" on palpation

category: Enlist causes of male infertility with semen analysis
front: A 32-year-old male with long-standing infertility presents with small, firm testes and gynecomastia. Chromosomal analysis reveals a 47,XXY karyotype. The expected finding on semen analysis is [___].
back:
• Azoospermia (total absence of sperm)
• Underlying Condition: Klinefelter syndrome
• Pathophysiology: Seminiferous tubule hyalinization and fibrosis with loss of germ cells
• Hormonal Profile: Primary hypogonadism with elevated FSH and LH levels

category: Enlist causes of male infertility with semen analysis
front: Contrast the mechanism of testicular atrophy in cryptorchidism with that caused by progressive atherosclerosis in old age.
back:
• Cryptorchidism: Thermal injury due to abdominal temperature inhibits germ cell maturation and triggers tubular hyalinization
• Atherosclerosis: Chronic ischemia from narrowing blood supply leads to parenchymal shrinkage
• Both culminate in sterility and azoospermia

category: Enlist causes of male infertility with semen analysis
front: Contrast the semen analysis findings and underlying pathology of Obstructive Azoospermia versus Non-obstructive (Secretory) Azoospermia.
back:
• Obstructive: Normal hormone levels; normal spermatogenesis on biopsy; caused by post-infectious scarring (Gonorrhea)
• Non-obstructive: Abnormal hormones (High FSH/Low Testosterone); impaired spermatogenesis; caused by Klinefelter or cryptorchidism
• Both show zero sperm count

category: Enlist causes of male infertility with semen analysis
front: Identify the primary pharmacological effect on the testes and fertility when a patient is treated with long-term antiandrogens for prostatic carcinoma.
back:
• Progressive testicular atrophy
• Mechanism: Blockade of androgen-dependent trophic signals to the seminiferous tubules
• Semen Analysis: Results in profound oligospermia or azoospermia depending on the duration of treatment

category: Enlist causes of male infertility with semen analysis
front: In clinical diagnostics, the presence of [___] in a postpubertal male one week following parotitis is highly suggestive of viral-induced testicular failure.
back:
• Acute Interstitial Orchitis
• Causative agent: Mumps virus
• Diagnostic Criteria: Occurs in 20-30% of postpubertal cases; leads to edema, congestion, and eventual fibrous scarring with sterility

category: Enlist causes of male infertility with semen analysis
front: A 28-year-old male presents with infertility. Semen analysis shows <40% sperm motility. Identify this clinical finding and its classic association with Kartagener syndrome.
back:
• Asthenospermia (Asthenozoospermia)
• Kartagener Association: Primary ciliary dyskinesia
• Pathophysiology: Lack of dynein arms in the axoneme of sperm tails results in total immobility despite normal sperm counts

category: Enlist causes of male infertility with semen analysis
front: Explain the biological mechanism behind 'Obstructive Azoospermia' as a complication of a neglected Neisseria gonorrhoeae infection.
back:
• Suppurative epididymitis and orchitis lead to tissue destruction
• Healing phase: Extensive fibrous scarring obliterates the lumen of the efferent ducts
• Result: Permanent blockage of sperm transport despite continued production in the seminiferous tubules

category: Enlist causes of male infertility with semen analysis
front: Contrast the physiological feedback loop of FSH and LH in Primary Testicular Failure versus Secondary (Hypopituitary) Failure.
back:
• Primary Failure: Hypergonadotropic hypogonadism (Low testosterone leads to compensatory high FSH/LH)
• Secondary Failure: Hypogonadotropic hypogonadism (Pituitary failure leads to low FSH/LH)
• Both show reduced sperm production and oligospermia

category: Enlist causes of male infertility with semen analysis
front: Define "Teratospermia" and list the clinical significance of "vanishing testis" in the context of male infertility.
back:
• Teratospermia: Presence of sperm with abnormal morphology exceeding reference limits
• Vanishing Testis: Complete regression of testicular tissue following extreme atrophy
• Significance: Irreversible sterility; often follows severe torsion or end-stage inflammatory orchitis

category: Enlist causes of male infertility with semen analysis
front: A common and often surgically correctable clinical finding in the spermatic cord that acts as a contributing factor to male infertility is a [___].
back:
• Varicocele
• Involves dilated veins in the pampiniform plexus
• Impairs spermatogenesis through increased scrotal temperature and venous stasis.

category: Enlist causes of male infertility with semen analysis
front: A 28-year-old male with a history of untreated bilateral cryptorchidism presents for fertility evaluation. Semen analysis is most likely to demonstrate [___].
back:
• Azoospermia (absence of sperm)
• Pathophysiology: Loss of spermatogonia and thickening of basement membranes
• Tubular atrophy prevents sperm production despite prominent Leydig cells.

category: Enlist causes of male infertility with semen analysis
front: Explain the role of postpubertal mumps infection in the development of male infertility.
back:
• Causes acute interstitial orchitis in 20-30% of cases
• Leads to edema and mononuclear inflammatory infiltrates
• Resultant tissue pressure and scarring can cause permanent seminiferous tubule destruction.

category: Enlist causes of male infertility with semen analysis
front: Contrast the typical testicular findings of infertility caused by Klinefelter syndrome with those caused by chronic epididymitis.
back:
• Klinefelter: Genetic primary failure; small, firm testes with hyalinized tubules.
• Epididymitis: Inflammatory/obstructive; fibrous scarring of ducts (epididymis) with potential abscess formation.

category: Enlist causes of male infertility with semen analysis
front: Enlist the triad of findings that define Testicular Dysgenesis Syndrome (TDS).
back:
• Cryptorchidism
• Hypospadias
• Poor sperm quality (low count or motility)
• Proposed to arise from in utero environmental exposures.

category: Enlist causes of male infertility with semen analysis
front: In male infertility resulting from hypopituitarism, the primary hormonal abnormality leading to testicular atrophy is a deficiency in [___].
back:
• Gonadotropins (FSH and LH)
• Leads to secondary failure of sperm production
• Semen analysis shows azoospermia or severe oligospermia.

category: Enlist causes of male infertility with semen analysis
front: A patient with a history of neglected N. gonorrhoeae infection presents with obstructive azoospermia. The primary site of anatomical blockage is usually the [___].
back:
• Epididymis
• Mechanism: Suppurative inflammation leads to abscesses and extensive fibrous scarring
• Prevents sperm from reaching the vas deferens.

category: Enlist causes of male infertility with semen analysis
front: Directly describe the impact of acute testicular torsion on long-term fertility if not corrected within 6 hours.
back:
• Triggers hemorrhagic infarction of the testis
• Venous drainage is obstructed leading to intense vascular engorgement
• Results in complete coagulative necrosis and non-functional parenchyma.

category: Enlist causes of male infertility with semen analysis
front: Contrast the semen analysis terminology: Azoospermia vs. Oligospermia.
back:
• Azoospermia: Complete absence of sperm in the ejaculate.
• Oligospermia: Reduced sperm concentration in the ejaculate (low sperm count).

category: Enlist causes of male infertility with semen analysis
front: Identify the rare cause of testicular atrophy associated with chronic liver disease.
back:
• Cirrhosis
• Mechanism: Hyperestrinism due to failure of the liver to metabolize estrogen
• Leads to feedback inhibition of gonadotropins.

category: Enlist causes of male infertility with semen analysis
front: The failure of intra-abdominal testes to descend (cryptorchidism) typically results in the loss of spermatogonia, often leaving the seminiferous tubules containing only [___] cells upon histological examination.
back:
• Sertoli cells
• Histologically characterized by basement membrane thickening and an apparent increase in interstitial Leydig cells
• Clinically results in sterility if bilateral.

category: Enlist causes of male infertility with semen analysis
front: A 24-year-old male presents with parotid swelling followed a week later by acute, painful testicular enlargement. Identify the likely viral pathogen and its chronic effect on fertility.
back:
• Mumps virus
• Pathophysiology: Acute interstitial orchitis occurring in 20-30% of post-pubertal cases
• Chronic sequelae: Fibrous scarring leading to decreased sperm quality or sterility.

category: Enlist causes of male infertility with semen analysis
front: Explain the biological function of Prostate-Specific Antigen (PSA) as it relates to the physical properties of semen.
back:
• It is an androgen-regulated serine protease
• Primary function: Cleaves and liquefies the seminal coagulum formed immediately after ejaculation
• Essential for releasing sperm to facilitate motility.

category: Enlist causes of male infertility with semen analysis
front: Contrast the typical semen analysis findings and morphological changes in obstructive azoospermia caused by Gonorrhea versus primary testicular failure in Klinefelter syndrome.
back:
• Gonorrhea: Extensive epididymal scarring/abscesses causing physical blockage (obstructive)
• Klinefelter: Primary failure with genetic origin; characterized by small, firm testes and exhaustion atrophy
• Both result in azoospermia.

category: Enlist causes of male infertility with semen analysis
front: Enlist four non-infectious systemic or environmental conditions mentioned as causes of testicular atrophy and decreased fertility.
back:
• Progressive atherosclerosis (old age)
• Generalized malnutrition or cachexia
• Irradiation
• Prolonged administration of antiandrogens (e.g., for prostate cancer).

category: Enlist causes of male infertility with semen analysis
front: The clinical condition characterized by the triad of cryptorchidism, hypospadias, and poor sperm quality, often linked to in utero pesticide exposure, is [___].
back:
• Testicular Dysgenesis Syndrome (TDS)
• Associated with in utero exposures to nonsteroidal estrogens
• Carries a higher risk for germ cell neoplasia.

category: Enlist causes of male infertility with semen analysis
front: A male patient presents with a 'bag of worms' sensation in the scrotum and decreased sperm count. Identify the vascular lesion and its potential treatment.
back:
• Varicocele (dilated vein in the spermatic cord)
• Pathophysiology: Impairs fertility likely through altered thermoregulation
• Management: Surgical repair can correct the infertility factor.

category: Enlist causes of male infertility with semen analysis
front: How does the anatomical 'bell-clapper' abnormality contribute to acute male infertility via a vascular mechanism?
back:
• Mechanism: Causes increased testicular mobility, predisposing to torsion
• Result: Twisting of the spermatic cord cuts off venous drainage
• Outcome: Hemorrhagic infarction and soft, necrotic tissue if not corrected within 6 hours.

category: Enlist causes of male infertility with semen analysis
front: Contrast the histological target of idiopathic Granulomatous Orchitis with that of chronic Epididymitis regarding the development of sterility.
back:
• Granulomatous: Granulomas are specifically restricted to the spermatic tubules, destroying them directly
• Epididymitis: Scarring usually begins in the interstitium and spreads to tubules, causing obstructive sterility.

category: Enlist causes of male infertility with semen analysis
front: Identify the primary hormone responsible for the first (transabdominal) phase of testicular descent.
back:
• Müllerian-inhibiting substance (MIS)
• Note: The second (inguinoscrotal) phase is androgen-dependent
• Failure of either phase results in cryptorchidism and potential sterility.

category: Enlist causes of male infertility with semen analysis
front: In the morphology of cryptorchidism, the specialized interstitial cells that are characteristically spared and appear prominent despite tubular atrophy are [___].
back:
- Leydig cells
- While spermatogonia are lost and basement membranes thicken, Leydig cells remain intact.
- This causes an apparent increase in interstitial stroma relative to the scarred, hyalinized tubules.

category: Enlist causes of male infertility with semen analysis
front: A 1-year-old boy presents for a routine check-up where one testis is found in the inguinal canal. If this condition is not corrected by orchiopexy, describe the impact on sperm production.
back:
- It results in deficient spermatogenesis and potential sterility.
- Histologic changes like basement membrane thickening begin by age 2.
- Even after surgical correction, sterility risk remains in 10% to 60% of patients.

category: Enlist causes of male infertility with semen analysis
front: Explain the role of inflammation and fibrous scarring in the development of sterility following acute epididymitis.
back:
- Bacterial infection (e.g., Gonorrhea) induces acute suppurative inflammation.
- The resulting inflammatory response destroys the tubular epithelium.
- Resolution via fibrous scarring causes permanent ductal obstruction, preventing the passage of sperm.

category: Enlist causes of male infertility with semen analysis
front: Contrast the clinical triad of Testicular Dysgenesis Syndrome (TDS) with the features of isolated cryptorchidism.
back:
- TDS: A spectrum including cryptorchidism, hypospadias, and poor sperm quality.
- Isolated Cryptorchidism: Incomplete descent without other urethral malformations.
- Both conditions are markers of gonadal developmental defects and increase testicular cancer risk.

category: Enlist causes of male infertility with semen analysis
front: Enlist the two most frequent sexually transmitted pathogens responsible for epididymitis and potential subsequent infertility in men younger than 35 years.
back:
- Chlamydia trachomatis
- Neisseria gonorrhoeae
- These organisms typically spread from the posterior urethra to the epididymis, often sparing the testis initially.

category: Enlist causes of male infertility with semen analysis
front: The primary trophic hormone from the anterior pituitary, the deficiency of which leads to 'exhaustion atrophy' of the testis and decreased fertility, is [___].
back:
- Follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH)
- Persistent stimulation by high levels of FSH or its total absence in hypopituitarism can lead to progressive testicular atrophy and vanishing tubules.

category: Enlist causes of male infertility with semen analysis
front: A 24-year-old male presents with sudden testicular pain and swelling one week after recovering from parotitis. Identify the condition and its long-term risk to fertility.
back:
- Mumps Orchitis
- Postpubertal mumps causes acute interstitial orchitis in up to 30% of cases.
- Chronic sequelae include permanent testicular atrophy and subsequent sterility due to follicular destruction.

category: Enlist causes of male infertility with semen analysis
front: Explain the biological mechanism behind the 'bell-clapper' abnormality and its relationship to testicular infarction.
back:
- It is a bilateral anatomic defect providing increased testicular mobility.
- This allows the testis to twist, cutting off venous drainage from the spermatic cord.
- The resulting intense vascular engorgement leads to rapid hemorrhagic infarction.

category: Enlist causes of male infertility with semen analysis
front: Contrast the anatomic origin and contents of a Spermatocele with those of a Varicocele.
back:
- Spermatocele: A cystic accumulation of semen occurring in the dilated efferent ducts of the rete testis.
- Varicocele: A dilated vein within the spermatic cord.
- Varicoceles are more commonly implicated as a major contributing factor to infertility.

category: Enlist causes of male infertility with semen analysis
front: Directly enlist four diverse non-congenital clinical conditions that can lead to permanent testicular atrophy.
back:
- Chronic ischemia (e.g., severe atherosclerosis)
- Irradiation or chemotherapy exposure
- Prolonged administration of antiandrogens (prostate cancer treatment)
- Generalized malnutrition or cachexia
- These lead to tubular hyalinization and loss of spermatogenesis.

category: Enlist causes of male infertility with semen analysis
front: The primary histologic change seen in the seminiferous tubules of a cryptorchid testis by age 2 is [___], which eventually leads to a complete loss of spermatogonia.
back:
• Thickening of the basement membrane.
• Results in tubules containing only Sertoli cells.
• Clinically manifests as deficient spermatogenesis or sterility.

category: Enlist causes of male infertility with semen analysis
front: A 28-year-old male with a history of childhood mumps presents with bilateral testicular shrinkage. Semen analysis is likely to show [___] due to end-stage inflammatory scarring.
back:
• Azoospermia (total absence of sperm).
• Pathophysiology: Acute interstitial orchitis leads to tubular destruction and fibrous scarring.
• Leydig cells are typically spared, maintaining testosterone levels.

category: Enlist causes of male infertility with semen analysis
front: Explain the role of the genitofemoral nerve and androgens in the pathogenesis of male infertility related to cryptorchidism.
back:
• Androgens trigger the release of calcitonin gene-related peptide from the genitofemoral nerve.
• This mediates the inguinoscrotal phase of testicular descent.
• Failure leads to high-temperature arrest and tubular atrophy.

category: Enlist causes of male infertility with semen analysis
front: A 32-year-old male presents with primary infertility and a palpable 'bag of worms' in the left scrotum. Contrast the mechanism of infertility in this patient with that of 'Testicular Dysgenesis Syndrome' (TDS).
back:
• Varicocele (Patient): Infertility via elevated scrotal temperature and venous stasis.
• TDS: In utero developmental defect involving cryptorchidism, hypospadias, and intrinsic poor sperm quality.

category: Enlist causes of male infertility with semen analysis
front: Enlist four non-inflammatory, systemic causes of testicular atrophy that result in decreased sperm count on semen analysis.
back:
• Hypopituitarism (lack of FSH/LH).
• Hyperestrinism (e.g., Cirrhosis).
• Nutritional cachexia/malnutrition.
• Prolonged administration of antiandrogens.

category: Enlist causes of male infertility with semen analysis
front: In the setting of male reproductive failure, the clinical triad of [___], [___], and poor sperm quality collectively defines 'Testicular Dysgenesis Syndrome'.
back:
• Cryptorchidism.
• Hypospadias.
• Linked to in utero environmental exposures (e.g., pesticides/estrogens).

category: Enlist causes of male infertility with semen analysis
front: A male patient with a 47,XXY karyotype presents with small, firm testes and infertility. Identify the specific histological pattern found in the seminiferous tubules that explains the azoospermia.
back:
• Klinefelter Syndrome.
• Histology: Atrophy and hyalinization of seminiferous tubules.
• Leydig cells appear prominent due to the loss of surrounding tubular mass.

category: Enlist causes of male infertility with semen analysis
front: Describe the morphologic progression from acute bacterial epididymitis to obstructive azoospermia.
back:
• Acute stage: Neutrophilic infiltration/abscess in interstitium and tubules.
• Chronic stage: Resolution via fibrous scarring.
• Result: Permanent ductal obstruction preventing sperm transport despite preserved production.

category: Enlist causes of male infertility with semen analysis
front: Contrast the initial sites of infection in the male genital tract for Tuberculosis (TB) versus Syphilis.
back:
• Tuberculosis: Almost invariably begins in the epididymis.
• Syphilis: Almost invariably involves the testis first (testicular gumma or endarteritis).

category: Enlist causes of male infertility with semen analysis
front: Identify the characteristic cells that remain in the seminiferous tubules when spermatogonia are lost due to cryptorchidism or irradiation.
back:
• Sertoli cells.
• Known as 'Sertoli-cell-only' syndrome morphology.
• Appears as atrophic tubules with prominent hyaline connective tissue cords.

category: Enlist causes of male infertility with semen analysis
front: In the malpositioned testis of a patient with cryptorchidism, the characteristic histological change resulting in azoospermia is the loss of spermatogonia, leaving the tubules populated by [___].
back:
• Sertoli cells (Sertoli-cell-only syndrome)
  • Thickened tubular basement membranes
  • Scarring into dense cords of hyaline connective tissue
  • Relative prominence of spared Leydig cells

category: Enlist causes of male infertility with semen analysis
front: A 25-year-old male develops sudden painful testicular swelling one week after the onset of parotid gland inflammation. Identify the condition and its long-term consequence for fertility.
back:
• Diagnosis: Mumps Orchitis
  • Occurs in 20-30% of postpubertal cases
  • Pathology: Acute interstitial orchitis
  • Consequence: Testicular atrophy and permanent sterility

category: Enlist causes of male infertility with semen analysis
front: Explain the mechanical mechanism by which nonspecific epididymitis and subsequent orchitis leads to male infertility.
back:
• Acute inflammation starts in the interstitial tissue and extends to the tubules
  • Resolution involves extensive fibrous scarring
  • Scarring causes ductal obstruction, preventing sperm exit despite normal androgen production

category: Enlist causes of male infertility with semen analysis
front: Contrast the histological features of testicular atrophy in cryptorchidism versus end-stage inflammatory orchitis.
back:
• Cryptorchidism: Thickened basement membranes with Sertoli-cell-only tubules
  • Inflammatory Orchitis: Massive fibrous scarring and replacement of entire epididymal/tubular structures with abscess or necrotic debris

category: Enlist causes of male infertility with semen analysis
front: Enumerate four systemic or iatrogenic causes of testicular atrophy associated with decreased fertility.
back:
• Cirrhosis (altered hormone metabolism)
  • Prolonged administration of antiandrogens (prostate cancer therapy)
  • Chronic malnutrition or cachexia
  • Therapeutic or accidental irradiation

category: Enlist causes of male infertility with semen analysis
front: In the pathogenesis of male infertility, sexually transmitted [___] are the most frequent causes of epididymitis in men under 35, while [___] are responsible for infections in older men.
back:
• Under 35: Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae
  • Over 35: E. coli and Pseudomonas (urinary tract pathogens)
  • Mechanism: Direct extension via vas deferens

category: Enlist causes of male infertility with semen analysis
front: A 16-year-old presents with sudden-onset excruciating testicular pain and a high-riding testis. If this condition is not manually untwisted within 6 hours, what is the impact on future fertility?
back:
• Diagnosis: Testicular Torsion
  • Outcome: Hemorrhagic infarction and total necrosis
  • Fertility: Contralateral testis may be affected due to the bilateral nature of the 'bell-clapper' abnormality

category: Enlist causes of male infertility with semen analysis
front: Describe the three essential clinical components that define Testicular Dysgenesis Syndrome (TDS) and its associated semen analysis finding.
back:
• Cryptorchidism and hypospadias
  • Poor sperm quality on semen analysis
  • Mechanism: Linked to in utero environmental exposures (pesticides, estrogens) disrupting gonadal development

category: Enlist causes of male infertility with semen analysis
front: Contrast the primary hormonal mechanism of infertility in Klinefelter syndrome with that of hypopituitarism.
back:
• Klinefelter Syndrome: Primary genetic gonadal failure with resulting germ cell depletion
  • Hypopituitarism: Secondary atrophy due to failure of trophic hormonal stimulation from the pituitary

category: Enlist causes of male infertility with semen analysis
front: Identify the vascular lesion of the spermatic cord implicated as a common contributing factor to male infertility and its management.
back:
• Lesion: Varicocele (dilated vein in the spermatic cord)
  • Impact: Impairs sperm production and quality
  • Management: Can be corrected by surgical repair

category: Describe pathological features of testicular torsion
front: The bilateral anatomic defect that allows for increased mobility of the testes and predisposes adolescents to torsion is known as the [___].
back:
• Bell-clapper abnormality
• Prevents normal posterior anchoring
• Results in intravaginal twisting of the spermatic cord

category: Describe pathological features of testicular torsion
front: A 14-year-old male presents with sudden-onset, severe scrotal pain and swelling without prior trauma. Identify the most likely underlying vascular pathophysiology.
back:
• Testicular torsion (Adult type)
• Twisting of the spermatic cord
• Mechanical obstruction of venous drainage and arterial supply

category: Describe pathological features of testicular torsion
front: Explain the role of venous drainage obstruction in the development of the morphological features seen in testicular torsion.
back:
• Venous outflow is cut off first due to thin walls
• Leads to intense vascular engorgement
• Followed by hemorrhagic infarction as arterial flow persists initially

category: Describe pathological features of testicular torsion
front: Contrast the anatomic basis of neonatal torsion with that of adult (adolescent) testicular torsion.
back:
• Neonatal: Occurs in utero or shortly after birth; lacks a specific anatomic defect
• Adult: Typically occurs in adolescence; caused by the bell-clapper abnormality

category: Describe pathological features of testicular torsion
front: Describe the typical gross morphological appearance of the testis in advanced stages of untreated torsion.
back:
• Dark discoloration (hemorrhage)
• Soft, necrotic consistency
• Widespread hemorrhagic infarction and swelling

category: Describe pathological features of testicular torsion
front: In a suspected case of testicular torsion, the critical time window for manual or surgical untwisting to prevent orchidectomy is approximately [___] hours.
back:
• 6 hours
• Early intervention prevents irreversible infarction
• Success rate for salvage drops significantly after this period

category: Describe pathological features of testicular torsion
front: A newborn is found to have a firm, painless scrotal mass shortly after delivery. If this is identified as neonatal torsion, what anatomical defect is likely present?
back:
• None
• Neonatal torsion lacks the bell-clapper defect
• Associated with extravaginal twisting during descent

category: Describe pathological features of testicular torsion
front: How do the thick walls of the testicular arteries contribute to the characteristic 'hemorrhagic' nature of the resulting infarction during torsion?
back:
• Arteries remain patent longer than veins
• Continued arterial inflow into obstructed venous bed
• Forces blood into tissues, causing hemorrhage and engorgement

category: Describe pathological features of testicular torsion
front: Contrast the clinical priority and surgical management of the unaffected contralateral testis in adult torsion compared to other scrotal pathologies.
back:
• Mandatory contralateral orchiopexy (fixation)
• Necessary because bell-clapper defect is usually bilateral
• Prevents future torsion in the remaining viable testis

category: Describe pathological features of testicular torsion
front: Identify the standard histologic hallmark of the tissue reaction in a testis that has undergone prolonged torsion.
back:
• Coagulative necrosis
• Widespread interstitial hemorrhage
• Ghost-like cellular outlines and loss of nuclei

category: Describe pathological features of testicular torsion
front: Testicular torsion typically obstructs venous drainage while thick-walled arteries remain patent, initially leading to intense [___].
back:
• Vascular engorgement
• Subsequent hemorrhagic infarction
• Soft, necrotic tissue in advanced stages

category: Describe pathological features of testicular torsion
front: A 15-year-old male presents with sudden-onset, severe testicular pain without preceding injury. Identify the likely underlying bilateral anatomic defect.
back:
• Bell-clapper abnormality
• Causes increased testicular mobility
• Predisposes to spermatic cord twisting

category: Describe pathological features of testicular torsion
front: Explain the role of vascular pressure differentials in creating the 'dark discoloration' seen grossly in a twisted testis.
back:
• Low-pressure veins are occluded first
• High-pressure arteries remain patent
• Continued arterial inflow into blocked venous system causes capillary rupture and hemorrhage

category: Describe pathological features of testicular torsion
front: Contrast neonatal and adult testicular torsion regarding their associated anatomic defects and timing.
back:
• Neonatal: Occurs in utero or shortly after birth; lacks a specific anatomic defect
• Adult: Typically seen in adolescence; results from the bell-clapper abnormality

category: Describe pathological features of testicular torsion
front: Identify the critical therapeutic time window for manual untwisting to prevent permanent testicular infarction.
back:

category: Describe pathological features of testicular torsion

category: Describe pathological features of testicular torsion
front: Contrast the arterial and venous status during the initial phase of testicular torsion.
back:

• Arteries: Initially remain patent due to thick muscular walls

category: Describe pathological features of testicular torsion
front: Define the anatomic term 'synorchism' as it relates to congenital testicular anomalies.
back:
• Fusion of the testes
• Classified as an extremely rare congenital anomaly
• Distinct from undescended testes (cryptorchidism)

category: Describe pathological features of testicular torsion
front: The bilateral anatomic defect predisposing adolescent males to testicular torsion by increasing testicular mobility is known as the [___].

• Characterized by increased mobility of the testis within the scrotum.

category: Describe pathological features of testicular torsion
front: A 15-year-old male presents with sudden-onset excruciating scrotal pain. If untreated, the initial obstruction of [___] drainage will lead to hemorrhagic infarction.
back:
• Venous drainage.
• Thick-walled arteries remain patent initially, causing intense engorgement and pressure buildup.

category: Describe pathological features of testicular torsion
front: Explain the role of the time-to-intervention window in determining the morphological outcome of testicular torsion.
back:
• 6-hour window: Restoration of flow within 6 hours often spares the testis.
• Beyond 6 hours: High risk of irreversible hemorrhagic infarction and necrotic tissue loss.

category: Describe pathological features of testicular torsion
front: A newborn is found to have a swollen scrotum from torsion. Contrast the likely anatomic cause in this patient with the typical adolescent presentation.
back:
• Neonatal: Occurs in utero or shortly after birth; lacks a specific anatomic defect.

category: Describe pathological features of testicular torsion

category: Describe pathological features of testicular torsion
front: In the morphology of advanced testicular torsion, the swollen organ is composed entirely of [___] tissue.
back:
• Soft, necrotic, and hemorrhagic tissue.
• This represents end-stage infarction resulting from complete vascular compromise.

category: Describe pathological features of testicular torsion
front: A 14-year-old male presents with sudden testicular pain after exercise. Pathologically, why does the testis appear dark and discolored rather than pale and white?
back:
• Hemorrhagic infarction.
• Venous occlusion occurs first while arteries stay open, pumping blood into a closed system that cannot drain.

category: Describe pathological features of testicular torsion
front: In a patient presenting with an 'acute scrotum,' explain the specific vascular mechanism that progresses from congestion to full infarction.
back:
• Torsion first compresses low-pressure veins.
• Arterial inflow continues, producing intense congestion and engorgement.
• Rising interstitial pressure eventually stops arterial inflow, causing necrosis.

category: Describe pathological features of testicular torsion
front: Contrast the early-stage microscopic features of testicular torsion with those seen in the advanced stage.
back:
• Early stage: Intense vascular congestion and interstitial edema.
• Advanced stage: Widespread hemorrhage, interstitial blood extravasation, and coagulative/liquefactive necrosis.

category: Describe pathological features of testicular torsion
front: True or False: Neonatal testicular torsion is primarily caused by an inherited bell-clapper deformity.
back:
• False.
• Neonatal torsion lacks an associated anatomic defect; the bell-clapper defect is associated with adolescent torsion.

category: Describe pathological features of testicular torsion
front: In testicular torsion, the twisting of the spermatic cord primarily obstructs [___], while thick-walled arteries remain patent, leading to intense vascular engorgement and eventual hemorrhagic infarction.
back:
• Venous drainage
• Obstruction causes massive hydrostatic pressure backflow
• Results in interstitial hemorrhage and soft, necrotic tissue
• Leads to total infarction if not corrected within 6 hours.

category: Describe pathological features of testicular torsion
front: A 15-year-old male presents with sudden-onset, severe scrotal pain and a high-riding testis. This urologic emergency is frequently caused by a bilateral anatomic defect known as the [___].
back:

• Predisposes the spermatic cord to spontaneous twisting
• Requires bilateral orchiopexy to prevent recurrence in the contralateral testis.

category: Describe pathological features of testicular torsion
front: Explain the morphologic progression of a testis undergoing torsion from the acute phase to the advanced necrotic stage.
back:
• Early phase: Intense venous congestion and interstitial edema
• Intermediate: Widespread hemorrhage throughout the testicular parenchyma
• Late stage: Hemorrhagic infarction resulting in a soft, swollen, and entirely necrotic organ.

category: Describe pathological features of testicular torsion
front: Contrast neonatal testicular torsion with adult (adolescent) torsion regarding their timing and predisposing anatomic factors.
back:
• Neonatal: Occurs in utero or shortly after birth; lacks a specific identifiable anatomic defect

category: Describe pathological features of testicular torsion

category: Describe pathological features of testicular torsion

back:

category: Describe pathological features of testicular torsion
front: In the pathophysiology of testicular torsion, the primary vascular event that initiates tissue damage is the obstruction of [___].

• Thick-walled arteries remain patent initially, pumping blood into the congested organ.

category: Describe pathological features of testicular torsion

category: Describe pathological features of testicular torsion

category: Describe pathological features of testicular torsion
front: Explain how the duration of torsion dictates the transition of microscopic and gross pathological findings in the testis.
back:
• Short duration: Characterized by intense congestion and edema
• Long duration: Progresses to widespread interstitial hemorrhage, thrombosis, and total hemorrhagic infarction.

category: Describe pathological features of testicular torsion
front: Contrast the clinical presentation of 'adult' torsion with idiopathic granulomatous orchitis regarding the onset of symptoms.
back:
• Testicular Torsion: Sudden onset of severe pain, often in adolescence
• Granulomatous Orchitis: Middle-aged presentation with sudden or insidious tender mass mimicking a tumor.

category: Describe pathological features of testicular torsion
front: Identify the lesion of the tunica vaginalis frequently encountered as a sequela of testicular trauma or torsion.
back:
• Hematocele
• Defined as a collection of blood within the mesothelial-lined tunica vaginalis sac.

category: Describe pathological features of testicular torsion
front: In testicular torsion, twisting of the spermatic cord primarily obstructs [___], while thicker-walled arteries remain patent in the early stages.
back:
• Venous drainage.
• Twisting of the spermatic cord cuts off outflow first.
